💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the bustling city of Cancún to the somewhat more tranquil bohemian beach town of Tulum, the Riviera Maya is home to some of Mexico’s most idyllic beaches along the Caribbean.
  • As wonderful as the beachfront views, jungle tranquility, and local activities are here, the vacation rentals in the Riviera Maya are equally as impressive.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the bustling city of Cancún to the somewhat more tranquil bohemian beach town of Tulum, the Riviera Maya is home to some of Mexico’s most idyllic beaches along the Caribbean. Featuring turquoise waters, windswept bays, and wide swaths of verdant jungle harboring hidden cenotes, this region of the Yucatán Peninsula delivers equal parts serenity and adventure. After living in Mexico for over 10 years, I’ve stayed in and driven through many of the towns and beaches that make up this region, and it's hard to choose a favorite.

As wonderful as the beachfront views, jungle tranquility, and local activities are here, the vacation rentals in the Riviera Maya are equally as impressive. They have a way of making the surrounding nature feel even more pristine. Whether you’re venturing to the region solo or traveling with friends and family, there are gorgeous options for nearly every type of traveler, each offering a personalized way to visit this corner of the Caribbean. Read on for my favorite vacation rentals in the Riviera Maya, from city escapes in Cancún to beachy stays in Tulum and everything in between.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1020 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.
  • Sources indicate that on the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the latest Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill.
  • At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

Sources indicate that on the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the latest Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”.

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Industry observers note that trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Sources indicate that virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”.

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he stated Tuesday.

It has been revealed that "We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”.

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality.".

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the upcoming Congress, noted on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

Sources indicate that “Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he noted. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his newly introduced White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”.

Kaine mentioned congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

It has been revealed that “Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”.

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”.

Recent findings suggest that getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon states his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve significant problems, instead of just beating the other side,” mentioned Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”.

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he noted Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”.

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”.

Sources indicate that members of House Republicans’ fresh leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Sources indicate that michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up.".

Industry observers note that “Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she mentioned. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”.

Sources indicate that to that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, remarked Republicans should heed one substantial takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”.

What US Airlines Owe You After An Overnight Diversion: See The Full List

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when a flight diverts late in the day, passengers can find themselves spending the night at an airport, sometimes hundreds or thousands of miles from their destination.
  • Some of the rules are also set to change from January 2027, when a new US Department of Transportation (DOT) rule will reclassify several common causes of diversions.
  • According to recent reports, A recent high-profile example of diverted passengers being stranded overnight occurred earlier this month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when a flight diverts late in the day, passengers can find themselves spending the night at an airport, sometimes hundreds or thousands of miles from their destination. What the airline provides in these situations, from hotel rooms and meals to ground transportation, varies between US carriers and depends largely on what caused the diversion.

Some of the rules are also set to change from January 2027, when a new US Department of Transportation (DOT) rule will reclassify several common causes of diversions. Here's what federal rules guarantee, what each major US airline promises passengers, and what the changes mean for travelers in the new year.

According to recent reports, A recent high-profile example of diverted passengers being stranded overnight occurred earlier this month. On November 7, Alaska Airlines flight AS322 from Dallas/Fort Worth to Seattle diverted to Yakima, around 100 miles from Seattle, due to storms. However, the flight was then held overnight because of a fuel-related issue, leaving 137 passengers in a difficult situation.

Sources indicate that around 50 of those passengers would end up sleeping in cots provided by the Red Cross, as Alaska declined to provide hotel rooms or meal vouchers because the diversion was weather-related. The airline told Simple Flying that "for weather delays or cancellations, airlines typically do not provide accommodations," and no federal rule required it to do otherwise.

Sources indicate that this is because federal protections for passengers stranded after a diversion remain limited. The DOT's tarmac delay rule requires airlines to let passengers off a diverted aircraft within three hours for domestic flights and four hours for international flights, while also ensuring access to food, water, working lavatories, and medical treatment.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, its automatic refund rule also entitles passengers to a refund if they reject an alternative following a significant change to their journey, which includes a change of arrival airport. However, neither rule requires airlines to provide hotel rooms or meals. Instead, passengers must largely rely on voluntary commitments from airlines through the DOT's Airline Cancellation and Delay Dashboard.

While some airlines explicitly include diversions in their accommodation policies, others only cover disruptions within their control, leaving passengers in a grey area when the cause is less clear. American Airlines is the only US carrier that explicitly names a diversion as a reason to provide a hotel.

It states that if "the disruption is our fault or you're diverted to another city," and passengers are not boarded before 11:59 PM local time on their scheduled arrival day, the airline will arrange or cover an approved hotel. Regarding the details covered in the table below, American lists diversions as a hotel trigger, but also says passengers pay their own costs when a delay is beyond its control.

Hotel if diversion is airline's fault.

Hotel if diversion is weather-related.

Sources indicate that however, it also indicates passengers must cover their own expenses when a delay is outside American's control. It also does not clearly explain which provision applies when a diversion is caused by weather. JetBlue also includes diversions in its definition of a controllable disruption and provides a hotel when such a disruption delays arrival by at least three hours overnight.

Meanwhile, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Alaska Airlines take a different approach, only offering hotel accommodation for disruptions they are responsible for. Low-cost carriers generally offer less protection: for example, Frontier Airlines considers diversions within its control to be controllable disruptions, but indicates it does not provide hotel accommodation for delays or cancellations. However, it does offer meal vouchers after three hours.

The way airlines classify diversions could also have an impact on what passengers receive when they are stranded overnight. Right now, airlines report delays and cancellations using different cause codes, including an 'Air Carrier' code for disruptions attributed to the airline. However, under a new DOT rule coming into effect in January, ten events will be removed from this category.

Recent findings suggest that among these events are certain unscheduled maintenance, unruly passenger removals, medical emergencies, and aircraft damage caused by weather or foreign object debris. Consequently, this could make it easier for airlines to exclude certain incidents from warranting hotels or other assistance.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the American Express® Gold Card has a $325 annual fee (Rates & Fees), which is obviously on the steep side. While I’ve published a full Amex Gold Card review, in this post I’d like to talk more broadly about whether the Amex Gold Card is worth it, with my firsthand experience.

    According to recent reports, the Amex Gold Card is an absolute powerhouse for dining purchases, whether you spend money at restaurants or supermarkets, so those are bonus categories that have real value for people. However, when it comes to making the math on the card work, it’s all about how much of the $400+ in annual credits that you can take advantage of, to help offset the fee.

    Sources indicate that so rather than just summarizing the Amex Gold benefits, I’d like to take a first-person look at how I get value from this card, to account for the points I’m earning and redeeming, and how much of the credits I’m easily able to take advantage of. After all, we shouldn’t judge cards by their published perks, but instead, by our actual use.

    Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card.

    Before getting into individual categories and credits on the Amex Gold Card, here’s where I am on the math over the past year, at the time of this post:.

    In a recent development, quite honestly, the math on this card has worked out quite well for me. I don’t want to say I’m coming out ahead on the Amex Gold Card purely in terms of the card’s credits, but they greatly help offset the annual fee, and then the 4x points is what makes the card worthwhile for me. If I could just remember to be a little more consistent with using the dining credits or using the Dunkin’ credits at all, I’d be coming out even further ahead with this product.

    The Amex Gold Card has an improved welcome offer where you can earn a bonus as high as 100,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $8,000 within the first six months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, those 100,000 points are worth $1,700 (assuming that’s what you’re eligible for).

    With a full six months to hit the spending requirement — a little over $1,300 per month — this should be easy enough for many people to complete (and if not, there are always creative ways to complete minimum spending). Thanks to Amex’s “apply with confidence” feature, there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

    When I applied for the card, the welcome offer was “only” 60,000 points, so this is quite a bit better. I received instant approval on the card. I should also emphasize that the product isn’t available to those who at the moment have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past.

    On top of that, you may not be eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had American Express Platinum Card® (learn more). That’s why I always recommend applying for the Amex Gold before the Amex Platinum, since that will allow you to eventually earn the welcome offer on both cards. As I see it, you get the Amex Gold for the return on spending, and the Amex Platinum for the perks. In the interest of being thorough, let me also mention that if you have some Chase cards you’re considering applying for, perhaps get those first, given the limitations of the Chase 5/24 rule.

    I’ve of course already redeemed a lot of the points earned from the welcome offer on the card, including for a flight in All Nippon Airways first class, which I booked with Air Canada Aeroplan points (moved over from Amex).

    Sources indicate that this is where the Amex Gold Card really becomes exciting, and where the personal version of the card is nicely differentiated from the business version of the card — the bonus categories are broad, everyday, and hard not to use. The Amex Gold offers:.

    Sources indicate that based on my valuations, that’s like an 8.5% return on prepaid hotel stays, a 6.8% return at restaurants and at U.S. supermarkets, and a 5.1% return on eligible flights. The 4x points on dining and 4x points on supermarket categories are the two that matter for most people, and they’re genuinely best-in-class.

    I’ve just gone over how much spending I’ve put on the card over the past year, and it’s not pretty… yow, food is expensive, especially when you add two little kids to the equation! I’ll simply say that I’ve earned six figures worth of points from the 4x points categories on this card.

    I’m not a huge fan of doing math this way, but just to do the breakeven math on the Amex Gold annual fee, based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, spending just under $4,800 per year (just under $400 per month) in the 4x points categories would earn you enough points to help offset the annual fee, not even factoring in any of the other benefits.

    I do want to add two caveats to the Amex Gold earning structure, just to balance things:.

    Eligibility is always determined by how the merchant is categorized, so some places you’d consider a restaurant or grocery store may not code that way, and that’s something to be aware of. It’s certainly an problem I’ve faced a few times with the card, where it didn’t code exactly as I expected.

    According to recent reports, for example, you typically expect a coffee shop to code as a restaurant for these purposes, but I’ve had a few that didn’t code that way. Fortunately I’m not spending a fortune at coffee shops, so it’s not a huge deal.

    It has been revealed that here’s the heart of the “worth it” question, as I see it. The Amex Gold Card offers statement credits that could save you up to $424 per year, more than offsetting the annual fee (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

    But they’re fragmented across several buckets, most of them monthly use-it-or-lose-it, so the advertised number and the amount you’re actually able to use can be very different. Here’s how each Amex Gold credit has worked for me, ranked from easiest to hardest to redeem. But first, below is a chart summarizing the basics of the Amex Gold credits (Enrollment is required for select benefits)..

    Amex Gold cardmembers receive a $10 Uber Cash credit every calendar month, valid toward Uber and Uber Eats purchases in the United States An Amex Card must be selected as the payment method for your Uber or Uber Eats transaction to redeem the Amex Uber Cash benefit. In order to use this, you need to pay for your purchase with an Amex card, and the Uber Cash can only be deposited in a single account.

    It has been revealed that this is the Amex Gold credit I maximize most reliably, because it’s effectively cash toward something almost everyone uses — a ride or food delivery. Even if you don’t take Ubers, the credit works on Uber Eats.

    Industry observers note that personally, I generally use Lyft for rideshare and Uber Eats for food delivery, so I easily get the full value of this credit each month on food orders alone. I wish I didn’t use Uber Eats so much that I consider it to be “good as cash,” but that’s the current reality.

    Amex Gold cardmembers receive a semi-annual Resy credit — a $50 credit in January through June, and a $50 credit in July through December — valid at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants, Resy.com, and in the mobile Resy app. There’s no need to even make a reservation, as long as you pay at an eligible restaurant.

    Because it’s semi-annual rather than monthly, it’s lower maintenance, but it requires you to actually dine at a Resy restaurant in each half of the year — which is easy in a major city and harder elsewhere.

    Recent findings suggest that as someone who lives in Miami, there’s absolutely no shortage of Resy restaurants, so I get full value out of this with minimal effort. Fortunately whatever part of the meal isn’t covered by the credit still earns 4x points. So over the past year, I’ve gotten the full value out of this… yay! But if you live in a more rural area, you may not have any Resy restaurants near you, and the credit may not be worth much unless you’re traveling.

    It has been revealed that amex Gold cardmembers receive a $10 monthly dining credit, for a total of up to $120 each year, valid for purchases with Grubhub (including Seamless), Buffalo Wild Wings, Five Guys, The Cheesecake Factory, and Wonder. Only purchases in the United States qualify, and you’re limited to a single credit no matter how many authorized users you have.

    The catch is that it’s tied to a specific list of merchants, so it’s only “easy” if one of those fits your routine. Grubhub is the flexible one for most people.

    Industry observers note that it goes without saying we all have different spending patterns. Personally, I sort of struggle with the credit. I don’t remember the last time I went to a Buffalo Wild Wings, Five Guys, or The Cheesecake Factory (nothing against them, I sort of love the SkinnyLicious menu, but they’re just not near me), and I don’t even know what Wonder is. So that leaves Grubhub.

    Sources indicate that I try to use the dining credit on Grubhub whenever I can, but to be honest, many months I forget. That’s because Uber Eats and DoorDash are the primary delivery apps I use. The $10 isn’t necessarily that huge of an incentive to remember, which is why it sometimes slips my mind.

    Amex Gold cardmembers receive a $7 monthly Dunkin’ credit, earned after using your enrolled card to pay at more than 9,000 Dunkin’ locations nationwide.

    Recent findings suggest that this is the most polarizing credit on the card. If there’s a Dunkin’ on your commute and you actually like Dunkin’, enjoy some coffee on Amex. If there isn’t, you may forfeit $84 of the headline credit total — and it’s worth subtracting from the card’s advertised value when you do your own math. Keep in mind that there aren’t even Dunkin’ locations in some states, like Oregon and Washington.

    I have read that a $ 7-per-month reload would trigger the credit as well, so you could accrue it. I probably should’ve been taking advantage of that all along, but this is also where “credit card fatigue” kicks in, and I just forget to even focus on this.

    Sources indicate that after all, on some level this credit card game is supposed to be fun, rather than just spending every month chasing dozens and dozens of credits. Or maybe I just have too many cards? 😉 So yeah, unfortunately I’ve been losing $84 per year in value with this credit by not taking advantage of it.

    Two more perks on the Amex Gold Card are worth a brief mention, because they round out the card without being the reason to get it.

    First, Amex Offers. One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which provides savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. The more Amex cards you have, the more offers you’ll have access to, and they could save you hundreds of dollars per year.

    For example, I recently had an Amex Offers deal for 1,200 bonus points when spending $150 with Amazon, and that could be used up to three times. Since I shop on Amazon all the time, that’s an easy bonus of 3,600 points as I see it.

    Second, The Hotel Collection. For staying two or more nights at select luxury hotels, you can receive extra benefits through The Hotel Collection, including a $100 hotel credit and a room upgrade if available. This is different than Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, which requires having the Amex Platinum. I can’t say that I’ve used this, because when it comes to Amex’s hotel programs, I typically gravitate toward FHR.

    Lastly, while I wouldn’t consider it to be particularly valuable either, I should also mention that the Amex Gold offers Hertz Five Star status, which is at least worth being aware of (Enrollment is required for select benefits). This gets you an upgrade to a higher car class on rentals when available as well as a 25% bonus on all Hertz rentals.

    The Amex Gold Card has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use it for purchases globally — and because the 4x dining category applies at restaurants worldwide, this is genuinely one of the better cards to carry abroad for meals. Just remember the 4x supermarket category is U.S.-only, so that bonus doesn’t follow you overseas.

    According to recent reports, I use this card all the time for dining abroad, and it’s a good way to maximize rewards. For example, on my summer trip to the Dolomites, I used the Amex Gold Card for all my dining outside hotels, which included some great meals.

    I should acknowledge that Amex doesn’t quite have the global acceptance of Mastercard or Visa, for example, though the gap is much smaller than in the past.

    I think the Amex Gold Card is a product that has bonus categories that are about as well rounded as one could imagine, in terms of appealing to the average consumer. Everyone eats, and this card is great for those people, whether you get your food at restaurants or supermarkets.

    I will say, the math on this card may break down for you if you fall into one of the following two categories:.

    Personally, the math on this card is working great for me. I do wish I more consistently maximized the credits, as I do a pretty good job, but not a great job. Based on my own usage patterns, I basically view this as a card costing me well under $100 per year (after subtracting the value of the credits), and then I get a very well balanced return in some bonus categories for that. I guess I just need to do a better job of actually using those Dunkin’ credits, and at least reloading my account.

    I also think it’s worth emphasizing that the Amex Gold might not be the right style of card for some people, depending on your consumer preferences:.

    For me, the Amex Gold Card is proving to be a keeper, and I initiative to renew on my account anniversary, while paying the annual fee. The rewards structure on this card is excellent and simple, while the credits help make this an affordable card to hold onto. So if you ask me, the card is a clear “yes” if:.

    If you’d forfeit two or more of the credits, do the math on the credits you’ll actually take advantage of before counting the full $424 — the card can still win on dining and supermarket earning alone, but the real math is different than the marketed amount.

    The other nice thing is that if you get the Amex Gold and decide after a year or more that the card is no longer a good fit for you, you can typically product change it to another card. This allows you to preserve the rewards, credit history, etc.

    The Amex Gold Card is one of American Express’ best rewards cards for earning points, with 4x points on dining and U.S. supermarkets, which is hard for any other card to beat. The earning side is the easy part — almost everyone can use it.

    Whether the card is worth its $325 annual fee on an ongoing basis comes down to one honest question: how many of the up to $424 in annual credits will you actually capture? The credit is real — up to $120 for dining, up to $120 in Uber Cash, up to $100 with Resy, and up to $84 with Dunkin’ — but it’s fragmented, and the gap between the headline and your real capture rate is the whole decision.

    It’s easiest to make the math work if you actually spend a substantial amount on the 4x points categories, since the value of that will promptly make a material difference to your points earning.

    What’s your take on the value proposition of the Amex Gold Card? Which credits do you actually capture each year, and which ones do you forfeit?

    #30606. Latest Update: Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

    Latest Update: Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.
    • A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.
    • The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any latest bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

    A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

    The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any latest bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

    Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

    The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

    It has been revealed that the House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

    Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances.

    Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

    “Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

    In a recent development, “Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”.

    The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

    At matter in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

    The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

    The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

    The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura noted his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

    Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change.

    But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

    Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”.

    Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

    He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”.

    Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely upcoming bill.

    No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

    He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

    A newly introduced Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

    According to recent reports, congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

    Pasco remarked he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

    The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a upcoming version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

    Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

    Why This It-Girl Ski Brand Is My Go-To Every Single Winter

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that if there’s one thing I take almost as seriously as chasing some good snow, it’s having the right wardrobe to go with it.
    • But that doesn’t mean style needs to take a backseat.
    • Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is wearing the Halfdays Ashton jacket and Alessandra pant in Stowe, Vermont.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that if there’s one thing I take almost as seriously as chasing some good snow, it’s having the right wardrobe to go with it. I’m a lifelong snowboarder, a fairly recent convert to skiing, and someone who has spent plenty of winters bouncing between mountains on the east coast and out west. I’ve learned that the best of the best ski gear needs to do a lot more than look good in a lodge photo. It has to hold up through long lift rides, changing conditions, unexpected snowfall, and the occasional unglamorous tumble.

    But that doesn’t mean style needs to take a backseat. In fact, I’d argue that the two should go hand in hand. That's a substantial part of why the popular ski brand, Halfdays, first caught my attention three years ago—and why I keep coming back season after season. Founded in 2020 by former Olympic freestyle aerial skier Kiley McKinnon and Ariana Ferweda, Halfdays came onto the ski scene with a refreshing take: women's ski apparel that actually considers women. Not just smaller versions of men’s gear or the usual boxy, so-called unisex silhouettes, but (finally) thoughtfully designed outerwear that takes fit, function, and fashion all very seriously.

    Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is wearing the Halfdays Ashton jacket and Alessandra pant in Stowe, Vermont.

    In a recent development, the outdoor apparel industry has come a long way, but finding technical pieces that feel just as considered aesthetically as they are functional on the mountain can still be a bit of a treasure hunt. So as someone who has accumulated her fair share of ski and snowboard gear over the years, I immediately fell in love with the brand’s mission, and eventually, the gear itself.

    While I’ve come to adore its ski suits, bibs, and winter jackets, Halfdays' assortment has expanded beyond the big-ticket ski uniform. The brand offers sweat-wicking baselayers, cozy fleeces, everyday outdoor staples, and chic accessories that make sense well beyond your stay at a ski resort. My favorite pieces from Halfdays keep me feeling comfortable and put together on harsh winter days in Upcoming York City too, from knit headbands that cover my ears to winter leggings and warm socks that aren’t too thick.

    Of course, Halfdays isn’t the same brand it was when I first discovered it. What began as a ski-focused label has evolved into an outdoor brand with spring and summer collections spanning hiking, running, and more warm-weather pursuits. Its arrival at major retailers like Nordstrom, REI, and Backcountry, the opening of its Denver flagship (along with plenty of other storefronts), and a string of collaborations have helped solidify it as a functional brand for every outdoor adventurer.

    Chapel is wearing the Parks Projects x Halfdays set on the slopes in Park City, Utah.

    Recent findings suggest that that remarked, the brand has been having some fun with its fashion credentials, most recently teaming up with Gigi Hadid’s Guest in Residence on an eight-piece winter capsule. The result is a nostalgic take on mountainwear, bringing Guest in Residence’s signature knitwear looks to Halfdays' mountain-ready vibes, with playful retro details that feel just as at home at après-ski as they do on the slopes.

    On the performance side, though, I’m excited about the brand’s newest launch: Halfdays has officially joined forces with Gore-Tex for its most technical outerwear collection yet. From down jackets and shells to bibs and mittens, the colorful collection brings together trusted waterproof, windproof, and breathable technology with the fit and design that initially made me fall for Halfdays in the first place.

    Recent findings suggest that as another winter of snow chasing commences, I’m giving my cold-weather wardrobe yet another Halfdays refresh. Below, my tried-and-true ski season favorites from Halfdays, along with a few winter staples I’ve got my eye on.

    It has been revealed that the Lawrence jacket is designed with Primaloft insulation, keeping you warm on the coldest winter days. It features underarm vents and an exterior chest pocket with an attached phone leash. Plus, the hood is adjustable, so you’ll get a perfect fit over your helmet every time. The jacket is best for bluebird days given its cropped length, but it’s also available in a longer version too.

    I like to pair the Lawrence jacket with these matching shell pants. With a slim fit, an adjustable waistband, a water-resistant exterior, and zippered hems for snow boots, this pair is just as practical as it is stylish. Pro tip: Try these bad boys on with a pair of your favorite winter leggings underneath before hitting the mountain, just so you know that you’ll be comfortable and warm all day long.

    Sources indicate that don’t underestimate the importance of a solid baselayer. The Johnson top features mesh underarms and a sweat-wicking finish, so you don’t have to worry about overheating in your ski gear. The long-sleeve layer also has a silicon grip on the inside hem, preventing it from sliding up as you move.

    Recent findings suggest that pair the Johnson top with these leggings for a stylish, mountain-ready set. They’re sweat-wicking and feature a layer of mesh on the calves for added breathability. Even better, they’re versatile enough to wear off the mountain too, whether you’re shopping at a holiday market or strolling through the park.

    Made with 100% merino wool, this chic Jacquard headband will keep your head and ears warm on the slopes—and it tastefully reps the brand too. I have (and love) it in the color Blue Fog, but it’s also available in black and red.

    Sources indicate that I’m obsessed with these Gore-Tex x Halfdays mittens. Along with the insulated, breathable, and waterproof design, there’s also a leather palm construction for added grip and durability.

    I can’t wait to put this three-layer shell jacket to the test on my trip to Stowe, Vermont, this December. It has all the classic Gore-Tex technologies that make the collaboration so enticing in the first place: engineered with durable water- and wind-proof material, and breathable protection without added insulation.

    Recent findings suggest that for a matching set, grab this three-layer shell bib constructed with the same Gore-Tex build. With adjustable shoulder straps, a drop-seat construction, thigh vents, and gusseted hems, you’ll be covered and ready for anything, from head to toe.

    Ah, one of the early Halfday classics. The tried-and-true Ashton jacket does it all, from ski trips to cabin getaways. With an adjustable (and removable) belt buckle enclosure, a helmet hood, and its many pockets for your phone and ski pass, it offers every bit of function you need for a full day on the mountain.

    According to recent reports, for those who favor a puffy yet packable one-piece, the Murphy ski suit is another one of Halfdays' original bestsellers. I own this bad boy in red, and wear it when I need extra warmth on the mountain. One thing to note: I’m 5'3", and it’s just a bit long on my legs when I’m not in snow boots—but it’s not very often that I wear the suit without them.

    Sources indicate that while I haven’t shopped the new Guest in Residence collection yet, I’m eyeing this chic ski sweater that looks straight out of a ’70s après-ski scene. I can already picture myself wearing it post-slopes, sipping on a spiked cider at the ski lodge.

    In a recent development, for another vintage-inspired piece from the Guest in Residence collection, this cable knit inspired down jacket is all about staying warm in style. (And I’ve already added it to my cart.).

    Get your hands on one of the Parks Project x Halfdays ski jackets while you still can. This gorgeous print is inspired by the Rocky Mountains—and I always receive compliments from other shredders when I wear it out on the slopes. Not to mention, it keeps me warm and comfy while doing so!

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Amex Membership Rewards program has just introduced a new bonus for points transfers to Avianca Lifemiles.

    #30603. Why Qantas Picked A 'Proven' Rolls-Royce Engine Over A Theoretically Better One For Project Sunrise

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1411 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Qantas Picked A 'Proven' Rolls-Royce Engine Over A Theoretically Better One For Project Sunrise

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1411 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that ultra-long-haul flights have exploded in popularity over the past decade, largely because the current generation of long-range widebodies is exceptionally fuel-efficient.
    • The longest of these, Sydney to London Heathrow, will last over 20 hours.
    • Sources indicate that what's unusual is that the 777X has been relatively popular while being equipped with the world's most advanced jet engines.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that ultra-long-haul flights have exploded in popularity over the past decade, largely because the current generation of long-range widebodies is exceptionally fuel-efficient. Recent advances in efficiency and capability are now allowing Qantas to launch Project Sunrise, two ultra-long-haul nonstop routes that will both be longer than today's longest flights (Singapore to Fresh York JFK and Newark) by a wide margin.

    The longest of these, Sydney to London Heathrow, will last over 20 hours. Qantas placed its official order for the Project Sunrise aircraft in 2022, selecting the Airbus A350-1000ULR after an intense competition between the A350 and the Boeing 777X.

    Sources indicate that what's unusual is that the 777X has been relatively popular while being equipped with the world's most advanced jet engines. However, Qantas still selected the older A350-1000 to operate the world's longest flights, a move that solidifies the Airbus A350's position as the world's ultimate long-range airliner.

    The core of Project Sunrise is the launch of newly introduced ultra-long-haul nonstop flights connecting Sydney to London Heathrow and New York JFK. The longer of the two, Sydney to London Heathrow, will be 9,188 NM (17,016 km), and will also be the first Project Sunrise route to launch in October 2027.

    According to recent reports, the first A350-1000ULR will arrive in April and will operate short-haul crew familiarization flights, while the London route will launch once Qantas has three examples to hand. Sydney to Newly introduced York will be the second route to launch, and Qantas will subsequently place the A350-1000ULR throughout its current route network, mainly displacing Boeing 787s to launch new routes.

    While Qantas has previously stated that it will also connect Melbourne to London and New York, these routes appear to be less of a priority based on Qantas's most recent announcements. They may only come with the final A350-1000ULR deliveries as the carrier increases its focus on Sydney. Flight times from Sydney to London will last over 20 hours, or about two hours longer than the Singapore-JFK service.

    Recent findings suggest that some have expressed skepticism over whether passengers would prefer a 20-hour nonstop over a 24-hour one-stop route. However, there was similar skepticism a decade ago about the commercial viability of 17 to 18-hour flights, like Singapore-JFK or Qantas's own Perth-London route. By and large, these routes have proven popular with passengers and have become quite lucrative.

    In a recent development, technically, the Airbus A350-900ULR could likely operate the Project Sunrise routes, but Qantas desired more capability. The A350-900ULR is a fairly minimal modification to the A350-900, featuring weight reductions and software changes to enable more fuel to be carried in the plane's center tank. With a deactivated forward cargo hold, it essentially trades payload for fuel.

    Recent findings suggest that qantas desired a larger aircraft that could carry significantly more payload than the A350-900ULR. Airbus offered the A350-1000ULR, while Boeing offered the 777X. Initial discussions centered around an optimized version of the smaller 777-8. It's unclear what exactly Boeing planned for the 777-8, but as delays with the program continued, the 777-9 also came into the picture.

    319 tons (current), 322 tons (future).

    9,000 NM (16,700 km) with 322-ton MTOW.

    8,500 NM (15,750 km) with 283-ton MTOW.

    While the plane's current brochure range is too short for Project Sunrise, the 777-9 could have received a higher gross weight and auxiliary fuel tanks to make the route, albeit with a reduced capacity. It's generally believed that this was offered as an interim solution until the 777-8 was ready, and it was even reported that Boeing also offered the 777-200LR as another alternative solution.

    Industry observers note that ultimately, Qantas announced the A350 as the preferred choice for Project Sunrise in 2019 for flights to commence in 2023, and then placed its official order in 2022 (the order was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic). The timeline is crucial because the 777X is one of the most delayed aircraft programs in recent history.

    The Boeing 777X will be exclusively powered by the General Electric GE9X. While the Rolls-Royce Trent XWB on the A350 is a remarkable engine, the GE9X will be unrivaled in terms of thermal efficiency, in large part due to the extensive use of advanced materials like ceramic matrix composites. It can almost be considered half a generation ahead of the Trent XWB/Trent 1000/General Electric GEnx.

    However, the GE9X and the 777X are also unproven. Qantas's desired timeline for Project Sunrise would have made it one of the first operators of the 777X. While General Electric has a proven track record in delivering dependable large turbofan engines, any new engine experiences teething issues upon introduction, which can be problematic to deal with.

    What's more, early production of the GE9X and the 777X will be limited (as is the case with any latest aircraft), resulting in slow deliveries during the 777X's first few years. In comparison, the Trent XWB is a proven engine that has been remarkably trouble-free, while the A350 is an established type.

    While deliveries of the A350 have presently been slow due to supply-chain constraints, this has been affecting the entire airline industry and is hardly unique to the A350. As a whole, it's less risky to go with the aircraft and engine type that has been in service for nearly a decade compared to the brand-latest plane/engine.

    It has been revealed that the GE9X will be an excellent engine once it enters service, but this doesn't mean that the 777X will burn less fuel than the A350-1000. The aircraft still retains a heavy-metal fuselage, while also featuring massive wings. It's a fundamentally larger, heavier plane that will be significantly thirstier than the A350-1000, and the 777-9 addresses this through its massive capacity, giving it competitive per-seat economics.

    The 777-8, however, is smaller than either, while costing almost the same to operate as the 777-9, making it an uneconomical aircraft. The advantage of the 777-8 is its field performance and range, but for Project Sunrise, the A350-1000 is more than capable with the ULR improvements.

    As a whole, the 777-8 has been an extremely slow seller due to these problems. In addition, the 777X's delays were also very problematic. In 2019 (the same year as when Qantas publicly selected the A350), Boeing planned to start delivering the 777-9 in 2021, while the 777-8 was delayed to 2023, the same year that Qantas intended to start Project Sunrise flights at the time. At the time, there were already concerns about whether the timeline would stick.

    Recent findings suggest that these concerns have proven valid, as the 777-9's entry into service is now set for 2027. Meanwhile, development of the 777-8 has been paused due to a lack of demand, with Boeing instead focusing on the 777-9 and then the 777-8F, as these models are more popular. For Qantas, relying on the 777-8 would have been significantly riskier than going with a derivative of the in-service A350-1000.

    While it has the same 'ULR' designation as the A350-900ULR, the engineering to create the A350-1000ULR is closer to how Airbus created the A321XLR. Key to the plane's range is the addition of a new 20,000-liter integrated Rear Centre Tank, derived from the design of the RCT on the A321XLR. In addition, the A350-1000ULR features a higher Maximum Takeoff Weight of 322 tons.

    It has been revealed that this will be available on all future A350-1000s. However, Qantas has an exclusivity deal on the A350-1000ULR variant specifically. To further extend the plane's range, Qantas is installing just 238 seats, making it the lowest-capacity A350-1000 configuration in the world. There will be six first class suites built by Safran, 52 business class seats based on the Safran Unity, 40 premium economy seats based on the Safran Z535i, and just 140 economy seats based on the Recaro R3.

    Sources indicate that in addition, the A350-1000ULR will also come with a latest crew rest facility for the pilots, of which there will be four on each flight. Some have questioned Qantas's decision to install economy seats on the A350-1000ULR, considering that Singapore Airlines' A350-900ULRs lack this cabin.

    However, Qantas is catering to a much larger leisure and visiting friends/relatives market than Singapore Airlines, and it specifically bought the A350-1000ULR for its size as well as its payload capacity. Economy was always part of the plan, and Qantas will be configuring the economy seats with more legroom while also offering an onboard 'Wellness Zone.'.

Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best hotels in the world as voted by you, our readers.

    View all of the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here, and the best resorts in the Caribbean here.

    Turks and Caicos’s bustling yet beautiful island of Providenciales (affectionately dubbed “Provo”) has had its moment in the proverbial sun. Consider venturing southeast to South Caicos for a more intimate and undeveloped look at what are arguably the Caribbean’s most jaw-dropping beaches. The first property to put down literal roots with nearly 800 acres of primarily local vegetation is Sailrock South Caicos: a stunning, 40-unit property on the southeastern island’s northern tip where the Atlantic Ocean and Caicos Bank converge to house the area’s latest and greatest escape. Travel to South Caicos is also more convenient than ever with two direct flights from Miami on Wednesdays and Sundays via American Airlines. This means guests can now bypass a layover in Providenciales and reach paradise in less than two hours.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    At the Ritz-Carlton Turks and Caicos, guests can sandwich sun-soaked days of lounging in a private cabana or on Grace Bay’s idyllic slice of beach with plenty of on-site experiences. A favorite for its white-sand beachfront and unrivaled centrality on famed Grace Bay, there’s no shortage of pursuits here—it’s a choose-your-own-adventure property with great amenities for young kids. 147 luxury ocean-view rooms and suites—with the Ritz-Carlton standard—awe and delight. There’s also a collection of luxury residences and penthouses for longer stays, each, of course, with stunning floor-to-ceiling views of Grace Bay’s turquoise waters. Interiors are all creams and whites with gentle pops of beachy colors, large windows, and pristine linens. As the most central property in Grace Bay, everything is within walking distance: the best restaurants, shops, and even a grocery store. For families with little ones, the Ritz Kids club is the place to be for guests ages 4–12. Drop the kids off and embark on the resort’s luxury sailing catamaran, the Lady Grace.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Salterra balances solitude and serenity with grace. Backgrounding the sprawling complex is a skirt of rugged cliffs and leafy tropical flora—the stuff of our beach getaway daydreams. With staff-organized excursions across the gin-clear Caribbean, a seaside garden sprinkled with lounge chairs begging for sunbathers, and a state-of-the-art spa with eight treatment rooms, whether you're up for an adventure or down for a little R&R, the choice is truly yours. While the island is only home to 1,100 total residents, guests in search of an even greater sense of privacy can book private cabanas looking over the four sun-lit pools that bleed into the horizon.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Basking on a coveted stretch of Grace Bay, this well-appointed resort is as lax as it is luxe. While there’s plenty of opportunities for R&R at the blissful on-site spa and for romance to blossom over candlelit dinners, the Sands at Grace Bay also know a thing or two about picking up speed. It wouldn’t be a proper Turks and Caicos vacation without hitting the water, and the resort provides complimentary access to a variety of water sport equipment ranging from sea kayaks to snorkeling gear to explore the mirror-clear seas. If you’re traveling with little ones who aren’t quite ready for the open ocean yet, there’s also kid-friendly pools and sprawling perfect for their next adventure. If you’re looking for a resort that grows up alongside your family, look no further.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Recent findings suggest that wymara Resort + Villas sits on the western curve of Grace Bay in Providenciales, just a 10-minute drive from the airport. It’s a place for travelers who like their luxury understated and favor the clean lines of minimalist design. Rooms and suites open to sea views and sun-washed balconies, while the villas—set apart from the main resort on a 15-acre peninsula—offer private pools, over-water decks, and personal hosts. The food is sustainably sourced: Indigo serves refined Caribbean dishes, and the Pink Bar is a magnet for sunset watchers. The spa, using island-grown botanicals and 111SKIN products, is intimate and calm. Service is polished yet relaxed, with staff who are friendly and will remember your preferences. Eco credentials are strong, from solar-powered electricity to refillable amenities. Complimentary wellness activities include yoga, pilates, HIIT, and sound baths, while evening entertainment leans local and cultural.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Recent findings suggest that this mega-resort sets itself apart from other all-inclusive properties throughout the region with its family-friendly activities. There is a 45,000-square-foot waterpark and kids clubs for different ages, including one with Caribbean-ified Sesame Street characters, the Xbox Play Lounge, and a teen disco. For the rest of the family, there are 10 swimming pools, 21 restaurants, 15 bars (some of them swim-up), and access to the 12-mile Grace Bay Beach. The 758 rooms and suites are spread across five themed villages, with architecture that represents different regions: France, Italy, the Caribbean, and Key West. With 43 room categories, the resort truly offers something for everyone.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Grace Bay Club offers not one, but three distinct accommodations to its discerning guests: the adults-only Hotel building, the family-friendly Villas Suites, and the Estate, a resort within a resort, with exclusive access to dedicated amenities, such as a separate pool, cabanas, and more. Despite catering to different crowds, they do have a few common features, including spectacular oceanfront views and personal concierge service. Head to the oceanfront Infiniti Restaurant & Bar for bites of such fresh local fare as a warm South Caicos lobster salad, garnished with shaved carrots and crispy basil, or the Mahi Mahi carpaccio, with a kick of jalapeño, served to the sound of breaking waves. Looking to stake your umbrella in the sand a little while longer? Rent one of the homes in the Private Villa Collection, a cluster of five freestanding private beachfront residences that come with all the amenities and services of a superior hotel stay, including roundtrip airport transfers, daily housekeeping, and complimentary breakfast.

    It has been revealed that A fan-shaped trio of seven-story buildings curve around a beachfront pool and patio at this Grace Bay resort, close to Providenciales's shopping district. Enormous rooms in soft colors have marble baths and soaking tubs, proving that bigger can mean better. Staff members always serve with a smile and make a point of remembering names. The restaurant Seven dishes up Caribbean-inspired cuisine, with entrees like house-made stone crab ravioli, or you can opt for private beachfront dining, complete with a personal butler and a playlist of your choosing. If you're traveling with the family, the kids camp provides diversions such as lizard hunting and sand-castle building—or you can all go for a dip in the island's only heated saltwater pool.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, artificial intelligence could be playing a role in the cascade of high-profile technology failures seen over the last week, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin remarked Monday.

    Mullin told FOX News’ Sean Hannity that he spoke with someone in the tech industry, “one guy who is very smart with tech,” who identified AI as a possible culprit.

    “He stated, ‘I believe that it’s the SI, because the programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is,'” he said.

    Recent findings suggest that the individual suggested that the technology’s ability to move fast and fix itself created “ripple effects” that overwhelmed older conventional systems. The secretary noted that theory “kind of makes sense to me.”.

    The Trump administration uses the term “super intelligence,” or SI, in place of AI.

    Mullin said his source did not want to be identified but ruled out at least one famous personality from the tech sector.

    Multiple large, U.S.-based networks have crashed over the past week, including the FAA’s air traffic control communications system, United’s internal applications, Microsoft’s business services, and software used by banks such as JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo.

    Mullin noted there is no indication from the intelligence and cybersecurity communities that the outages are part of a cyberattack.

    The FAA has blamed Friday’s nationwide ground stop on a faulty or improperly installed router, which flooded other routers with data and ultimately crashed the system.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the airport lounge wars aren't heating up only among premium credit card issuers.
    • American Airlines has been on a tear of its own lately, including upgrades and a huge new Admirals Club at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) Terminal C, a massive (and much-needed) new lounge complex at its Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT) hub and the reopening of its Flagship Dining offering at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).
    • Now, Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) is the airline's next base scheduled for a glow-up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the airport lounge wars aren't heating up only among premium credit card issuers. Airlines are stepping up their own lounge investments, too.

    American Airlines has been on a tear of its own lately, including upgrades and a huge new Admirals Club at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) Terminal C, a massive (and much-needed) new lounge complex at its Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT) hub and the reopening of its Flagship Dining offering at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    Now, Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) is the airline's next base scheduled for a glow-up.

    Read more: 3 reasons why this is the best credit card for Admirals Club access.

    American Airlines at the moment fields three Admirals Clubs at PHX — two in Concourse A and one in Concourse B at Terminal 4 — all of which are being updated.

    The first lounge where flyers will see changes is this diminutive lounge in Concourse A. Effective immediately, there will be a new food service area and expanded food and beverage offerings.

    More importantly, though, the airline intends to nearly triple the combined lounge footprint of its Concourse A lounges, which include another Admirals Club near gates A7 and A9; it will increase seating capacity by around 150%, and add new furniture and finishes. Hopefully those will reflect the more sophisticated aesthetics American Airlines has been pivoting toward, starting with its Ronald Reagan National Airport (DCA) outpost.

    Over in Concourse B, one of the airline's other Admirals Clubs will see a latest self-service food and beverage area (aka a buffet and bar), a 20% increase in seating capacity and new interiors.

    It has been revealed that “Phoenix continues to be an crucial hub in our network, and these investments reflect our commitment to giving customers more space, comfort and convenience when they travel through PHX,” American’s chief customer officer Heather Garboden said in an online statement. “While we look forward to the development of the new West Terminal, these enhancements will help create an even more seamless travel experience for the millions of customers who pass through Phoenix each year.”.

    The updates make sense and are badly needed at an American Airlines hub where the Admirals Clubs frequently become overcrowded.

    The airline carries over 20 million passengers through PHX each year and operates over 300 peak daily departures, so expanding and refreshing its lounges there is a priority to continue attracting premium passengers.

    Read more: The ultimate guide to American Airlines Admirals Club access.

    Recent findings suggest that though details are still scant, American Airlines is updating its three Admirals Clubs at PHX. Passengers should see immediate changes at its Concourse A club near gates A19 and A21, but travelers will have to wait for the larger changes, which will include an expanded footprint and updated interiors. It remains to be seen what other amenities might be available.

    Industry observers note that isn’t this a little surreal? After years of reading OMAAT, here I am writing my very first post.

    Recent findings suggest that first of all, a huge thank you to Ben for such a lovely introduction, and for everyone who gave me such a warm welcome in the comments already. I’m really looking forward to getting to know the OMAAT community Ben has built over the years.

    In the first of what will undoubtedly be a lot of posts for One Mile at a Time, I thought I’d share a bit about who I am and what you can expect from me going forward.

    I’m literally asking myself that as I write this.

    Sources indicate that funnily enough, it was never my dream to be a writer, journalist, blogger, or anything similar. The only thing I can ever remember wanting to be “when I grew up” was a pilot. Despite several applications and reaching the final stage of cadet schemes with Aer Lingus and British Airways, it didn’t work out for me.

    Industry observers note that determined to work in the industry, I quit my soul-destroying city job in London to do a Master’s in Air Transport Management at the University of Loughborough in the U.K. I was then offered 2 very different jobs: a junior marketing role with Air Transat, or to be part of a small team starting up TPG’s U.K. office. As a natural risk-taker, I took the latter. After almost 8 years of writing for various publications and dabbling in some video content, I’ve realized that this is what I was meant to be doing all along — the job just didn’t exist when I wanted to be a pilot as a kid.

    It has been revealed that so why OMAAT? Why now? I spent the last 2 years traveling the world, working remotely, in search of somewhere I felt connected enough to call home. In my heart of hearts, I always knew that was going to be Rio, so I moved here in September this year. I’ve also been considering a more permanent home for my writing and my online presence, so when happenstance did its thing and Ben offered me a full-time online home at OMAAT, it was the perfect opportunity.

    In a recent development, I’m honored to have been entrusted to write alongside Ben, whose expertise I’ve learned from over the years. While I don’t promise to be an expert on everything, my almost 8 years of experience in this industry should hopefully mean my expertise meets the standard expected here.

    What started out as a passion for planes and aviation has turned into a love of all things travel, loyalty, and the miles and points that help make it happen. I’m really looking forward to sharing some of my learnings, experiences, and tips and tricks from the past couple of years that should complement Ben’s breadth of knowledge.

    To start with, much of what you’ll see from me will be written. But as Ben said, the initiative is to gradually bring in more video and social content, which I’m really looking forward to helping OMAAT with.

    I’m also a self-proclaimed expert on Rio and Brazil (I’ve been coming here since 2009), so if there’s any specific Rio, Brazil, or wider South American travel advice, reviews, or insights you’d like, I’d be more than happy to help, even if it means I have to hop a plane for the research. 😝.

    I’ll leave it at that for now, as I need to get packing to fly across the Pond for an exciting aviation event this week. All will be revealed soon. 🤓✈️.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Irish flag carrier Aer Lingus has become the latest airline to join the premium economy revolution, with the airline having just unveiled its upcoming product offering ahead of its launch next October.
    • While the introduction of premium economy for the first time in the Irish flag carrier's history is the main headline, Aer Lingus will also use this refurbishment as an opportunity for a nose-to-tail reimagining of its A330 interiors, with business and economy class also changing.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Irish flag carrier Aer Lingus has become the latest airline to join the premium economy revolution, with the airline having just unveiled its upcoming product offering ahead of its launch next October. It plans to fit 28 spacious recliner seats on ten of its Airbus A330 widebody twinjets. This will represent the bulk of its twin-aisle fleet, with ch-aviation showing that it currently has two Airbus A330-200s and 12 A330-300s.

    While the introduction of premium economy for the first time in the Irish flag carrier's history is the main headline, Aer Lingus will also use this refurbishment as an opportunity for a nose-to-tail reimagining of its A330 interiors, with business and economy class also changing. Passengers flying on Aer Lingus' US routes will be the first to benefit from the patch, with Dublin to New York JFK being the first route.

    Aer Lingus has chosen the RECARO R4 seat for its new premium economy cabin on the Airbus A330, which will be able to accommodate 28 passengers in four seven-abreast (2-3-2) rows. These flyers will be able to look forward to an increased seat pitch of 38 inches, with the seats measuring 18-19 inches in width. They will also offer guests a greater deal of recline, at eight inches. The soft product is strong too.

    Recent findings suggest that on this front, Aer Lingus says that its premium economy passengers can expect, among other things, "an upgraded three-course dining experience, complimentary drinks throughout the flight, comfortable bedding, an amenity kit and noise-reducing headphones." All the while, Starlink WiFi will help them to stay more connected inflight than ever before. Lynne Embleton, the CEO of Aer Lingus, remarked that:.

    Sources indicate that "Our ambition here is simple. We want to give our customers greater choice, comfort, and connectivity, while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus.".

    Sources indicate that it is no secret in the world of modern commercial aviation that the transatlantic market between Europe and North America is one of the most lucrative corridors around. As such, premium demand is often high, and Aer Lingus is set to tap into this trend by launching its newly fitted A330s on the long-haul route from Dublin (DUB) to New York (JFK). These flights will begin in just under a year, on October 1, 2027.

    According to recent reports, initially, Aer Lingus looks to deploy its premium economy-equipped A330s on the EI104/105 rotation. These flights are operated today by the A330-300, which is the larger and more numerous of Aer Lingus' two variants of the Airbus A330. At the time of writing, these widebody twinjet aircraft feature a two-class configuration with 30 business class flatbeds and either 283 or 287 economy class seats on board.

    As more and more of Aer Lingus' Airbus A330s are retrofitted with the fresh cabins, the carrier will be able to roll the product out on a growing variety of, as it puts it, "additional North American routes." According to Cirium, an aviation analytics firm, its present A330 services across the pond from Dublin serve Boston, Chicago, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Miami, New York, Orlando, and San Francisco.

    It has been revealed that with ten of Aer Lingus' A330s being taken out of service for the premium economy refit, this presents an opportunity for the Irish flag carrier to undertake a nose-to-tail reimagining of its widebody twinjet fleet. This is exactly what it looks to do, hence the aforementioned addition of Starlink WiFi. This will also see it refit its business class cabins with 28 Collins Elevation suites in a four-abreast 1-2-1 layout.

    Sources indicate that found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

    This setup will provide every passenger with direct aisle access, and, when converted to a bed, Aer Lingus states that these seats stretch to a length of 78 inches (1.98 meters). The carrier is also reimagining its business class catering offering and fitting its A330s with a snack bar. As for economy class, Aer Lingus promises "ergonomic seating, six-way adjustable leather headrests, [and] refreshed dining options.".
