    Delta Reserve Credit Card Review: Benefits Worth It For Delta Loyalists?

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Express and Delta have had a close relationship for many years.
    • Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card.
    • Before I get into my Delta Reserve Card review, here are some of the card’s key details, from its current welcome bonus to its annual fee and the perks you get with Delta:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Express and Delta have had a close relationship for many years. As part of that, they matter seven co-branded Delta Amex cards. The Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card is the most premium of these cards, and in this post, I’d like to take an in-depth look at the product. The Delta Reserve Card is worth it if you’re a frequent flyer with Delta, or if you want to earn elite status through credit card spending. Let’s take a look at all the details of the card.

    Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card.

    Before I get into my Delta Reserve Card review, here are some of the card’s key details, from its current welcome bonus to its annual fee and the perks you get with Delta:.

    I also put together my list of top pros and cons for the Delta Reserve Card:.

    Industry observers note that let’s look at the Delta Reserve Card‘s welcome bonus offer, eligibility rules, and fees. All of these are probably top of mind if you’re considering applying for this card.

    According to recent reports, the Delta Reserve Card currently has the following welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 125,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $5,000 in eligible purchases on your latest Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

    According to recent reports, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Delta SkyMiles to be worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the 125,000-mile bonus is worth $1,375. While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have quite a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

    The welcome bonus offer on the Delta Reserve Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. However, eligibility for the Delta Reserve Card (including the welcome offer) is unrelated to whether you have any other personal card in the portfolio. You’re also eligible for the personal card if you already have the business card, and vice versa.

    You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

    It has been revealed that the Delta Reserve Card has a $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees). Obviously that’s on the high side, though you also get quite a few perks. You can add authorized users for $175 each, and authorized users get some card benefits, including airport lounge access and inflight savings on Delta.

    If you spend on the Delta Reserve Card, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can efficiently use the card abroad.

    Beyond the welcome bonus, how does the Delta Reserve Card earn rewards on your spending, both in terms of miles earned and in terms of elite status qualification? Let’s look at the ongoing earning rates and Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you can earn through spending on the card.

    The Delta Reserve Card has fairly limited bonus categories for spending. The Delta Reserve Card earns:.

    Ironically, other Delta cards with lower annual fees have more robust bonus categories. The logic is probably that this is the most rewarding card for spending counting toward elite status, and therefore Delta believes that’s enough of an incentive.

    It has been revealed that nowadays, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status is earned exclusively based on how many Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you rack up. When it comes to earning MQDs through credit card spending, the Delta Reserve Credit Card is as good as it gets:.

    For context, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status has the following annual MQD requirements:.

    Therefore if you wanted to earn elite status exclusively through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following amounts:.

    While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

    Delta One (business class) awards can be a great option, especially on roundtrip awards rather than one way itineraries. Using SkyMiles for shorter hops on Delta can be great, too. I’ve seen award flights between New York (LGA) and Orlando (MCO) for less than 20,000 miles roundtrip.

    Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles.

    You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air. You can also redeem SkyMiles on some airlines that aren’t part of SkyTeam but still partner with Delta, like LATAM and WestJet.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the primary things that sets the Delta Reserve Credit Card apart from other Delta Amex cards is the lounge access perks that it offers. The card offers Delta Sky Club® access, Centurion Lounge access, and even several Sky Club passes. How does that work?

    The Delta Reserve Card offers 15 Delta Sky Club visits each Medallion year for the primary cardmember. Each visit is defined as all entries within a 24-hour period, including at different airports. In other words, if you have a connecting itinerary, you can visit multiple Sky Clubs at different airports while using only one visit allotment.

    It’s possible to unlock unlimited Sky Club visits after spending $75,000 in purchases on your card in a calendar year. Once all 15 visits have been used, eligible cardmembers may purchase additional Sky Club visits at a per visit rate of $50 per person using the card.

    In addition to the primary cardmember getting Sky Club access when flying Delta the same day, they also receive four Sky Club guest passes annually.

    These can be used by the primary cardmember to guest others into the lounge, allowing you to skip the $50 guesting fee four times annually.

    The Delta Reserve Card also offers complimentary Centurion Lounge access when traveling on a same-day Delta flight booked with the card. The primary cardmember is entitled to access, and bringing additional guests costs $50 each.

    Centurion Lounges, for the most part, offer a significantly improved food and beverage offering compared to most domestic airline lounges in the United States, so this is a nice option to have.

    The Delta Reserve Credit Card has a good bonus, though if I were just looking for the best welcome bonus offer, I would go for the Gold or Platinum version of the card, since the cards have significantly lower annual fees.

    It has been revealed that the reason you want to get the Reserve version of the card is because of the valuable long term perks that it offers. Above I’ve talked about how the Reserve Card can help you earn status and can help you access lounges, though there are lots of perks beyond that. Let’s take a look at some of those benefits.

    Every year upon renewal of the Delta Reserve Card, you receive a roundtrip companion certificate valid within the United States (including Alaska and Hawaii), and to Mexico, the Caribbean, and Central America. This can be used for fares ranging from first class to economy, so the flexibility offered by that is pretty awesome, and for many will more than justify the annual fee.

    Sources indicate that you just have to pay the government-imposed taxes and fees for the companion. There are some things to be aware of when redeeming the Delta companion certificate, including:.

    It has been revealed that just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive a $200 Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you receive up to $200 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a upcoming Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

    Industry observers note that while I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $200, if you wanted to. If used right, the value here is considerable.

    Recent findings suggest that just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive up to $240 in Resy credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $20 in statement credits each month after using your card on eligible purchases at U.S. restaurants that offer reservations on Resy.com and the Resy app, purchases made directly on Resy.com or in the Resy app, and purchases made via Resy Pay.

    Recent findings suggest that just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive up to $120 in rideshare credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers, including Uber and Lyft.

    Just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you get a first checked bag free. With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up:.

    Depending on how many bags you’re checking, a few trips with a companion could pay for the card’s annual fee.

    You can receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Reserve. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you must ensure the primary cardmember’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation.

    If you have the Delta Reserve Amex then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food, alcoholic beverages, and audio headsets, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

    Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card you can redeem miles for one cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

    Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn MQDs for taking those flights.

    Sources indicate that with the TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta. Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

    Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

    Having the Delta Reserve Card gets you priority for complimentary upgrades, assuming you have Medallion status. That’s because the card acts as a tiebreaker.

    It has been revealed that if you have the Reserve Card you get upgrade priority over other Medallion members within the same Medallion level and fare class. Given how competitive upgrades are, this can make a material difference in terms of whether you clear or not.

    Industry observers note that the Delta Reserve Card offers complimentary Delta First and Delta Comfort upgrades on eligible flights for non-elite members. You will be toward the bottom of the upgrade list, but there are lots of situations where this could help you score a good extra legroom seat, or in some cases even a first class seat.

    Those with the Delta Reserve Card receive a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit. This benefit applies once every four years. This can save you significant time both at security and immigration, and is something I highly recommend signing up for if eligible.

    Recent findings suggest that just for having the Delta Reserve Card, you receive Hertz President’s Circle elite status, which is Hertz’s top-tier status. Status is valid for as long as you’re a cardmember. This should take the pain out of renting cars, and offers the following perks:.

    The Delta Reserve Card comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:.

    #30594. Industry News: At Our Annual Points of View Summit, Experts Make Their 2027 Travel Predictions

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: At Our Annual Points of View Summit, Experts Make Their 2027 Travel Predictions

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When planning our 2026 Points of View Summit, we wanted to be sure to set time aside to hear directly from our travel specialists—the behind-the-scenes experts who work tirelessly work to curate ambitious and deeply personal itineraries around the world.
    • Jim Berkeley, founder and CEO of Destinations and Adventures International, speaks on culinary moments.
    • Inspired by Hilton Head Island's rich tapestry of culinary traditions, senior features editor Megan Spurrell and editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez led a discussion on traveling for taste—from the rising interest in foraging over traditional cooking classes to the draw of massive-name chefs contrasted with harder-to-find local gems, and the hotspots that deserve to be on our food maps.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When planning our 2026 Points of View Summit, we wanted to be sure to set time aside to hear directly from our travel specialists—the behind-the-scenes experts who work tirelessly work to curate ambitious and deeply personal itineraries around the world. Spliced between compelling panels on Lowcountry heritage, summer travel trends, and the evolving appeal of all-inclusive stays, the breakouts allowed for extended discussions with Traveler editors on a range of themes. From culinary experiences inspired by Hilton Head Island's Gullah cuisine, to the evolving dynamics of multigenerational travel and a new guard of ultra-luxe globetrotters, we got the inside scoop on where travelers are going and how they're getting there.

    Jim Berkeley, founder and CEO of Destinations and Adventures International, speaks on culinary moments.

    Inspired by Hilton Head Island's rich tapestry of culinary traditions, senior features editor Megan Spurrell and editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez led a discussion on traveling for taste—from the rising interest in foraging over traditional cooking classes to the draw of massive-name chefs contrasted with harder-to-find local gems, and the hotspots that deserve to be on our food maps.

    According to recent reports, our specialists all agreed that travelers yearn for “authentic” food moments, though defining authenticity—and actually finding it—often becomes tricky. To Omolola Campbell, sixth-gen Gullah descendant and executive producer of Gullah short documentary The Spirit We Move With, it's about who provides the experience. “Taking a cooking class is much different than getting it from a local chef who can tell stories about why a dish means so much to this locality,” she said, explaining how so many of South Carolina's Gullah dishes contain okra because its seeds were sown into the hair of West Africans who were brought to the South for slavery. The plant has come to represent resilience, and it's that integral context, according to her, that gives a meal its soul. “That's how you differentiate the person who really knows why they're cooking what they're cooking,” Campbell concluded.

    Dana Kravis, Madison Flager, and our travel specialists explore multigenerational travel trends.

    Industry observers note that when it comes to multigenerational trips, the grandchildren are choosing the destinations and the grandparents are paying—it's their way of leaving a legacy amongst those dearest to them. During a discussion led by global executive director of video Dana Kravis and commerce director Madison Flager, our travel specialists observed that, because people today tend to wait longer to have children, grandparents are older than they used to be. Travelers in their 80s and 90s are increasingly joining trips, shifting the multigenerational travel dynamic away from the traditional picture of grandparents in their 70s. To trip designers, this means there must be layers of options catering to different activity and exertion levels.

    Industry observers note that many in this session agreed the most successful family trips provide opportunities for separating and coming back together. Three itinerary choices in one day are ideal, so younger folks can be out and about, with the whole family reuniting for mealtimes and perhaps an afternoon activity. Boat and yacht experiences were especially recommended as spaces where the family is forced to be together—grandkids cannot simply run off and do their own thing.

    What's luxury to one traveler might seem the furthest from it to another; some long for jam-packed, once-in-a-lifetime itineraries, while others want total disconnection and the privilege to do absolutely nothing for a week. Features director Rebecca Misner and commerce writer Jessica Sulima led this breakout, as specialists debated the definition of luxury itself. “Luxury is being able to pass on meaning to kids [and] exposing families to the broader world and its cultures,” Virgi Schiffino Kennedy, managing partner at Lux Voyage, said of its intangible appeal. To Ruchi Harnal, founder of Harnal Travel, true luxury “is not about the resort or the villa but the personalization of the trip.” As for who’s spending money on trips? Thomas Robinson, MR at Dehouche, has observed that Gen Z and Millennials are more inclined to spend but want to know where that money goes. Additionally, the specialists largely agreed they’re seeing a shift away from parents taking their children on trips, and towards 30- and 40-somethings treating their parents to a vacation. In Harnal's experience, milestone birthdays and anniversaries are driving clients to book a trip.

    Between rising temperatures and overtourism, our specialists discuss the factors impacting European summer destinations.

    Recent findings suggest that what is the impact of overtourism, price inflation, and rising temperatures on our Euro summers? Director of special projects Lale Arikoglu and commerce editor Meaghan Kenny opened the floor for our specialists. “If you’re thinking of traveling to the Dolomites, consider Switzerland instead. There’s history and beautiful scenery with fewer crowds,” Brian Dore, owner of CIU Travel, said. For the hiking curious, some added that Switzerland offers plenty of one-day hiking trails or “soft adventure” travel—three-to-four days combined with a lake or city destination. Others agreed that traveling to the Alps offers a significant advantage—higher elevations means cooler temperatures—and that Slovenia is a great alternative to Italy. To dodge the crowds, travelers might also consider Belgium, Denmark, or Norway (where ocean ships and river cruises are opening earlier in March). For families, consider Umbria (hot tip: plenty of festival and craft opportunities for kids), Austria, Ireland, or Croatia.

    According to recent reports, for those who want to stick with more tried-and-tested European itineraries next summer, consider going as early as possible, for instance, in May instead of August. When it comes to traveling to France specifically, folks advised flying into Paris or Nice, then venturing out to the countryside or oft-overlooked Atlantic Coast. And our specialists could not stress it enough: Always, always check the temperatures in advance of your trip.

    Recent findings suggest that as discussed by Mei Zhang, chairman and founder at WildChina, during the panel on summer travel, the demand for travel to Asia is only increasing. Global features director Erin Florio and editorial assistant Kat Chen continued the conversation with travel specialists on the destinations and experiences driving this growth. For Silk Road Treasure Tours president Zulya Rajabova and her clients, it's the destinations with indispensable craft identities, such as Samarkand in Uzbekistan with its millennia-old design traditions, that make the continent so varied yet distinct. Meanwhile, Marigold Wood, travel designer at Blonde Atlas, explained that she's been recommending routes going through China, such as Yunnan's tea trails, which offer trekking and hiking opportunities. For Ethan Crowley, lead trip designer at Asia Desk Ltd, educating his travelers on navigating countries like Cambodia, beyond their most-visited landmarks, is key.

    Sources indicate that if 2026 was the year of the fan, 2027 is ushering in even more reasons to travel for entertainment. Associate editor Charlie Hobbs and commerce writer Jessica Chapel helmed this breakout on the sporting events, music festivals, and art fairs that specialists are seeing people travel for (and the subsequent hurdles they must overcome to). From Pink at the Sphere, where access requires a Venetian hotel package to the Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, where full-house and package buyouts, high-demand events are increasingly forcing bundled purchases.

    The specialists also highlighted how limited legal protections in the States enables extreme ticket scalping for stadium concerts and makes domestic events increasingly unaffordable. Stephanie Malakie, founder of Empress Travel Club pointed to a related challenge: With so many events and providers, travel advisors find it hard to filter the options and identify the right fit for clients. Rather than just acquiring a ticket, specialists agreed the focus should be on curating the surrounding experience or tapping into evergreen and niche experiential travel, with events like the Jets playing in London or F1 in Shanghai. Cultural milestones like Vatican City trips featuring Papal Blessings or European Christmas markets pair well with entertainment, too. To Zhang, set-jetting to filming locations also offers value, minus the headache of peak-event ticketing.

    Hannah Towey co-leads the breakout session on outdoor travel.

    Everyone is hiking, or so it seems. Helmed by Jamie Spain, travel bookings commerce editor, and Hannah Towey, news editor, this breakout explored nature as wellness and why it is we're increasingly longing for all things outdoorsy. However, our specialists offered a frank reality check on our dumbphone fantasies. “Guests all want to have access [to Wi-Fi] for emergency reasons at a minimum… I don’t have a single guest who wants to [fully] digital detox," Kate Doty, trip designer at Geographic Expeditions, remarked. It seems that many travelers want to be disconnected until the time comes for true disconnection, and Lou Lagrange, trip consultant at Luxury Travel Advisor, added, “Even planning for national park trips, [you have to] warn them there won’t be Wi-Fi.” However, the group observed that services such as having photographers on small ships, helps reduce a traveler's dependency on their phones.

    There's still a real demand for glamping, as guests want access to nature but with a side of luxury. And when it comes to extreme weather events, instead of having travelers write off entire regions or countries, Doty has figured out collaborative ways to shelve them for potential future trips. In Travel Studio founder Kerri Lisa's case, it's a matter of reframing the perks of a destination and its seasons; the rainy season, for example, might be exceptionally lush and green. There's always something to be learned in welcoming a bit of playful unpredictability into our itineraries.

    Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.
    • Industry observers note that the possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections.
    • Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

    Industry observers note that the possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

    Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

    Sources indicate that vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

    In a recent development, "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself remarked so last night.".

    Trump has remarked that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over.".

    Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”.

    In a recent development, “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!".

    The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

    Trump, Vance and other administration officials have noted in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

    Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday highlighted that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

    The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

    Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "promptly.".

    “Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers mentioned in one campaign ad.

    On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

    In a recent development, as the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

    According to recent reports, “With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”.

    Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

    Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

    Recent findings suggest that asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”.

    It has been revealed that through November 21, 2026, Hilton Honors is offering a buy points promotion, which is the program’s best-ever bonus on purchasing points! While Hilton Honors ordinarily offers up to a 100% bonus on purchased points, this time around the program is offering up to a 120% bonus, which is a cost of 0.45 cents per point. This could represent a great value for hotel redemptions, especially with an immediate use in mind, as members can purchase up to 528,000 points in one transaction.

    As always, I only recommend buying points with a short term use in mind, and if you understand the mechanics of how award redemptions with a program work, including what redemption costs are like.

    Link: Buy Hilton Honors points with this promotion with a 120% bonus.

    Hilton Honors ordinarily charges one cent per purchased point, including all taxes and fees. That’s before any discounts or bonuses. If you’re eligible for the 120% bonus and maxed out the offer, you’d receive a total of 528,000 points at a cost of $2,400, which is a rate of 0.45 cents per Hilton Honors point.

    Ordinarily, Hilton Honors lets members buy up to 160,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased by 50%, to 240,000 points. With a 120% bonus, that means you could purchase up to 528,000 points.

    The purchase of Hilton Honors points is non-refundable, and points purchased don’t count toward elite status. Purchased points will post within 48 hours of finalizing the purchase (though in my experience, much faster than that).

    While Hilton Honors has a strict limit on how many points you can buy, note that there are ways to acquire more points than that limit without violating the rules.

    Hilton lets members combine points across accounts at no cost, so in reality you could acquire substantially more points by simply buying them across accounts and then consolidating them. Hilton Honors lets members transfer up to 500,000 points, and receive up to two million points, per calendar year. Each member can make up to six transfers to other members per calendar year, and latest Hilton Honors members can only transfer or receive points a minimum of 30 days after enrollment.

    Hilton also allows points pooling, whereby Hilton Honors members can combine points with up to 10 other members, with the same limitations.

    When Hilton Honors offer a promotion on purchased points, it’s most common to see a 100% bonus (the equivalent of a 50% discount). So this 120% bonus is the best-ever promotion we’ve seen from the program, so that’s awesome.

    Below is a chart with some of the recent buy points promotions we saw from the Hilton Honors program, before this one.

    In a recent development, hilton Honors point purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with a Hilton credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s Hilton spending.

    I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

Hilton’s partnership with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) is also awesome, and offers great redemption opportunities.

    However, people shouldn’t blindly buy Hilton Honors points, as there are also lots of redemptions where you won’t come out ahead. As I see it, the biggest value with buying Hilton Honors is for aspirational redemptions at expensive properties. Let me give some examples, based on current redemption rates.

RiverView Ranch Retreat is located in Montana, and is bookable for 220,000 points per night for a standard room. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $990. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be over $3,800 (the screenshot below is for two nights, since that’s the minimum stay), so that’s close to three-fourths off.

Unfortunately I find that for your run of the mill Hilton properties, including many limited service hotels, the value just isn’t there in the same way.

    Industry observers note that for example, take the Hilton Garden Inn Tampa, which is bookable for 45,000 points per night. At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, you could acquire those points for $203. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be under $180, so there’s absolutely no reason to buy points, only to redeem them for less value than what you paid.     In a recent development, hilton Honors doesn’t have a published award chart, but rather the program has dynamic award pricing. This means that the cost of a standard free night award can vary depending on the day of the week, time of year, etc.

    As a general rule of thumb, Hilton Honors free night awards start at 10,000 points per night, and go up to 250,000 points per night (which is a shame, because up until last year, properties maxed out at 150,000 points per night).

    It has been revealed that sometimes you’ll see award costs that are way higher than these amounts. That’s generally not nearly as good of a use of Hilton Honors points, and you’ll find that some awards even cost one million or more points per night. Obviously that’s a lousy value.

At a rate of 0.45 cents per point, that’s like the equivalent of paying $540 per night. As a point of comparison, the cash rate would be over $1,800 per night, so that represents absolutely massive savings.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Hilton Honors points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively.     How I Travel: Audra McDonald Needs a Humidifier in Her Hotel Room

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Theater legend Audra McDonald possesses one of the most powerful, lauded voices of her generation, a soprano so stunning that she’s been nominated for more Tony Awards than any other performer in history.
    • While her role in the period drama The Gilded Age doesn’t require singing—yet!—McDonald and the many Broadway legends in the cast released a holiday album this month, ‘Voices of the Gilded Age: The Christmas Album,’ and the fourth season is currently airing on HBO.
    • In a recent development, I don't think you can beat Fresh York City.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Theater legend Audra McDonald possesses one of the most powerful, lauded voices of her generation, a soprano so stunning that she’s been nominated for more Tony Awards than any other performer in history. So what elixirs, potions, and special teas does she keep with her to ensure the quality of her voice as she travels the world to sing? “I mask up on planes. I’m traveling all over the country to do concerts; I can’t land and be sick,” she says. “And I try to make sure there's a humidifier in the hotel room. Those are the two main things.”.

    While her role in the period drama The Gilded Age doesn’t require singing—yet!—McDonald and the many Broadway legends in the cast released a holiday album this month, ‘Voices of the Gilded Age: The Christmas Album,’ and the fourth season is currently airing on HBO. She spoke with Condé Nast Traveler from Australia, where her husband Will Swenson is currently starring in the Oz production of A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical, about traveling with their 10-year-old daughter, the unspeakable glories of Fresh Zealand, and why you simply can’t top New York City in the final months of the year.

    The world’s best city for the holidays:.

    In a recent development, I don't think you can beat Fresh York City. I've lived there for 36 years and it's always such a beautiful time. We have dear friends with a kid around my youngest child's age, and we've been going to the holiday spectacular at Radio City. My sister makes sure that she takes my daughters to The Nutcracker every year at City Ballet. We always try to go see the tree at Rockefeller Center. The one day I don't like in New York City during the holidays is Santa Con, but other than that, I'm down.

    Her favorite venue on Earth in which to perform:.

    Recent findings suggest that there's something about Carnegie Hall [in Manhattan] that is magic. I last sang at Carnegie Hall about six, seven months ago—I'm on the board there now, as well—and the nerves I normally get [before a performance] are always tenfold when I'm getting ready there.

    Sources indicate that then the minute I step out on that stage, the hall just gives you a hug that says, You're here to do what you're supposed to do. You're supposed to make music, you're supposed to celebrate music, you're supposed to commune with your audience, and glorious sounds are supposed to be heard. Carnegie Hall is built for all the sound to be glorious. That [venue] takes care of me.

    Her advice for traveling with kids:.

    Industry observers note that don't worry about how they act up on a plane. Do what you can, but it's not the flight attendants’ first time at the rodeo. You're never going to see any of these other people again. When we flew out to Australia, my daughter got some weird stomach bug that started the minute they shut the door, and she vomited for the first eight hours of that 15-hour flight. The flight attendants just kept bringing bags and stuff and were like… [mimes a blasé hand gesture]. There was nothing we could do! We were over the ocean. I was giving myself grace. I was giving my poor daughter grace. I just wanted her to feel better, and I was doing the best I could. That’s what I would say to other parents. They’ve seen it all, so don’t worry about what other people are thinking. Everybody has headphones now! We’re fine!

    How she spends her flight time:.

    According to recent reports, I am not preparing for work! That's the ADHD in me. I am also not sleeping because I cannot sleep on planes very well, unless I'm really knocked out with the help of sleeping pills or something, and I don't like to do that. I try to watch movies, but I'm not good at it, either. My dad was killed in a plane crash about 20 years ago, so normally what I'm doing on a plane—when I'm not taking care of my daughter vomiting—is watching the flight path and seeing where we are in the sky. Then, if there's Wi-Fi, I check to see the weather ahead. Like I'm helping! I don't know what I'm doing, but it calms me down to be like, “Okay, I see that there is weather up ahead, so I should expect that it's probably going to be bumpy.” I don't know if in my mind, I'm thinking [as if] I can warn the pilot. I’ve got to go to therapy, but that's what I do on a plane.

    The best vacation she’s ever taken:.

    Recent findings suggest that new Zealand, holy wow. My husband and I were asked to sing on a Playbill cruise in Tahiti. We flew to Tahiti with our two daughters, and then I had three and a half weeks off before I started my Australian tour, so we went to New Zealand. I'm going to get emotional talking about it. Every place we visited—the North Island, the South Island, Queenstown, Rotorua, Hahei Beach, the Southern Alps, Christchurch, Wellington—all of it was just one wow after another. The people were lovely. We went to Hobbiton. We drove everywhere, and every second of it was mind-blowing. We even did the mailboat, where you go with this guy on a boat to deliver the mail in an area you can only access by water. I want to go back!

    The destination she swears she loved before everyone else:.

    In a recent development, when we first start going, I wasn’t hearing about a lot of people there, but now everybody goes to Portugal. We have friends who live there, so we started visiting a lot, and not just Lisbon or the Algarve or Porto, though we love Porto. It was also the beautiful countryside and hills and tiny little villages. The topography there is stunning. It’s getting more expensive now, but we used to get incredible bottles of wine for €3! In fact, we have a farm there now, we love it so much.

    The hotel amenity she always checks for:.

    Sources indicate that toothbrush and toothpaste. Not every hotel provides that, and I just love it when they do. If they've got a toothbrush and toothpaste in there, they've probably gotten a lot of the other amenities right too.

    The farthest flung place she’s ever been recognized:.

    Industry observers note that here in Australia. I was in the South Melbourne neighborhood we've been living in, and I went into a little bookstore near my daughter's school, and someone recognized me. They stated, “Were you the one who recorded Emily Wilson's translation of The Iliad book on tape? I loved your work in that.” And I was like, “Whoa, what? Yes I did, wow, thank you.” Doing The Iliad on tape almost killed me. It was the hardest thing I've ever done, so the fact that she wanted to thank me for it? I don’t think my mom knows I did that!

    Industry observers note that I really want to take a trip to Africa. Obviously, I want to go to Ghana and see where our journey started. I want to go to Kenya and do a safari. I want to go on a trek to see the gorillas. I've been to Egypt, to Cairo, but that's the only time I've been to Africa. I want to wait a couple more years, until my daughter's about 13, and then I will take her. That's going to be our trip.

    #30590. The Hub Delta Air Lines Threw Away After Merging With Northwest

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1675 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The Hub Delta Air Lines Threw Away After Merging With Northwest

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The 2008 merger between Delta Air Lines and Northwest Airlines was the first to create one of the US's current 'mega legacy carriers.' Delta Air Lines and its contemporaries today have hubs spanning the entire country while operating over 1,000 mainline aircraft each.
    • Industry observers note that the main benefits of these mergers were scale, including network size, and all three legacy carriers have largely used the hubs that they inherited from their mergers to their advantage, enabling further growth and boosting relevance in more markets.
    • Industry observers note that northwest had traditionally been heavily focused on its Asia network, competing primarily against United Airlines to be the dominant US airline across the Pacific.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The 2008 merger between Delta Air Lines and Northwest Airlines was the first to create one of the US's current 'mega legacy carriers.' Delta Air Lines and its contemporaries today have hubs spanning the entire country while operating over 1,000 mainline aircraft each.

    Industry observers note that the main benefits of these mergers were scale, including network size, and all three legacy carriers have largely used the hubs that they inherited from their mergers to their advantage, enabling further growth and boosting relevance in more markets. One of the biggest exceptions, however, came with Northwest's hub at Tokyo Narita International Airport.

    Industry observers note that northwest had traditionally been heavily focused on its Asia network, competing primarily against United Airlines to be the dominant US airline across the Pacific. Ever since the merger, Delta has attempted to still be competitive in this market space, but has moved away from the Narita hub, slowly de-prioritizing it and then pulling out of Narita entirely in 2020.

    Going into the merger, Atlanta-based Delta had hubs in Atlanta, New York, Cincinnati, Salt Lake City, and Los Angeles, while Northwest Airlines brought hubs in Memphis, Detroit, Minneapolis, and Narita. In addition, the carrier often labeled Amsterdam and Paris as hubs, but these were joint venture hubs dominated by joint venture partners KLM and Air France.

    Narita, on the other hand, was a fully Northwest operation with a large number of US-bound flights and intra-Asia routes. Memphis was dehubbed after the merger due to the decline of the city's economy as well as its proximity to Atlanta, while Cincinnati was also eventually dehubbed in favor of Detroit. After the merger, Delta also began pursuing hubs in Boston and Seattle, with some success.

    As a whole, Delta's network changes were primarily from growth and rationalizing some elements of the hub structure to remove redundancy, but the Narita hub was different because, to an extent, the carrier still has not added back the lost capacity. At the time of the merger, Northwest served 19 cities from Narita, but in the 2010s, Delta slowly cut away at the hub until pulling out of Narita entirely.

    The US routes were mainly replaced by services to Tokyo Haneda Airport, but Delta also cut services to many Asia-Pacific destinations. This includes Beijing, Guangzhou, Busan, Guam, Palau, Manila (which will be returning in 2027 from Los Angeles), Saipan, Singapore, and Bangkok. As of 2026, Delta still does not fly to most of these cities.

    Industry observers note that the Narita hub made sense in the 20th century, when the longest-ranged Boeing 747-200s couldn't reliably fly routes longer than Upcoming York to Tokyo. Northwest would have all of its US services stop in Narita, and passengers would then transfer to flights bound for other Asian destinations.

    However, aircraft like the Boeing 747-400 and 777, along with the later Airbus A350 and 787, could fly nonstop from the US to most cities in Asia, making the stop in Narita redundant. While this helped fill the intra-Asia flights, the US hubs had much greater connecting feed as well. Delta had already operated a hub in Los Angeles, which has a strong local market for Asia travel, but also heavy competition.

    Delta Air Lines Long-Haul Destinations Served From Seattle In 2026.

    Amsterdam Schiphol Airport (AMS).

    Seoul Incheon International Airport (ICN).

    Josep Tarradellas Barcelona–El Prat Airport (BCN).

    Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG).

    Taipei Taoyuan International Airport (TPE).

    Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG).

    Rome Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO).

    In 2012, it elected to begin building Seattle as its primary hub for transpacific flights, inheriting former Northwest services to Narita, launching Beijing (previously announced by Northwest), while later adding Osaka, Shanghai, Haneda, Seoul, Hong Kong, and most recently, Taipei. Not all of these services stuck around, but Delta committed to Seattle for transpacific flights, while also growing its domestic and European network from its upcoming hub. Operating smaller widebodies nonstop from Seattle to Asia proved more lucrative.

    As such, Delta rapidly built a much larger domestic network in Seattle compared to the US network out of Narita. In recent years, Delta has experienced difficulties competing with Alaska Airlines and foreign carriers out of Seattle, and is therefore planning to grow its transpacific network out of Los Angeles as well. It's already added Hong Kong, and Manila will be coming in 2027, while Singapore is also rumored to be returning as a nonstop.

    In a recent development, delta has replaced its intra-Asia operations out of Narita with nonstops from the US, but there's still a large number of Asian cities that have lost service on Delta metal. The reason for this is that, for all intents and purposes, Delta has replaced its Narita hub with a hub in Seoul, except that the intra-Asia flights are now operated by fellow SkyTeam member, Korean Air, rather than using widebodies with the Delta livery.

    According to recent reports, this is possible due to the metal-neutral joint venture that became effective in 2018. As part of their joint venture, Delta and Korean Air coordinate schedules, pricing, and codeshare on each other's flights, while also sharing revenue. They essentially act as one airline across the Pacific.

    Hong Kong International Airport (HKG).

    Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    Seoul Incheon International Airport (ICN).

    Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW).

    Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL).

    Minneapolis-St Paul International Airport (MSP).

    Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC).

    Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA).

    Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG).

    Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW).

    Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    Seattle Tacoma International Airport (SEA).

    Taipei Taoyuan International Airport (TPE).

    Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA).

    Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW).

    Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL).

    Honolulu Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL).

    Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    Minneapolis-St Paul International Airport (MSP).

    Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA).

    Recent findings suggest that this allows Delta to still sell one-stop tickets to destinations like Singapore or Bangkok, but with a layover in Seoul and a segment operated by Korean Air. To the carrier, it makes essentially no difference whether the second leg is flown by a Delta or Korean Air jet, except that codesharing with a partner costs less money. In recent years, Delta has been practically allergic to adding newly introduced long-haul and ultra-long-haul routes if a destination can be conveniently served by partner airlines.

    However, customers in the US are increasingly seeking out nonstops to major international destinations, while the carrier's latest contract with its pilots mandates a one-for-one increase in widebody flying relative to any capacity growth by foreign partners. As such, the airline is increasing its US-to-Asia nonstops, with the Seoul hub filling in the gaps that were previously served by Narita.

    Recent findings suggest that in short, Delta was able to fully replicate its intra-Asia network out of Narita with Korean Air's operations out of Seoul after their joint venture agreement went into effect, and Delta also benefited from not having to operate these flights with its own metal. The cities with the highest demand got their own nonstops from the US.

    The 2018 joint venture agreement officially rendered Narita redundant within Delta's network, relegating it to just a spoke airport. However, Delta also had a better airport with which to serve Tokyo directly. Upon Narita's opening in 1978, the Japanese government moved all international flights away from the older Haneda Airport, but in 2010, it began permitting foreign carriers to serve Haneda again on a limited scale.

    Sources indicate that haneda is closer to the city center than Narita, making it more desirable, but it's also a slot-controlled airport. As such, Delta had to build up its Haneda operations slowly, as it had to wait for the Japanese government to release and award slots, while rivals American Airlines and United Airlines still serve both airports. Today, Delta serves Haneda from Atlanta, Detroit, Honolulu, Los Angeles, Minneapolis, and Seattle.

    According to recent reports, while its Tokyo network is smaller than rivals, it lacks a major Japanese partner, which makes Tokyo less notable to Delta than American and United. Delta has recently confirmed that it will be returning to Narita in 2027 with a single daily flight from Seattle, but in all likelihood, this is due to a lack of slots at Haneda. If Delta could, it almost certainly would have added a second daily flight to Haneda, but has to return to Narita instead.

    Similar to Northwest, United Airlines also formerly had a significant intra-Asia operation out of Narita due to aircraft range limitations. These routes went away as the carrier began taking latest Boeing 787s that could serve destinations like Singapore nonstop, but United still serves Narita nonstop from the US alongside its newer Haneda routes due to its joint venture with All Nippon Airways.

    Haneda is primarily for origin & destination traffic, whereas Narita is for additional Asia-Pacific connections. Within the past few years, however, United has begun adding upcoming flights within Asia out of Narita again, using Boeing 737s to serve Cebu, Kaohsiung, Koror, Saipan, and Ulaanbaatar.

    Sources indicate that naturally, these are destinations that can't be economically served nonstop from the US with a widebody, but the major reason why United has begun these routes is due to issues with its Guam hub. Travel demand to Guam remains significantly down from pre-COVID levels, while United operates crew bases and specially configured 737s out of this hub located thousands of miles away from the mainland.

    Rather than operate half-empty 737s out of Guam or move planes and crews to the mainland US, United has instead opted to move some of its 737s to Narita. It's notably operating routes that are not at the moment served by All Nippon Airways (ANA) , and it's also allowed the carrier to operate direct flights to destinations not served by any other US airline. United still relies on nonstop flights from the US to serve Asia, while the Narita operations today are mainly a creative use of assets.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

    Recent findings suggest that the Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

    Industry observers note that dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

    “Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, mentioned in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”.

    LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

    LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

    Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

    Industry observers note that “I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden noted in a social media post last week.

    Industry observers note that dunlap initially introduced his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

    Atmos Rewards Upgrade Certificates: How Do They Work, Are They Worth It?

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.
    • It has been revealed that as I’ve worked my way through the elite ranks, I’ve become eligible for the milestone perks program, whereby you can select perks when passing various elite thresholds.
    • I’m intrigued by Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, given the increasingly global route network of Alaska and Hawaiian.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. The program has four elite tiers — Silver, Gold, Platinum, and Titanium — and somehow I’m actually going to end the year as a top tier member, it looks like, without having once stepped foot on an Alaska or Hawaiian flight.

    It has been revealed that as I’ve worked my way through the elite ranks, I’ve become eligible for the milestone perks program, whereby you can select perks when passing various elite thresholds. Along those lines, At the higher tiers, one of the choices becomes upgrade certificates, so I’d like to talk about those a bit, as I’m trying to decide whether or not I should select these.

    I’m intrigued by Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, given the increasingly global route network of Alaska and Hawaiian. At the same time, the execution of this upgrade program definitely leaves a lot to be desired, including the lack of confirmable upgrade availability.

    Sources indicate that I have to make a selection soon, so I’d like to talk through the Alaska and Hawaiian upgrade certificate program, and then get some feedback from Atmos Rewards loyalists. The last time I was focused on upgrade certificates at the airline was when Alaska Mileage Strategy had Gold Guest Upgrades as the upgrade currency, and MVP Gold was the top tier status… those were the days!

    Atmos Rewards complications upgrade certificates as part of the Atmos Rewards milestone perks program. This can be unlocked based on how many status points you earn over the course of a calendar year. Let me emphasize that these upgrade certificates are intended for confirming upgrades in advance, and they’re separate from the complimentary space available upgrades offered.

    Specifically, Atmos Rewards members could earn upgrade certificates at the following thresholds:.

    Titanium status requires 135,000 status points, and I expect to end the year with roughly that many status points. That means I could select up to eight upgrade certificates. However, that would come at the opportunity cost of 70,000 bonus points, for example. Of course I could also mix and match, like selecting four upgrade certificates and 50,000 bonus points.

    Now let’s talk a bit about the rules for redeeming Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, at least on paper. Upgrades are valid across the Alaska and Hawaiian route networks, and fall into one of two categories:.

    According to recent reports, upgrade certificates can be shared with others, but of course can’t be bartered or sold. One other interesting quirk is that if you cancel or change an itinerary that was upgraded, the certificate will be forfeited. However, a replacement upgrade certificate code can be requested through customer care. Let’s cover the details of upgrades based on the region.

    When it comes to upgrading within North America, an Atmos Rewards upgrade certificate can be confirmed at the time of booking, as long as the “U” fare class is available. If it’s not available, the upgrade will be waitlisted.

    To cover the very basics, the upgrade certificate is valid for one-way travel (with no connections longer than four hours), for tickets issued by and flown on Alaska and Hawaiian. Tickets purchased in Y, B, H, K, M, L, V, S, or N fare classes, are eligible for upgrades using certificates, while tickets purchased in Q, O, G, or X fare classes, are not eligible.

    To search if a flight is upgrade eligible, select “Upgrade Certificate” in the dropdown in the “Upgrade type” section, during the booking process.

    Then on the search results page, you should be looking for two things:.

    When it comes to upgrading outside of North America, Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates have completely different rules, both for better and worse. First, it’s worth understanding that an upgrade requires either one or two upgrade certificates, depending on the route, per the below chart.

    When it comes to using Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates on global (non-North America) flights, there are both pros and cons:.

    I have to say, the execution of this perk is odd. Keep in mind that Atmos Rewards has a one-of-a-kind upgrade perk for top tier Titanium members, whereby they receive space available upgrades globally on the day of departure. So what’s odd is that if you’re a Titanium member you’re eligible for a complimentary upgrade close to departure, but having applied an upgrade certificate previously gives you no priority. You’d think they’d prioritize members who requested an upgrade, but I suspect it’s a technology limitation of some sort.

    I’d like to address the question of whether Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates are worth it both broadly, and more specifically to my situation.

    In a recent development, I hear all the time from Atmos Rewards members who are frustrated by the lack of confirmable upgrade space. And indeed, compared to back in the day, upgrade space that can be confirmed is incredibly limited. At the same time, that’s true across airlines nowadays, given how much better airlines have become at actually selling their first class seats, rather than filling them with those upgrading.

    For example, looking at the route between my home airport of Miami (MIA) and Seattle (SEA) as far out as the schedule opens, I don’t see a single date that has confirmable upgrade space. Now, you’ll sometimes find confirmable upgrade space up and down the West Coast, especially during off peak times, so I don’t want to suggest it’s impossible to find a confirmable upgrade.

    According to recent reports, but just broadly speaking, confirmable upgrades with “U” class available for transcontinental and Hawaii flights are exceedingly rare, and it’s like winning the lottery. So it’s really hard to get excited about that.

    Sources indicate that in theory, I of course love the idea of being able to upgrade a long haul flight with upgrade certificates. The catch is that an upgrade clearing at most 72 hours before departure really limits flexibility. I suppose you could always apply an upgrade, hope it clears, and then cancel your ticket if it doesn’t, but this would be a last minute scramble.

    According to recent reports, to me, that’s just too risky. It’s not that I’d be unwilling to fly economy on a long haul flight, but by strategically using points, it’s really not necessary in a vast majority of situations, at least based on my own travel patterns.

    The thing is, it’s also notable to view Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates in terms of the opportunity cost of selecting them.

    Recent findings suggest that for example, as I mentioned above, at 55,000 status points I can select two upgrade certificates or 5,000 bonus points. At an opportunity cost of 2,500 points per upgrade certificate, I think it might be worth selecting upgrade certificates. Based on my latest points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, so the opportunity cost per upgrade is $37.50. That’s a rate at which I’d probably be happy to gamble, because if the upgrades expire, it’s not the end of the world.

    Sources indicate that meanwhile at 95,000 status points, the opportunity cost becomes 7,500 bonus points per upgrade, so that’s a value of $112.50 per upgrade. Then at 125,000 status points, the opportunity cost becomes 12,500 bonus points per upgrade, so that’s a value of $187.50. That’s the point at which I’m definitely more inclined to take the “sure thing,” rather than take my chances with an upgrade.

    It has been revealed that atmos Rewards lets members select upgrade certificates as part of the milestone perks program. This always comes at an opportunity cost, and is a better value at some tiers than others.

    Industry observers note that upgrade certificates can be used on Alaska and Hawaiian flights globally, with most one-ways requiring one upgrade certificate, though some global routes requiring two upgrade certificates. While upgrades within North America can be confirmed at the time of booking (pending upgrade availability), global upgrades can only be confirmed at most 72 hours before departure.

    It has been revealed that the major issue with upgrades is the lack of availability. Alaska is just really bad about making confirmed upgrades available, and upgrades clearing at most 72 hours before departure on global flights is less than ideal.

    What do you make of the value of Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates?

    It has been revealed that they're not a sure thing, but as a Gold, I've still managed to clear SFO-JFK, though sometimes after booking only and after monitoring for availability. To me, the main frustrations are: lack of waitlisting (this is coming in 2027 but will probably hurt lower tier elites like me), and fare class minimums (I do not want to pay for a higher fare class for the *chance* of upgrading if there is no availability to confirm).     Recent findings suggest that the certs are hard to use domestically. Close in bookings on open flights in off season travel for anything but a 1-2 hr flight is the only hope.     #30585. The Subtle Signs That Give 1st Time First Class Passengers Away, According To Cabin Crew

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1576 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The Subtle Signs That Give 1st Time First Class Passengers Away, According To Cabin Crew

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that most of us don't have the luxury of affording a first class or business class airfare, but we can still dream of turning left instead of turning right at the aircraft door.
    • It has been revealed that there are the large signs and the more subtle signs that show a passenger is flying first class for the first time, but what are they?
    • Sources indicate that cabin crew assess passengers during the boarding process in order to spot any potential issues.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that most of us don't have the luxury of affording a first class or business class airfare, but we can still dream of turning left instead of turning right at the aircraft door. There is a huge difference between regular frequent premium class passengers and those who are upgraded or traveling in first class for the very first time, and cabin crew can spot the difference immediately.

    It has been revealed that there are the large signs and the more subtle signs that show a passenger is flying first class for the first time, but what are they? In this guide, we'll take a look in more detail. Usually, in just a few seconds, cabin crew will know. After all, they are well-used to assessing passengers during the boarding process.

    Sources indicate that cabin crew assess passengers during the boarding process in order to spot any potential issues. This may be an unruly, entitled, or drunk passenger, or it may be that a passenger needs some extra assistance. They will also monitor the cabin through situational awareness to assess if someone has become sick or is a nervous flyer.

    In a recent development, they also use emotional intelligence to understand passengers who are not in their usual environment; after all, the sky is home for many of us, and flying is an event for the passenger. It is easy to tell if someone is not used to being in a premium cabin such as first class. Those who are used to traveling in premium cabins will know exactly where to stow their personal items and be comfortable with the workings of the seat.

    Passengers who are new to the first-class cabin may be overwhelmed and hesitant and may well be clutching their ticket, especially if they received an upgrade or paid with points or were gifted the seat. Regular premium passengers have a calm demeanor and just walk to their seat. Usually, cabin crew can tell from the passenger's body language and mood.

    Sources indicate that however, how they are dressed can also give clues. Their familiarity with the aircraft cabin may also be a factor. First class passengers are usually dressed quite formally but also comfortably and have less hand luggage, whereas passengers more used to economy class are likely to be more casual or alternatively dress too formally and have more hand luggage. This is due to the increased checked baggage allowances offered by premium cabins.

    A passenger unfamiliar with the seat will fumble with the seat controls and try to figure out what does what, according to Yahoo Travel. They might not know the hidden storage areas or where to stow items and how to operate the privacy door, whereas a frequent flyer will handle everything with ease and confidence. The cabin crew will help passengers unfamiliar with the seat controls.

    In a recent development, the cabin is usually extremely quiet and private, the very opposite of the main economy cabin, so new passengers may have to adjust how they behave to fit in. Today's first class seats can be quite complex, with various recline and massage functions. This could be intimidating to a first time passenger, and they might be hesitant to try to figure out where the usually familiar armrest and tray table are.

    A frequent premium passenger will just move their tray table into the correct position without thought, once the seatbelt sign is off. For a first-timer, it can feel like a very expensive puzzle. Amenity kits are often prized and kept intact as souvenirs, or some passengers like to resell them to collectors, according to The Points Guy.

    Industry observers note that they are designed to be used inflight, mostly to help combat the dry air conditions, and are especially formulated with premium passengers in mind. However, more frequent premium passengers might only use one or two items and leave the rest behind.

    Service in the first class cabin is on demand and tailored to each passenger. The cabin crew will address the passenger by their name and introduce themselves. They will ask the passenger if they wish to eat or sleep or if they prefer not to be disturbed, which is sometimes the case. They will also bring any amenity kits or requested items and note any special requirements unique to each passenger.

    Industry observers note that this could be their favorite drink or what time they would like to eat. Someone who is not used to first class may be overexcited and want to try everything on the menu and ask for everything that's free. Some passengers may be overly apologetic when asking for something as they feel uncomfortable. Many first-timers like to document their experience with photographs or videos.

    On the other hand, more frequent first class travelers will barely glance at a menu or wine list and will choose decisively what they want and may ask focused questions. They won't just immediately go for the 'best' or the most expensive but may order more traditional items.

    It has been revealed that in general, they are less demanding than those who have been upgraded or paid with points. They are not scared of missing out on something as the flight is very routine for them, and they tend to prioritize sleep on long-haul flights.

    Some passengers like to 'be seen' when seated in a premium cabin, especially if they have not paid in full for it. They will look to see who notices them. Very experienced first class passengers rarely check out the rest of the cabin and usually their presence doesn't need to be acknowledged by other passengers in the cabin, according to an article at Yahoo Travel.

    Cabin crew are used to strange passenger behavior and observing the rules of passenger etiquette in each cabin. They are used to being closely observed by passengers who are in an unfamiliar environment. The fear of missing out on something can be noticeable to the crew, but in general, they don't mind as long as passengers are polite and not entitled. Being over apologetic? The crew don't mind: they are happy for a smile and a thank-you.

    Sources indicate that the cabin crew in premium cabins understand that regular passengers can get overwhelmed by an ultra-luxury experience, and they will understand it and explain things in detail to help out. The passengers tend to observe every detail: how the food is presented, how the wine is poured, and how they are spoken to, as it's all part of the luxury, and they become somewhat enthralled by everything that is going on.

    First class cabins are becoming quite rare these days, although some legacy carriers still have them, whilst other airlines have switched to improvements in premium economy and business class. Premium economy has become the latest business cabin in effect, and business is the new first class cabin. Upgrades to first class are very rare and are more likely to be a points purchase, if not a fully paid fare.

    Most airlines would rather first class seats went empty on flights than to upgrade passengers. This is because it protects their revenue model, and keeping the product exclusive forces people to pay if they want luxury. Giving luxury seats to random economy passengers undercuts the value for high-paying and loyal customers who spent thousands of dollars to sit there.

    In a recent development, cabin crew treat all passengers the same, whatever class they are seated in, but it's how you interact with them that is the most notable thing, and they notice it from the moment they first see you. Eye contact and a smile or a polite greeting are much appreciated. Politeness and please and thank you should not be an exception to the rule, and etiquette is expected.

    Recent findings suggest that A first-class seat comes with many privileges, like lie-flat beds in private suites, the best in fine wines and champagne, caviar service and a wide range of high-quality meals, plated in the galley and on demand. There may well be a designer amenity kit and pajamas to take home.

    A passenger latest to the luxuries of the cabin will probably want to try everything, take things home, and also take lots of photos or videos of their experience. Someone used to traveling first class will likely leave most of the amenities behind. They will either eat something immediately after take-off or avoid food entirely in order to sleep.

    Everything is routine for them, and they know the ropes, so they are often quite undemanding and do not require much attention, whereas upgraded or points passengers tend to want everything available to them. Most crew members don't mind this unless it's too demanding and distracts them from their duties and other passengers.

    According to recent reports, the cabin crew working in the first class cabin have a higher crew-to-passenger ratio. This allows them to tailor the service to each passenger in the cabin, as it is also on demand. They also receive training in silver service and how to operate the seats.

    Sources indicate that although most first class passengers are easy to please, they can also go the other way and assume the crew are their personal servant throughout the flight. It varies. Upgrades to first class are very rare and more likely to be a points purchase, loyalty upgrade, or for a special occasion.
