    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that in late 2023, we saw the opening of the Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport (TQO), in Tulum, Mexico.
    • While it could previously be accessed via Cancun International Airport (CUN), the hope was that by opening a latest international airport, visitor numbers would expand massively.
    • According to recent reports, in 2023, we saw airline after airline announce flights to Tulum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that in late 2023, we saw the opening of the Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport (TQO), in Tulum, Mexico. For those not familiar, Tulum is located on the eastern coast of the Yucatan Peninsula, and for years, it was a growing tourist destination.

    While it could previously be accessed via Cancun International Airport (CUN), the hope was that by opening a latest international airport, visitor numbers would expand massively. Unfortunately what has actually happened is exactly the opposite, as airline after airline has pulled out. What exactly is going on here? I think it makes for an interesting story, and thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this.

    According to recent reports, in 2023, we saw airline after airline announce flights to Tulum. Among US carriers, we saw American, Delta, JetBlue, and United, all launch flights to Tulum, while Spirit announced flights, but never rolled out them.

    That was only a small part of the overall international service to the airport, as we also saw flights to Tulum on Air Canada, Air Transat, Avianca, Copa, Discover, and WestJet, along with flights on domestic carriers like Aeromexico, Mexicana de Aviacion, Viva, and Volaris.

    In a recent development, less than three years after the airport opened, where do things stand? When it comes to international year-round service, we’ve now gone from service to 12 airports, to service to four airports, which is an absolutely massive reduction:.

    Recent findings suggest that just to put this into numbers, in the first half of 2026, the airport saw a 33.2% reduction in passengers. June 2026 was the worst month to date, with a 44.8% drop, as there were just 47,600 passengers, compared to 86,200 passengers the year prior.

    It goes without saying that for a newly built airport, this is rather catastrophic, and not what you hope to see.

    It has been revealed that in some ways, it feels like the whole concept behind Tulum Airport was sort of unnecessary. That’s also easily explained by the fact that the airport was well over a decade in the making, so while I can see how it might’ve seemed like a good idea at some point, tourism trends do evolve over time.

    It has been revealed that the reality is that there was a point where Tulum was cool, edgy, and a bit off the beaten path, compared to… whatever it is now. But when it comes to the struggles that airlines have had with flying to Tulum, it seems like the problems have been endless:.

    It’ll be interesting to see if Tulum can reverse any of these trends, and regain visitors….

    Recent findings suggest that A few years ago Tulum Airport opened to some fanfare, as a good number of airlines rushed to add service there. Unfortunately the excitement didn’t last long, as the airport has gone from a dozen year-round international routes, to just four.

    This reduction in demand particularly evident from the United States, as soon there will just be nonstop service on American and Delta, and even that will be with reduced frequencies and routes.

    Tulum Airport is facing endless challenges, not the least of which is a decline in visitors to Mexico from the United States, combined with increasing competition for those fewer visitors. Mexico just isn’t a value destination in the way that it used to be in places like Cancun, Tulum, Los Cabos, etc., and that’s understandably impacting demand.

    I’m curious if Tulum can find a way to turn things around, but it’s not a good situation.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The blue wave washed over a slew of state legislative chambers and six upcoming governorships.
    • Their vehicle is called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote, no matter which candidate carries each state.
    • John Fund is National Review’s national-affairs reporter.

    The blue wave washed over a slew of state legislative chambers and six upcoming governorships. Next year, a majority of Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governing trifecta. One of the biggest dangers of Democrats’ new political clout is that they will now push to override the Electoral College and effectively force the country into a nationwide presidential popular voting system as early as 2028.

    Their vehicle is called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote, no matter which candidate carries each state. The compact was born after former President George W. Bush’s narrow Electoral College victory in 2000, and it was turbocharged following Donald Trump’s 2016 win despite his losing the popular vote. The District of Columbia and 18 states have joined, accounting for 222 electoral votes.

    John Fund is National Review’s national-affairs reporter.

    Tech Report: Here's the perfect 4-day Cayman Islands itinerary — and how to earn points along the way

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Top-tier resorts, nature excursions and seven-mile stretches of clear water — there's much worth experiencing when visiting the Cayman Islands.
    • According to recent reports, the Cayman Islands’ luxury boom in hotels, restaurants and experiences made it an easy pick for our 2027 Where to Go list.
    • What really makes the Cayman Islands work as a points destination is how every part of your trip, from flights and hotels to dining and activities, can help you earn.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Top-tier resorts, nature excursions and seven-mile stretches of clear water — there's much worth experiencing when visiting the Cayman Islands.

    According to recent reports, the Cayman Islands’ luxury boom in hotels, restaurants and experiences made it an easy pick for our 2027 Where to Go list. But building the right itinerary can be a challenge when there’s so much to enjoy — especially when you're trying to maximize your point earnings and fit everything into a long weekend.

    What really makes the Cayman Islands work as a points destination is how every part of your trip, from flights and hotels to dining and activities, can help you earn.

    That's why TPG and Chase are teaming up to bring travelers everything they need to know to make the most of their trip to the Cayman Islands. Planning and earning are easier with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees), thanks to its recently refreshed benefits, including the annual $100 Chase Travel℠ Hotel Credit, a statement credit of up to $120 back every four years for a TSA PreCheck®, Global Entry or Nexus application fee charged to the card. Cardmembers also enjoy long-standing benefits, including no foreign transaction fees and a comprehensive suite of built-in travel protections.

    Here's how I spent four unforgettable days on the islands, and how you can use your Chase Sapphire Preferred card to do the same.

    Getting to the Cayman Islands is easy, as there are plenty of nonstop flight options to Owen Roberts International Airport (GCM) year-round from major U.S. hubs, including:.

    All three airlines are Chase transfer partners, meaning you can book through the Chase Travel or transfer points to any of these airline loyalty programs.

    It has been revealed that chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Getting to and from the airport is one of my favorite ways to earn some extra points on a trip. With the Chase Sapphire Preferred, you can earn 5 points per dollar on Lyft* if you opt for a ride, or 3 points per dollar on gas station purchases and EV charging if you decide to drive yourself, as I did.

    Either way, don't forget that your Chase Sapphire Preferred card offers a statement credit of up to $120 every four years toward a Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or Nexus application fee. If you choose Global Entry, membership also includes TSA PreCheck, making it easier to breeze through airport security.

    It has been revealed that once you land in Grand Cayman, you will need to take a taxi or book private transportation to your resort. Hotels, resorts and condo properties are not permitted to offer complimentary or in-house airport shuttle services to arriving and departing guests to protect the local taxi and licensed public transit trade. When exiting the airport, simply locate the taxi stand directly outside the main arrivals greeting area for a ride to your hotel.

    The best part of staying in Grand Cayman is that the island has no shortage of luxury hotel options in the Seven Mile Beach area, the ideal home base for island activities and excursions.

    I stayed at the Kimpton Seafire Resort + Spa, which has three on-site restaurants and bars, a Forbes Five-Star spa (trust me, book the massage) and daily yoga and fitness classes overlooking the ocean. The sprawling pool connects directly to Seven Mile Beach, and the hotel regularly hosts events ranging from mixology classes to live Caribbean music, so there is always something to do.

    Other TPG-recommended properties include:.

    Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Cardmembers can book hotels through Chase Travel and receive up to $100 in statement credits each account anniversary year on eligible hotel stays. The cherry on top? After the first $100 in hotel purchases that qualify for the credit, you'll earn 5 points per dollar on additional hotel purchases made through Chase Travel with your Sapphire Preferred card.

    All these recommended properties are part of a wave of luxury hotels elevating the Caribbean escape. Keep an eye out for additional resorts opening in 2027 and beyond, including the highly anticipated Grand Hyatt Grand Cayman Resort & Spa.

    Once you check in and freshen up, head downstairs at Kimpton Seafire to dine at Ave. The Mediterranean-inspired menu has plenty to choose from, and I can say the local snapper ($38) and the Mediterranean orzo salad ($22) were excellent — and don’t skip the creamy mashed potatoes ($9).

    Sources indicate that the cocktails were as beautiful as the sunset you'll watch from their outdoor patio. I sipped a colorful mocktail called the Butterfly Lemonade ($12), made with butterfly pea flower, ginger, rosemary, orange, cinnamon, lemon and soda, while my husband enjoyed the Ponoma, which features Beefeater gin, Dolin dry, grapefruit and hibiscus cordial, lemon and ginger ale. It was a perfect ending to day one.

    Recent findings suggest that spend day two on one of Cayman Island’s most popular and iconic excursions: a boat tour to Stingray City. The famous shallow sandbars on the North Sound sit in water that can only be described as Gatorade blue, where visitors can stand, swim and interact with dozens of friendly, wild southern stingrays. If you don’t feel like getting up close and personal with the rays, you are welcome to soak up the sun and enjoy the views from the boat.

    Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Activities and tours booked through Chase Travel, such as a boat excursion to Stingray City, earn 5 points per dollar when you pay with your Preferred Card.

    For a rooftop sunset dinner, make a reservation at Pom Pom at the neighboring Hotel Indigo, where you can enjoy Caribbean small plates and cocktails with some of the best views Grand Cayman has to offer. Since Hotel Indigo and the Kimpton Seafire are IHG sister properties, you can just take a quick three-minute golf cart ride to get there, no taxi required.

    After a long day in the sun, I sipped on the Raspberry & Chicha Tereré ($13), an alcohol-free refresher that blends yerba mate, raspberry, and purple corn. For food, our server recommended the Picanha ($39), a 10-oz. sirloin cap with a Brazilian vinaigrette and lava salt, and Pollo Anticuchos ($30), chicken skewers with Peruvian chilies puré and chimichurri that had a little kick without being too spicy. For dessert, do not skip the Quatro Leches ($15) cake; it was sweet, light and absolutely delicious. Needless to say, it was one of my favorite meals of the whole trip.

    In a recent development, wake up bright and early and take a taxi to Cayman Crystal Caves, an underground cave system that's part geology lesson, part adventure, and it’s safe for all ages. The caves are accessible through guided tours that last about an hour and a half, and take you through chambers filled with stalactites and stalagmites that formed over millennia.

    Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Transportation expenses such as taxi rides can earn 2 points per dollar with the Chase Sapphire Preferred card, helping you earn bonus points even when you're exploring beyond your hotel or resort.

    If you have time, visit the Queen Elizabeth II Botanical Gardens before heading back to the resort. It has 65 acres of maintained grounds with orchid gardens and woodland trails. You'll wind through native plant collections, endemic species and tropical pathways, home to endangered Grand Cayman Blue Iguanas and other Caribbean-native animals. I’d budget about 90 minutes to wander.

    Industry observers note that for sunset dinner on the beach, head over to Bonny Moon Beach Club. It’s a two-minute walk from the Kimpton, and the restaurant offers seating under their outdoor canopy or directly on the sand. You can’t go wrong with anything on the menu either: flatbreads, ceviches and hummus will all make for delicious accompaniments to another perfect view of the sun setting over the water.

    After a few days full of adventure and sightseeing, I prefer to slow it down on my last full day with a little R&R, and that, of course, includes a trip to the spa. Book a morning treatment at The Spa at Seafire, as I did, and enjoy the Artisan’s Touch massage ($250) or a facial that incorporates locally inspired ingredients and techniques to really lean into the Caribbean vibes. (Ask for Donna if she is available!).

    And of course, take advantage of the included amenities, such as the spa garden, steam room, cold plunge and hot tub.

    In the afternoon, take it easy with a poolside lunch, then head on over to the beach to unwind on a lounger and go for a calming swim in the Caribbean's clear waters.

    Chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: One of my favorite multipliers on the card focuses on dining. You’ll earn 3 points per dollar on dining, whether it’s happy hour at Tillie's or breakfast at Ave.

    For your final night, make your last dinner count at Cocoloba. The beachfront Mexican-inspired restaurant is elevated enough to feel like a celebration, but since it's located at the Kimpton Seafire, you can enjoy the meal and easily head back up to your room to pack and get proper rest before your flight home the next day.

    According to recent reports, after four days spent swimming with stingrays, exploring underground crystal caves and enjoying the Caribbean, leaving was definitely the hardest part. Thankfully, my Chase Sapphire Preferred card helped make the trip home easier. The card's application fee credit for Global Entry helped cover the cost of enrollment, and the program's expedited arrival process meant minimal wait times when we landed. Instead of standing in long lines, we had extra time to enjoy our layover before the final leg of our journey.

    In a recent development, chase Sapphire Preferred editor tip: Back home, my grocery delivery was waiting for me. The Chase Sapphire Preferred can earn 3 points per dollar on online grocery purchases to help make the reset from vacation a little easier.

    The growing number of hotels bookable with points in the Cayman Islands means your points stretch further when you visit. Plus, when you're making the most of everything the islands have to offer, the Chase Sapphire Preferred card makes it easy to earn along the way so you can easily redeem when you’re ready to come back and visit again.

    Learn more: Chase Sapphire Preferred.

    In a recent development, *Valid through Sept. 30, 2027; does not apply to Wait & Save, bike or scooter rides; activation required.

    #30567. FAA’s Flight Shutdown Fuels A $30 Billion Funding Push—Most Of The Money Isn’t Even For Air Traffic Control

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 25m • 📚 Deep Dive (5008 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    FAA’s Flight Shutdown Fuels A $30 Billion Funding Push—Most Of The Money Isn’t Even For Air Traffic Control

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that after the FAA communications breakdown brought departures across the country to a halt on Friday, the travel industry has its answer: give air traffic control another $30 billion.
    • Travel Association states Friday’s ground stop demonstrates that the FAA “lacks the resources necessary to modernize America’s aging aviation infrastructure.” It wants Congress to pass the Modern Skies Act sponsored by Senator Eric Schmitt (R-MO) before the end of this Congress.
    • According to recent reports, that legislation would provide $30.1 billion, including $15 billion for airport terminals.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that after the FAA communications breakdown brought departures across the country to a halt on Friday, the travel industry has its answer: give air traffic control another $30 billion. Most of the money in the bill they’re pushing wouldn’t even go to air traffic control. The U.S. Travel Association claims Friday’s ground stop demonstrates that the FAA “lacks the resources necessary to modernize America’s aging aviation infrastructure.” It wants Congress to pass the Modern Skies Act sponsored by Senator Eric Schmitt (R-MO) before the end of this Congress. That legislation would provide $30.1 billion, including $15 billion for airport terminals. It would leave the FAA running air traffic control under essentially the same institutional structure that’s spent decades failing to deliver promised improvements. We need modern equipment. We also need to modernize the organization buying and operating it. Using this failure to sell airport terminal subsidies does neither particularly well. A Local Equipment Change Disrupted Most Of The National Network The nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern Friday and lasted until 8:15 p.m. The airline recovery took much longer. There were over 18,000 cancellations from Friday through Sunday. Planes and crews wound up in the wrong places. Crew duty limits and missed connections kept the disruption going after communications stabilized. The FAA identifies two sites: a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, where contractor L3Harris was installing a router, and a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas. Excessive connection attempts flooded their ancient private network, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds at 17 of 22 en route centers and spreading into approach control facilities. Blocking the two sites stabilized the network. Officials also disabled the broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers. Some radio frequencies and radar feeds kept working, allowing aircraft already airborne to land. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford describes the work as routine maintenance, separate from the new $12.5 billion modernization program. That makes the question about managing the system day to day even more pressing if it can destabilize the whole system with only the third nationwide ground stop in U.S. history. Most Of The $30 Billion Would Go To Airports John Kefaliotis at Reason Foundation breaks down the spending. The introduced bill, S. 5572: Purpose Funding Terminal rebuilding pilot for up to three airports $10 billion Other airport terminal grants $5 billion Discretionary airport improvement grants $3 billion Common automation platform and controller workstation $7.2 billion Cloud computing and associated telecommunications $2 billion Air traffic control facilities, including digital towers $2 billion Air traffic flow management technology $600 million Consolidating terminal air traffic control facilities $300 million That’s $12.1 billion for air traffic control systems and facilities, versus $18 billion for airports. About 40% goes to air traffic control. The administration’s announcement includes building airports, but the sales pitch after Friday’s failure is that Congress needs to fund the air traffic control fix. The $10 billion terminal pilot is particularly brazen. It would cover up to 90% of costs at no more than three medium hub airports. Eligibility requires a principal terminal built before 1990 that hasn’t undergone comprehensive redevelopment since then, plus a project with environmental review complete and final design underway. The Transportation Secretary picks the recipients. The bill’s sponsor is a Missouri senator. At St. Louis airport last month, Duffy was asked whether the program appeared tailor made for the airport’s single terminal project. His answer: “That’s a fair assessment.” It’s not even clear whether other airports even qualify given the Rube Goldbergesque rules in the bill. It’s pure pork barrel spending. The same local report notes that Southwest Airlines, which operates more than half of Lambert’s flights, would otherwise bear the largest share of the terminal project’s cost. Moving that bill to federal taxpayers is a windfall for Southwest. The separate $3 billion airport grant pot also bypasses normal allocation formulas and minimum shares. Politicians get more discretion over where the money goes. Bundling that with air traffic control improvements makes it easier to portray objections to the airport spending as opposition to aviation safety. The FAA Has Already Been Spending Billions Congress provided roughly $12.5 billion in the One Substantial Beautiful Bill Act last year, also from taxpayers rather than airlines and passengers. That came on top of billions in earlier modernization spending largely lit on fire. The Transportation Department’s inspector general reports that the FAA spent more than $15 billion on NextGen through the end of 2024. The effort began in 2003, with completion originally envisioned for 2025. Major capabilities slipped to 2030 or later, costs rose, and the agency reduced what it would deliver. There are improvements underway. Duffy says 69% of copper communications have been replaced and electronic flight strips are installed at 25 towers. But he also acknowledged the FAA’s history during Saturday’s briefing: “They haven’t spent the money well.” Secretary Sean Duffy’s November 14 briefing on the ground stop and modernization funding The FAA set out a initiative in 1983 “to equip 150 to 250 airport control towers by 2000.” They went way over budget and didn’t accomplish much. Meanwhile, all of Nav Canada facilities went electronic 15 years ago (and all control towers and TRACONs even earlier). Their solution is used in Australia, Italy, the U.K. and Dubai. We could license the Canadian solution, or other commercial ones, but instead the FAA has been contracting for their own solution since three years before the Beastie Boys were fighting for your right to party. Wait until you explain paper flight strips!https://t.co/fyU7aSILWr pic.twitter.com/gOBIHME3oK — gary leff (@garyleff) July 2, 2023 Modernize The Organization That Runs Air Traffic Control When I reviewed the administration’s plan in May 2025, my concern was that the same institution that had failed to deliver for decades would be asked to execute another enormous upgrade, faster, without fixing its underlying incentives. And there wasn’t a plan to make real changes there. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA has operated since 1996 as a private nonprofit without equity shareholders. It funds operations and capital investment through customer charges and issuing bonds for long-term investments. Transport Canada regulates its safety. Commercial airlines elect four of its 15 directors. Government, employees, general aviation and independent directors also have roles. There’s no need to hand the system to an airline monopoly to get it out of congressional budgeting. The FAA, by contrast, regulates itself – which is a recipe for unaccountability. An outside regulator would have a clearer job: demand safe performance from an operator whose failures it isn’t also responsible for defending.     The bill’s sponsor is a Missouri senator. At St. Louis airport last month, Duffy was asked whether the program appeared tailor made for the airport’s single terminal project. His answer: “That’s a fair assessment.”.

    It has been revealed that it’s not even clear whether other airports even qualify given the Rube Goldbergesque rules in the bill. It’s pure pork barrel spending. The same local report notes that Southwest Airlines, which operates more than half of Lambert’s flights, would otherwise bear the largest share of the terminal project’s cost. Moving that bill to federal taxpayers is a windfall for Southwest. The separate $3 billion airport grant pot also bypasses normal allocation formulas and minimum shares. Politicians get more discretion over where the money goes. Bundling that with air traffic control improvements makes it easier to portray objections to the airport spending as opposition to aviation safety. The FAA Has Already Been Spending Billions Congress provided roughly $12.5 billion in the One Substantial Beautiful Bill Act last year, also from taxpayers rather than airlines and passengers. That came on top of billions in earlier modernization spending largely lit on fire. The Transportation Department’s inspector general reports that the FAA spent more than $15 billion on NextGen through the end of 2024. The effort began in 2003, with completion originally envisioned for 2025. Major capabilities slipped to 2030 or later, costs rose, and the agency reduced what it would deliver. There are improvements underway. Duffy states 69% of copper communications have been replaced and electronic flight strips are installed at 25 towers.     #30566. Calls for Nvidia probes, new chip export limits intensify

    Calls for Nvidia probes, new chip export limits intensify

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.
    • Industry observers note that huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech firm and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S.
    • According to recent reports, senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

    Industry observers note that huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech firm and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

    According to recent reports, senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

    “I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune remarked, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

    Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”.

    “The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., stated at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”.

    “We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries noted. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”.

    The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

    Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

    Industry observers note that “The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar stated. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”.

    Industry observers note that last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar said that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

    Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

    It has been revealed that moolenaar also mentioned that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

    “We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar noted. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole newly introduced light on that discussion.”.

    Sources indicate that also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns.".

    Sources indicate that A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

    However, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

    Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

    “The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he said.

    Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

    “There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu noted.

    It has been revealed that mast stated the Huang revelations could give newly introduced momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the concern came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

    In a recent development, “Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast noted. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”.

    Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

    In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

    The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

    Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

    The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

    Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”.

    Industry observers note that “If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”.

    Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, noted his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”.

    On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”.

    “This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

    Industry observers note that in a statement Thursday, Warren noted that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

    Industry observers note that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an upgrade on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

    According to recent reports, savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

    #30564. Delta CEO: “Customers Are Not Choosing Airlines Based On Wi-Fi”

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1232 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Delta CEO: “Customers Are Not Choosing Airlines Based On Wi-Fi”

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1232 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’ve gotta be honest, I don’t envy the situation that Delta CEO Ed Bastian is in.
    • In theory that’s fine, except Amazon Leo is years behind Starlink, and just faced a fresh setback, due to a rocket failure.
    • Recent findings suggest that there’s now an interesting patch, as Bastian made some comments about the carrier’s Wi-Fi choice, and overall customer preferences.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’ve gotta be honest, I don’t envy the situation that Delta CEO Ed Bastian is in. Unlike most other carriers in the United States, Delta hasn’t opted for SpaceX Starlink Wi-Fi, and has instead gone with Amazon Leo.

    In theory that’s fine, except Amazon Leo is years behind Starlink, and just faced a fresh setback, due to a rocket failure. Elon Musk has also repeatedly publicly ridiculed Bastian, regarding what Bastian reportedly said about Musk to employees.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s now an interesting patch, as Bastian made some comments about the carrier’s Wi-Fi choice, and overall customer preferences. It sure is amazing how narratives can change, based on what’s convenient….

    Sources indicate that this week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum 2026, Delta’s CEO was asked about the carrier’s decision not to choose Starlink, plus the public spat with Musk. Here’s what Bastian had to say about this:.

    Sources indicate that “We’ve been the leader in Wi-Fi, and in free and fast Wi-Fi, and we’ve been at it for five years. I’ve got a long history with Elon on that. We’ve looked at Starlink, we actually helped them started in aviation, we gave them our planes to use during COVID, when we weren’t flying, and they tested the system out. We just couldn’t come to agreement on a business model.”.

    According to recent reports, “We’ve been the leader in free, fast Wi-Fi. We are confident there will be more than one LEO product in the world other than Starlink, and I’m confident Amazon has the capability to do a great job. Customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi. We’ve been out with a great product from Viasat, which we’ve got two newly introduced satellites in the sky. It’s not Starlink caliber but it’s pretty darn close.”.

    “This is about the total experience, and customers are not choosing airlines based on the Wi-Fi.”At the #F500Innovation Forum, @Delta CEO Ed Bastian told @ajs that the airline helped Elon Musk’s satellite Wi-Fi “get started in aviation,” but the two sides “just couldn’t come to… pic.twitter.com/xmSERJNjjH.

    Look, before I get too deep into this, let me make several points that I think no one reasonable will disagree with (which is not to say some commenters won’t disagree!):.

    When Bastian formally unveiled prepares for free Wi-Fi at CES 2023 in Las Vegas, he remarked the following:.

    It has been revealed that “At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different. Our vision has long been to deliver an experience at 30,000 feet that feels similar to what our customers have available on the ground.”.

    “We didn’t just want free Wi-Fi to offer base-level service – we wanted it to be transformative for the entire onboard experience. It is imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home, and we’ve put this system through meticulous tests to make that possible.”.

    Any reasonable person could agree that:.

    Earlier this year, when announcing aims to partner with Amazon Leo for connectivity, Bastian stated that “we need to stay the leader” in inflight connectivity. Obviously that won’t be the case for a long time.

    As I see it, Delta’s problem here is pretty simple. Customers absolutely notice a difference between Viasat and Starlink. The concern isn’t that people will stop flying Delta altogether. The issue is that Delta has built its entire brand on being the industry leader, and on being on the forefront of technology.

    There’s no denying that this sentiment among the public changes over time, because inflight Wi-Fi is easily one of the top amenities that passengers notice nowadays. Seriously, I can’t count the number of people I’ve heard from or just overheard talking about their first Starlink experience, and how blown away they were.

    I guess to look at it from another angle, there’s no airline that loves talking about how premium it is more than Delta. What makes Delta premium? If we’re going to believe that Delta is premium, it’s not based on any one single thing, but rather, it’s based on the sum of the experience. And I think anyone who thinks a major Wi-Fi disadvantage lasting for years isn’t part of what contributes to consumer sentiment is lying to themselves.

    Delta CEO Ed Bastian is now downplaying the importance of inflight Wi-Fi. He’s arguing that “customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi,” which in isolation, is probably true. But he’s also arguing that Viasat is “pretty darn close” to Starlink, which is most definitely not true, as I see it.

    I wouldn’t be so critical of these statements if it weren’t for Bastian spending years hyping up how it’s “imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home,” while also saying “we need to stay the leader.” And for that matter, Delta has of course also long hyped how premium it is — if that’s to be believed, it’s not about any one feature, but instead, it’s about the sum of the experience.

    What do you make of Bastian’s inflight connectivity comments?

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • British Airways charges most members £50 per transaction to give Avios to someone else, and each transfer tops out at 60,000 points.
    • You can move British Airways Avios into a Finnair account, and Finnair charges €10 to transfer Avios to another member.
    • According to recent reports, I’ve written about moving Avios between airline programs to get the best redemption deal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    British Airways charges most members £50 per transaction to give Avios to someone else, and each transfer tops out at 60,000 points. Move the same points through Finnair and you can give someone 100,000 Avios for a single €10 fee. You can move British Airways Avios into a Finnair account, and Finnair charges €10 to transfer Avios to another member. I’ve written about moving Avios between airline programs to get the best redemption deal. The same flexibility lets you choose which program’s rules to use when giving points to another person. For two people with British Airways balances, the process is: Each person links their own British Airways and Finnair accounts. Names and email addresses need to match within each person’s accounts, and both programs need two-factor authentication enabled. The United States, which created and sustained that order, increasingly regards its maintenance as an excessive burden. The revolutionary, the reformer, and the reluctant guardian have become, in different ways, revisionists.

    A very small international airline plans to add long haul, international flights to the United States as of next spring, and I feel pretty confident in saying that 99% of people have never heard of this airline (I had to look it up after seeing one of their planes at an airport several weeks back, and I know a thing or two about identifying airplanes). 😉.

    Industry observers note that as reported by AeroRoutes, as of May 1, 2027, Parata Air will launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Los Angeles (LAX). The flight will operate with the following schedule:.

    WE301 Incheon to Los Angeles departing 12:00PM arriving 7:20AMWE302 Los Angeles to Incheon departing 9:50AM arriving 3:20PM (+1 days).

    Parata Air will operate the route with an Airbus A330-200, featuring 260 seats, including 18 business class seats and 242 economy seats. The 5,944-mile flight is blocked at 11hr40min eastbound and 13hr30min westbound.

    Tickets on the flight are now on sale, and I see fares starting at around $670 one-way in economy, and around $2,500 one-way in business class. Those aren’t exactly terribly attractive fares for a newcomer that appears to have a pretty lackluster onboard product.

    Recent findings suggest that for those not familiar with Parata Air, the airline released operations back in 2019, but it has a fleet of just a handful of planes, including three Airbus A330s and two Airbus A320s. This will be the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. As I hinted at in the headline, I imagine this is a fully unknown player to most people, and I had never heard of the airline until a few weeks ago.

    Random thought — can anyone think of a smaller international airline (in terms of fleet size) that added long haul flights to the United States? I know that’s very specific, but I can’t think of another one… it’s possible I’m missing something, though!

    The airline acquired its three A330s secondhand from different sources, with the planes having flown for Garuda Indonesia, Hainan Airlines, and Thomas Cook (though that plane doesn’t have business class).

    The Seoul Incheon to Los Angeles market is pretty well served in terms of capacity, but not so well served in terms of competition. That’s because no US carrier flies between Los Angeles and Seoul Incheon, and with Korean Air having acquired Asiana, there’s now only one South Korean flag carrier.

    If you look at the market, you’ll see that Korean Air operates up to four daily flights, and Air Premia operates up to two daily flights. Now we’ll see a third airline from the country operating in the market, though with the lowest capacity, and arguably the worst product.

    In a recent development, it’ll be interesting to see when we see some competition here on the US side. Delta might operate the route eventually, but that doesn’t actually increase competition, since the airline has a joint venture with Korean Air. American has (smartly, probably) given up on Los Angeles as a long haul hub. So that leaves United, and I could definitely see the airline eventually adding service in the market, as a competitive response against Delta and Korean Air, if nothing else.

    As of May 2027, Parata Air will be launching a fresh nonstop route between Seoul Incheon and Los Angeles, representing the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. The airline will be operating daily in the market with Airbus A330s. With this, there will be three South Korean carriers flying this route, though no airlines from the United States.

    In a recent development, saudia is the fourth-largest airline operating flights between the United Kingdom and the Middle East. The airline has been reviewing its UK network in recent years. In fact, earlier this year, it discontinued services to Birmingham and London Gatwick. With that being stated, the SkyTeam member now appears to be considering a new UK destination.

    This time, to the Scottish capital, Edinburgh. According to Airport Coordination Limited's (ACL) Edinburgh Summer 2027 Initial Coordination Report, Saudia has secured slots at Edinburgh Airport (EDI) for the upcoming summer season. If the airline proceeds with the planned service, it will become its third UK destination.

    According to the ACL report, Saudia has requested slots for four weekly flights to Edinburgh, using its 110-seat Airbus A320 aircraft. However, securing slots does not necessarily mean that the airline will operate the flights as planned. The aircraft type could also change, as airlines can revise their planned equipment after slots have been allocated.

    Sources indicate that given the distance involved and the range limitations of a typical A320, operating the route with this aircraft would be unusual. One possible alternative is the Airbus A321XLR, which airlines are increasingly using on long-haul routes with relatively limited passenger demand.

    According to ch-aviation data, the Saudi flag carrier presently operates five A321XLRs and is awaiting deliveries of another ten aircraft. It could therefore consider deploying the extra-long-range narrowbody on the Edinburgh route instead of the A320. In fact, Saudia already uses the A321XLR on its service between Jeddah’s King Abdulaziz International Airport (JED) and Manchester Airport (MAN).

    Sources indicate that interestingly, the 110-seat A320 is no stranger to the UK. Saudia previously deployed the aircraft on its service between Neom Bay Airport (NUM) and London Gatwick Airport (LGW). The airline at the moment has seven A320s in this configuration and regularly uses them on several European routes.

    According to scheduled data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, Saudia will deploy the aircraft on nine of its European routes in December, most of which originate from Jeddah. These include services to Barcelona, Rome Fiumicino, Frankfurt, Geneva, Istanbul, Munich and Zurich.

    The airline will also use the 110-seat A320 on its flights from Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport (RUH) to Rome Fiumicino and Geneva. Apart from this, the SkyTeam member also operates its 188-seat Airbus A321neo on some European routes and regularly deploys the A321XLR, which accommodates 144 passengers.

    Nevertheless, it will be interesting to see whether Saudia goes ahead with its intends to serve Edinburgh. At the moment, there are no nonstop flights between the Scottish capital and Saudi Arabia, meaning passengers have to travel via other airports, such as Doha, Dubai, Istanbul, or London Heathrow. Indeed, there is certainly demand for travel between the UK and Saudi Arabia. In 2025, more than 1.76 million passengers traveled between the two countries.

    According to Cirium data, four airlines have scheduled flights between the two countries for 2027; Saudia is by far the largest operator in the market. The airline serves four routes, three of which connect London Heathrow Airport (LHR) with King Fahd International Airport (DMM) in Dammam, RUH, and JED. The fourth connects Jeddah with MAN.

    London Heathrow – Dammam (3x weekly).

    London Heathrow – Riyadh (Up to 3x daily).

    London Heathrow – Jeddah (Up to 3x daily).

    London Heathrow – Riyadh (Daily).

    Manchester – Riyadh (3x weekly).

    Recent findings suggest that london Heathrow – Riyadh (Daily from Jan. 11).

    London Heathrow – Red Sea International (3x weekly)**.

In addition, the all-business-class carrier beOnd had planned to launch three weekly nonstop flights between Red Sea International Airport (RSI) and London Heathrow on December 15, 2026.     Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.
    • The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.
    • Recent findings suggest that and it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

    The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

    Recent findings suggest that and it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

    It has been revealed that it joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

    Recent findings suggest that her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

    The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

    According to recent reports, the GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

    Sources indicate that the House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

    It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

    Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

    “The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds notable efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

    It has been revealed that the Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

    The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tunisia is about to have a big year.
    • In a recent development, the latter will also draw “Star Wars” fans to many of the Tatooine filming locations to mark the franchise’s 50th anniversary of the movie’s release in 2027.
    • This 7-day itinerary covers a tour of Tunisia’s most crucial cultural and historic landmarks in a road trip from Tunis to Tozeur and back, plus tips for where to be during the 2027 eclipse and how to maximize the perks and benefits of the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) along the way.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tunisia is about to have a big year. On the morning of Aug. 2, 2027, a total solar eclipse will cut a path across the central part of the North African nation, bringing several minutes of darkness to sites like the ancient Roman amphitheater in El Jem, the Great Mosque of Kairouan and the dramatic Sahara Desert dunes and canyons surrounding Tozeur.

    In a recent development, the latter will also draw “Star Wars” fans to many of the Tatooine filming locations to mark the franchise’s 50th anniversary of the movie’s release in 2027. The capital of Tunis isn’t in the path of totality, but any trip in 2027 should also include a stop in the picturesque cliffside village of Sidi Bou Said, which UNESCO recently added to its World Heritage list, joining other culturally significant sites like the Medina of Tunis and the Archaeological Site of Carthage.

    This 7-day itinerary covers a tour of Tunisia’s most crucial cultural and historic landmarks in a road trip from Tunis to Tozeur and back, plus tips for where to be during the 2027 eclipse and how to maximize the perks and benefits of the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) along the way.

    At the moment, there are no nonstop flights between the United States and Tunisia, so you’ll need to proposal for at least one layover before connecting to Tunis-Carthage International Airport (TUN), the country’s largest airport.

    According to recent reports, I flew to TUN on Air France via Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), since I’m loyal to the SkyTeam alliance and it offered the most frequent connections. However, if you’re loyal to another airline alliance, you can also find connections to TUN on Lufthansa via Frankfurt, ITA via Rome, Royal Air Maroc via Casablanca and Turkish Airlines via Istanbul.

    Sources indicate that chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: When booking flights, check the Chase Travel℠ portal to see what routes and airlines are available to book using the Points Boost feature. I found several business-class fares offering the maximum Points Boost value of 2 cents per point. I ultimately transferred 142,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Air France-KLM Flying Blue after finding an amazing round-trip business-class fare directly on the Air France website, yielding a value of 5.83 cents per mile.

    It has been revealed that I landed in Tunis around 5 p.m. after a red-eye flight from Newly introduced York and a relaxed connection in Paris.

    It has been revealed that A pre-arranged car transfer whisked me to the Four Seasons Hotel Tunis, a luxury beachfront resort in the suburb of Gammarth, about 30 minutes from the airport. Upon arrival, staff greeted me warmly and took me directly to my upgraded Deluxe Sea-View Room for an in-room check-in. The spacious room had a balcony overlooking the Mediterranean, a walk-in closet and a marble bathroom with a separate tub and a shower.

    After a quick rinse, I wandered down to Blu, the hotel’s alfresco poolside restaurant, where I enjoyed a refreshing salad of a soft local cheese, tomatoes, onions and peppers served with a glass of Tunisian rosé. Since it was my first day in the country, the friendly staff made sure I tried some spicy Tunisian harissa, a smoky chili paste drizzled in olive oil that I sopped up with fluffy squares of focaccia.

    Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Book the Four Seasons Hotel Tunis through The Edit to use one of the twice-annual, up-to-$250 credits toward prepaid hotel stays of two or more nights reserved through Chase Travel. By booking through The Edit, I also received other perks like complimentary hotel breakfast for two and up to $100 property credit, which I used for meals but could have used toward spa treatments like the ceremonial hammam experience, which comes out to approximately $100.

    According to recent reports, since I only had one full day in Tunis, I headed out bright and early for a private tour of the capital’s major sites, booked through Chase Travel with Didon Tours. My guide, Baligh, and a private driver picked me up for a full 8-hour day that included lunch and fascinating storytelling about the city’s ancient and modern history and politics.

    To beat the cruise groups and midday heat, we visited the ancient ruins of Carthage first, taking in the views from Byrsa Hill before heading down to the circular Punic port and the massive seaside complex of the Baths of Antoninus.

    From there, we drove to the charming blue-and-white village of Sidi Bou Said, Tunisia’s newest UNESCO World Heritage site, for fresh juice and almond cakes at Cafe des Delices and iconic views of the beach below. While we didn’t have much time to browse the cliffside town’s shops, I did pick up some handmade souvenirs at the ceramic store at 16 Rue Habib Thameur.

    For lunch, we stopped in the coastal suburb of Le Goulette at Restaurant La Victoire for a traditional Tunisian meal of brick à l’oeuf, a deep-fried pastry stuffed with egg, tuna and onion and a freshly grilled dorade fish served with rice and carrots.

    Next, we turned inland toward the western side of the city to visit the Bardo Museum, set in a former palace and home to the world’s largest collection of Roman mosaics. (Don’t miss the mosaic of the Roman poet Virgil, flanked by the muses of history and tragedy, as it’s considered to be the Mona Lisa of Tunisia.).

    Finally, we hit the medina of Tunis, where we visited the courtyard of the Zitouna Mosque and made a quick pass through the souk's meandering lanes before returning to the hotel for a much-deserved swim in the indoor pool and a nap before a quiet room-service dinner.

    Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Earn 8 points per dollar spent on Chase Travel purchases, including activities and tours like the one I booked. Those with more time can add another day in Tunis and split this itinerary into two for a more relaxed pace in each location.

    Around midday, I returned to the airport to pick up a rental car from Avis and set the GPS to drive two hours south to Kairouan, a UNESCO-recognized city famous for its picturesque medina and Great Mosque, which dates to the 9th century AD. While Kairouan is considered one of the holy cities of Islam, film buffs may recognize it from “Raiders of the Lost Ark,” where it stood in for 1930s Cairo. It lies along the northern boundary of the 2027 solar eclipse’s path of totality.

    La Kasbah Hotel, booked via Chase Travel, provided a soft landing with its private parking lot, pool and strong air conditioning. The shops and sites in the medina tend to close in the late afternoon, so if you arrive after then, plan on a quiet night in the hotel, cooling off in the pool or lounging on woven rugs in its vintage café, drinking mint tea.

    Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Pay for car rentals with Chase Sapphire Reserve to receive primary auto rental coverage (just be sure to decline the agency's collision insurance). Though I didn’t end up needing it, I had peace of mind knowing I was covered for up to $75,000 of theft or collision damage to the rental car.

    It has been revealed that having arrived the previous afternoon after the mosque closed, I went first thing the next morning to admire the column-lined courtyard and three-tiered minaret before the tour groups arrived. The ticket to the mosque also included admission to the nearby Sidi Abid el Ghariani Mausoleum, built in the Moorish style with black and white marble arches. A few doors down, I stopped by the former home of the governor of Kairouan, an ornately decorated mansion that now serves as a rug shop. While I wasn’t in the market for a carpet, I enjoyed the architecture and left with a handwoven scarf for 40 dinars ($14).

    After checking out, I hit the road again for the 4.5-hour drive south to Tozeur, a city in the heart of the Sahara Desert. Though I drove straight through, making brief stops at gas stations along the way, it’s also possible to break up the drive with stops at either the well-preserved archaeological site of Sbeitla or the Roman baths of Gafsa.

    Sources indicate that just be mindful of timing: I wouldn’t recommend driving at night. Though the roads are well-maintained, speed bumps are common and harder to spot after dark.

    Once in Tozeur, I checked into Dar Saida Beya, a traditional Tunisian guesthouse, booked through Chase Travel. After a long drive, I had a quiet evening to walk around and explore the nearby old town center.

    Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Though the upscale Mora Sahara Tozeur resort west of town isn’t bookable via Chase Travel presently, it’s still possible to earn 4 points per dollar spent on direct hotel bookings made with the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

    The Atlas Mountains meet the salt flats and sands of the Sahara Desert in Tozeur, creating an otherworldly landscape that inspired many film directors. Most notably, the canyons and dunes around Tozeur served as the filming location for the desert planet of Tatooine in the “Star Wars” movies. The epic sci-fi series is celebrating the 50th anniversary of its release in 2027, and fans can experience the eclipse from here, since Tozeur falls along the southern boundary of the path of totality.

    According to recent reports, I booked a 7-hour tour with Attractive Discoveries via Chase Travel to see everything the area had to offer. Before diving into the area’s cinematic legacy, my driver and guide, Firas, began the day at Chebika Oasis, where a 45-minute hike wound through the ruins of a former Berber village and down to the oasis and its waterfall.

    Our next stop was the Grand Canyon of Tunisia, Mides Canyon, roughly a mile from the Algerian border and featured in films like “The English Patient.” During the 30-minute hike along the dry riverbed, I spotted no fewer than six falcons diving in and out of the cliff face while hunting.

    It has been revealed that to avoid the worst heat of the day, the tour included a break from 1 to 5 p.m., during which we stopped to pick some dates from my guide’s family’s oasis of palm trees. I also tried a makloub sandwich filled with chicken, cheese and harissa and took a short nap.

    At 5 p.m. on the dot, Firas picked me up again in his 4x4 to head out into the desert to watch the sunset over the dunes. Along our drive, we spotted a herd of camels, stopped to climb the Ong Jmal or “Camel’s Neck” rock formation and did some adrenaline-inducing 4x4 driving. We arrived at the remaining film sets that served as the desert trading post of Mos Espa in “The Phantom Menace” just before sunset.

    To cap off the day, we drank fresh mint tea with almonds — a local treat — and watched the sun set behind the dunes before heading back into town.

    Recent findings suggest that chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Put the card's up to $300 annual credit to work on travel purchases like the tour I booked. The credit is applied automatically to eligible purchases each account anniversary year.

    The biggest Star Wars fans may want to stay another day to visit other nearby filming locations, such as Sidi Bouhlel Canyon and the Lars family homestead exterior near the town of Nefta.

    Recent findings suggest that since I had another 4.5-hour drive ahead of me that day, I left around 11 a.m. to drive back north to the city of El Jem via Chott el Djerid. Before heading off across the massive salt lake, I filled up my gas tank and packed snacks for the long drive since there aren’t many places to stop in the first couple of hours.

    Built about 1,800 years ago, the Roman amphitheater of El Jem is roughly 70% the size of Rome’s amphitheater but has significantly fewer crowds and offers wide-open access to each level — even the underground level where animals were kept before they fought gladiators.

    According to recent reports, after checking into Hotel Julius, booked through Chase Travel, I dropped my bags and took the five-minute walk to the amphitheater before it closed. The 20 dinar ($7) ticket includes entrance to both the amphitheater and the nearby El Jem Archaeological Museum on the same day. Since I arrived a little later in the afternoon, I went to the museum first thing the next morning and justified the extra $7 by spending a leisurely morning taking in the incredibly detailed mosaics without being rushed.

    El Jem falls within the path of totality for the 2027 solar eclipse, so history buffs may want to make this city their home base for the celestial event.

    Chase Sapphire Reserve editor tip: Tunisia is still a predominantly cash-based society, so it may be hard to find restaurants that accept cards. I couldn’t earn 3 points per dollar spent on dining worldwide with my Chase Sapphire Reserve in El Jem, but the two fricassee (fried dough buns stuffed with egg, tuna, potato and harissa) I ordered at a street food stall on the way back from the amphitheater only cost 7 cents total (yes, really), so I wasn’t worried about missing out on too many points.

    After checking out the museum, I loaded up my rental car one last time for the two-hour drive back to Tunis. Those with more time and desire to sit on the beach than I did could easily add a day or two in the coastal town of Hammamet, which sits about two-thirds of the way back to Tunis from El Jem.

    Once I handed off my rental car keys at the airport, I met the taxi driver I had prearranged with my final hotel, Dar Ben Gacem, a traditional guesthouse in the Tunis medina. Since my tour of Tunis at the beginning of the trip only included a brief visit to the medina, I was glad to have the rest of the afternoon and evening to poke around the shops and alleys of the historic city center and do some final souvenir shopping before flying home the next day.

    Recent findings suggest that keep in mind that most stalls in the medina are open from around 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with more closed on Fridays and Sundays, so plan your visit accordingly. (Plus, many restaurants are closed for dinner on Sunday nights as well.).

    Though some flights depart in the evening, I opted to take a connecting flight back to Paris in the morning and stay an extra night to avoid a rushed final day.

    In a recent development, during my week-long road trip, I explored Tunisia’s ancient ruins, UNESCO-recognized Islamic architecture and otherworldly desert landscapes, many of which lie in the path of totality of the 2027 solar eclipse. Booking through Chase Travel maximized my Ultimate Rewards earnings, while the card benefits helped offset travel expenses along the way, like the $300 annual travel credit on tours, The Edit perks and $250 statement credit at the Four Seasons and primary rental car coverage through Avis. When I returned to Latest York, I was glad I had enrolled in Global Entry before my trip. The Sapphire Reserve's $120 Global Entry application fee statement credit helped offset the cost, and the program made reentering the U.S. much easier.

    Learn more: Chase Sapphire Reserve.
