    #30542. Lufthansa’s A380 Business Class Seat Retrofit Nearly Done, But It Isn’t Allegris

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1289 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Lufthansa’s A380 Business Class Seat Retrofit Nearly Done, But It Isn’t Allegris

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In January 2026, Lufthansa formally declared looks to retrofit its Airbus A380s with latest business class seats.
    • There’s now a positive update, as it looks like Lufthansa is running way ahead on that schedule, and all A380s should be retrofitted within the coming weeks….
    • Lufthansa is introducing a new business class product on its entire fleet of eight Airbus A380s.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In January 2026, Lufthansa formally declared looks to retrofit its Airbus A380s with latest business class seats. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026, and Lufthansa had committed to retrofitting all the planes by the middle of 2027.

    There’s now a positive update, as it looks like Lufthansa is running way ahead on that schedule, and all A380s should be retrofitted within the coming weeks….

    Lufthansa is introducing a new business class product on its entire fleet of eight Airbus A380s. Rather interestingly, it’s only business class that’s getting new seats, while first class, premium economy, and economy, remain the same, aside from some minor upgrades (like improved inflight entertainment).

    The first A380 with latest interiors entered service in April 2026, and AeroRoutes flags how as of December 18, 2026, Lufthansa is exclusively showing the new business class configuration on all routes. So starting in the coming weeks, you can expect the entire A380 network to feature the new cabins.

    Recent findings suggest that lufthansa A380s are based in Munich (MUC), and at the moment fly to Bangkok (BKK), Delhi (DEL), Los Angeles (LAX), Mumbai (BOM), San Francisco (SFO), and Washington (IAD). As you’d expect, there’s seasonal variation in the routes, though.

    What’s interesting is that Lufthansa isn’t introducing its latest Allegris business class on these planes, but instead, is introducing another “off the shelf” product. Specifically, the airline has opted for the Thompson Aero Vantage XL product, which is in a staggered configuration.

    Each seat has direct aisle access, seat width of 58cm, and a bed length of at least two meters. Seats feature bluetooth connectivity and flexible partitions. Lufthansa is calling this “Premium XXL,” which… I’m not sure if that’s supposed to describe the seat, or if Lufthansa is taking some liberties on a newly introduced Grindr profile, somehow turning Vantage XL into Premium XXL.

    As A380s are reconfigured, the business class cabin is shrinking in size by 10 seats, going from 78 seats to 68 seats. First class continues to have eight seats, premium economy continues to have 52 seats, and economy continues to have 371 seats.

    It’s pretty cool to note how Lufthansa has reversed course on the A380. At the beginning of the pandemic, Lufthansa grounded its fleet of Airbus A380s, and the intent was that these planes would be retired, and would only reenter service “in the event of an unexpectedly rapid market recovery.”.

    With the strong recovery we’ve seen in transatlantic leisure demand, the airline made the decision to start bringing back Airbus A380s as of the summer of 2023, and eight of the initial 14 are now back in service (six of them were sold). At first, the return of the A380s was mostly described as a temporary measure, in light of delayed Boeing 777-9 deliveries. The airline didn’t commit to keeping these planes around in the long run, though that changed over time.

    Sources indicate that in recent years it has become clear that the A380 will have a long term place in Lufthansa’s fleet. Clearly this investment in the business class product reflects that.

    It has been revealed that lufthansa of course has its new Allegris cabins, including the new Allegris business class and new Allegris first class. These cabins debuted on newly delivered Airbus A350-900s, and we’re also seeing them on newly delivered Boeing 787-9s (though without first class).

    Sources indicate that so why is Lufthansa not installing its fresh Allegris seats on the A380s? Well, I’d assume it comes down to a couple of factors. The biggest reason is quite straightforward — Lufthansa has had a really tough time getting its new Allegris seats certified, and these seats need to be certified on each individual aircraft. The idea is that by picking an “off the shelf” product, these seats are already certified, and therefore the airline could actually rely on getting them into service immediately.

    Second of all, I imagine that given the narrower fuselage of the A380 upper deck, it might’ve required even more complicated customization to fit the fresh Allegris seats up there.

    Recent findings suggest that for once, I’d say Lufthansa made a wise decision by just picking a generic product for its A380s. I think the significant mystery is why Lufthansa just didn’t do this for its other planes, to avoid this entire mess. Separately, Lufthansa is reconfiguring its Boeing 747-8s, in a complicated two-part process. Initially, we’ll see the latest Allegris business class seats on the lower deck, while the same business class seats will remain on the upper deck.

    Lufthansa is wrapping up the process of introducing a latest business class product on its Airbus A380s. The first plane with new cabins entered service in April 2026. While the initial initiative was for all planes to be reconfigured as of the middle of 2027, it looks like that project will instead wrap up by December 2026, which is amazing.

    Rather than installing the latest Allegris business class seats, the airline is instead installing a more generic product, the Thompson Aero Vantage XL seat, which is a significant improvement over the product you’ll otherwise find on these jets. As planes are reconfigured, business class capacity is being reduced by 10 seats, from 78 to 68.

    According to recent reports, lufthansa sure is all over the place when it comes to modernizing its cabins. Either way, this change is good to see.

    What do you make of Lufthansa’s newly introduced A380 business class?

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.
    • Industry observers note that chase is adding Qantas and Cathay Pacific as 1:1 transfer partners on November 18.
    • These are Chase’s first newly introduced airline transfer partners in more than five years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

    Industry observers note that chase is adding Qantas and Cathay Pacific as 1:1 transfer partners on November 18. For me, the biggest value is access to business and first class award seats that these airlines don’t make available to members of other frequent flyer programs.

    These are Chase’s first newly introduced airline transfer partners in more than five years. And they’re an unambiguously positive addition, even if neither becomes the program most cardmembers use most often.

    Industry observers note that eligible cards include Chase Sapphire Reserve, Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve for Business, Ink Business Preferred and J.P. Morgan Reserve. Both latest partners transfer at 1:1. Hyatt transfers are now less generous for Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred: 4 Chase points become 3 Hyatt points, while the Reserve cards retain 1:1. That distinction doesn’t apply to these new airline partners. Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) is a strong card for actual spending, with 4 points per dollar on flights and hotels booked directly and 3 points per dollar on dining. Adding more transfer partners makes the value of those points even greater. Why I Want Qantas Points Chase already had ways to book oneworld flights through programs like British Airways and Iberia. But being able to book an airline doesn’t mean having access to all of its award seats. Airlines increasingly keep more of their premium cabin availability for their own members. As I explained when Rove added Qantas transfers, Qantas offers its members award space that American AAdvantage, Alaska and British Airways members can’t book. I have family in Australia and have had real success finding Qantas business class awards when there’s flexibility over the U.S. gateway and travel date. I’ll set alerts across several flights rather than insist on one. Some flight between Australia and the U.S. will inevitably open up with a couple of business class awards, usually around 60 days out. Qantas can also be useful for Emirates redemptions. I’d generally rather book the same available Emirates business class seat through Copa ConnectMiles, though. Copa charges 80,000 miles one way between the U.S. and Dubai in business class without fuel surcharges. And Qantas is no longer an unrestricted way around Emirates’ first class award limits. Booking Emirates first class with Qantas points requires Qantas Silver status or higher, and passengers must be at least nine years old. Cathay Offers More Award Space And Lower British Airways Surcharges Cathay Pacific is similar. Its own members get access to far more premium cabin award space than members of partner programs. Asia Miles prices can be high, though. I also like Asia Miles for reducing fuel surcharges on British Airways awards, particularly compared with booking through American AAdvantage. It’s also notable that Chase’s Cathay transfer rate is better than American Express’s. American Express transfers 1,000 Membership Rewards points to just 800 Asia Miles. An award requiring 100,000 Asia Miles takes 100,000 Chase points versus 125,000 Amex points (without transfer bonus). American Express, Citi, Capital One and Rove already partner with both Qantas and Cathay. Chase is catching up with these. I wouldn’t transfer points just because these options have been added. Chase Is Finally Adding Airline Partners Again Chase’s last new transfer partner was Wyndham Rewards in February 2026. Its last new airline partner was Air Canada Aeroplan on August 3, 2021. I welcomed Wyndham because it revealed Chase was building out Ultimate Rewards, even though I had little interest in transferring points there. Qantas and Cathay are programs I can see myself using. They bring Chase to 12 airline transfer programs and four hotel programs. I also wonder whether these relationships could lead to more Points Boost opportunities. With Points Boost, Chase can use discounts it negotiates on paid tickets to offer more value per point through its travel portal. More airline relationships could help them offer more flights, more dates, or better redemption values. Qantas has already appeared in Points Boost, and American Airlines has participated without being a Chase transfer partner. But I’d love to see deeper relationships produce more opportunities to redeem at 2 cents per point for premium cabin tickets in the future.     I also like Asia Miles for reducing fuel surcharges on British Airways awards, particularly compared with booking through American AAdvantage.

    Industry observers note that it’s also notable that Chase’s Cathay transfer rate is better than American Express’s. American Express transfers 1,000 Membership Rewards points to just 800 Asia Miles. An award requiring 100,000 Asia Miles takes 100,000 Chase points versus 125,000 Amex points (without transfer bonus).

    In a recent development, american Express, Citi, Capital One and Rove already partner with both Qantas and Cathay. Chase is catching up with these. I wouldn’t transfer points just because these options have been added.

    Chase’s last latest transfer partner was Wyndham Rewards in February 2026. Its last new airline partner was Air Canada Aeroplan on August 3, 2021. I welcomed Wyndham because it demonstrated Chase was building out Ultimate Rewards, even though I had little interest in transferring points there. Qantas and Cathay are programs I can see myself using. They bring Chase to 12 airline transfer programs and four hotel programs. I also wonder whether these relationships could lead to more Points Boost opportunities. With Points Boost, Chase can use discounts it negotiates on paid tickets to offer more value per point through its travel portal. More airline relationships could help them offer more flights, more dates, or better redemption values. Qantas has already appeared in Points Boost, and American Airlines has participated without being a Chase transfer partner. But I’d love to see deeper relationships produce more opportunities to redeem at 2 cents per point for premium cabin tickets in the future.     #30538. Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (336 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that colorado Rep.
    • Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.
    • According to recent reports, the red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

    Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

    According to recent reports, the red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

    Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

    Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

    A newcomer to electoral politics, she rapidly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

    In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

    In a recent development, running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch unveiled he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

    This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

    Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

    World Of Hyatt Status Revamps For 2027—Award Stacking And New Benefit Choices, But Cuts Come Also

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 33 min read (6552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~33 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.
    • Industry observers note that hyatt will finally let members combine a free night certificate with a confirmed suite upgrade starting January 1, 2027.
    • Sources indicate that this isn’t an across the board improvement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

    Industry observers note that hyatt will finally let members combine a free night certificate with a confirmed suite upgrade starting January 1, 2027. I’ve wanted that for years. They’re also extending milestone free night certificates from 180 days to a year, and adding rewards after just 10 qualifying nights.

    Sources indicate that this isn’t an across the board improvement. Suite upgrades will expire sooner. The suite upgrade choice at 50 nights gets cut in half. And My Hyatt Concierge becomes something you select alongside other rewards, rather than something everyone automatically receives at 60 nights. Free parking will no longer be an automatic benefit on award stays for Globalists.

    Sources indicate that when I covered Hyatt’s last major status benefit refresh in November 2023, I liked it overall. They made awards transferable, added choices, and let members try Globalist benefits before earning Globalist. Guest of Honor became limited, but the Milestone Rewards themselves mostly got better.

    It has been revealed that this time there are new and better options. I genuinely like a lot of the choices, but there are real tradeoffs. Hyatt is pitching the changes as more choice and flexibility, based on listening to members. That’s actually fair for much of this, though I don’t think members told them what they really wanted was for suite upgrade to expire up to a year earlier.

    It has been revealed that hyatt will allow members to combine eligible awards on the same reservation, including Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards and the new Free Parking Awards. This fixes one of the problems I’ve been complaining about for years. A free night certificate is something you often want to use on a special leisure stay. That’s also when a suite may matter most, especially traveling with family. When I didn’t want to use a free night certificate was a work trip by myself. Free night awards had a lot less value to me because I had to give up a confirmed suite to use them. But being able to use the two awards together makes both more valuable. Combining Guest of Honor with a suite upgrade is useful, too. You can give someone Globalist treatment and confirm their suite ahead of time, rather than leaving the room upgrade to availability when they arrive. Hyatt also promises an enhanced Pay My Way experience, letting members mix awards, points, cash and Points + Cash by night. Online selection, gifting and redemption will be available for eligible awards. Pay My Way and stacking, by the way, really do all work together. Hyatt offers me this illustration, Let’s say a member is making a three night booking. Assuming both the Standard Suite was available for the duration, and there is award inventory available on the selected dates (just like today) – yes, a member could apply a Suite Upgrade Award to the whole stay, a Free Parking award to the whole stay, a Guest of Honor Award to the whole stay, and then pay for the reservation using points on one night, a promotional Free Night Award on another night, and cash on the third night.

    Milestone Rewards currently begin at 20 qualifying nights. Next year they’ll start at 10 nights or 20,000 base points. Here’s the new chart through 50 nights. Qualifying nights / base points   What you receive 10 / 20,000   Choose one: 1 qualifying night credit, $25 FIND experience credit, or $30 Inclusive Collection spa credit. 20 / 35,000   Choose one: 2 qualifying night credits, $30 spa credit, $25 Delta certificate, 2K Next Stay Award, or 2 Club Access Awards. 30 / 50,000   Choose 10,000 bonus points or a Category 1–4 free night. Also choose one: 2 qualifying night credits, $30 spa credit, $25 Delta certificate, 2K Next Stay Award, or 2 Club Access Awards. 40 / 65,000   Receive 1 Guest of Honor Award. Also choose one: 5 qualifying night credits, $200 Thompson Hotels credit, $75 Delta certificate, 5,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. 50 / 80,000   Choose one: $200 Thompson Hotels credit, $75 Delta certificate, 5,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. The qualifying night choices add up to 10 nights: one at the first milestone, two at the next, two at 30 nights and five at 40 nights. These count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. That creates a path to Globalist with 50 qualifying nights from other sources, if you select all four night rewards. The requirement remains 60, but 10 can come from these choices. And you earn qualifying nights with the The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) too – 5 qualifying night credits every year and 2 qualifying night every time you spend $5,000 on the card. The 30 night option to take 10,000 points instead of a Category 1–4 certificate is useful for someone who struggles to use the certificate. A good Category 4 redemption can be worth more, and the certificate will become easier to use with the longer expiration and ability to add a suite upgrade. One Fewer Suite Upgrade, And A Choice About Your Concierge The reduction at 50 nights is easy to miss. The current choice is two Suite Upgrade Awards. The new chart offers one. At 60 nights or 100,000 base points, members will receive: 2 Guest of Honor Awards. A choice of free nights: 2 Category 1–4 awards or 1 Category 1–7 award. Two selections from this menu: 7,500 bonus points, a Free Parking Award, a $100 Delta certificate, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, or My Hyatt Concierge. You can still select the two suite upgrades and concierge access, keeping the existing 60 night package. But if you want points or parking, something else has to go. And you can’t make the same two choices at 60 nights – you can’t have four upgrades, 15,000 points or two parking awards. You don’t have o select all of your awards at once, though you do have to make these two selections at the same time. Hyatt explains to me that you’ll still have 90 days to make your choices, and: In milestones where there are separate choices, such as 30 nights, the member can make those choices at different points within the 90 day selection window (e.g., could choose the Free Night Award one day, and the HIC Spa credit on a different day.) At 60 nights, the member can choose their free night award choice on a different day from the other selection, but the two selections within “Choose Two” must be made together at the same time. I do plan to keep the concierge benefit, even though mine has never been very responsive. I won’t give up the ability to email someone to address concerns. I just wish I would hear back more quickly, and didn’t need to follow up so often. Maybe that’s actually coming? Hyatt tells me they do plan greater investment in the concierge program: [B]y shifting to a choice, we will be able to further invest in My Hyatt Concierge and deliver even more proactive and personalized care. We will share more when available.

    Recent findings suggest that I do proposal to keep the concierge benefit, even though mine has never been very responsive. I won’t give up the ability to email someone to address concerns. I just wish I would hear back more rapidly, and didn’t need to follow up so often. Maybe that’s actually coming? Hyatt tells me they do plan greater investment in the concierge program:.

    [B]y shifting to a choice, we will be able to further invest in My Hyatt Concierge and deliver even more proactive and personalized care. We will share more when available.

    As before, lifetime Globalists retain their concierge without having to stay 60 nights.

    The upcoming parking award covers a qualifying paid or award stay of up to seven nights, and can be gifted. It appears among the choices at 60, 70, 80 and 90 nights. However it’s no longer simply a benefit for Globalists redeeming points for free nights. I wrote in that Hyatt was surveying turning automatic benefits into awards you could choose and they’ve done that with this one. The benefit is no longer unlimited It comes with a tradeoff – the benefit is instead of something else And you have to strategy ahead, one more thing to track and manage, rather than something that’s just ‘taken care of’ in recognition of your loyalty. Hyatt explains the decision to me as, [T]his decision was made as 70% of Globalists did not use the free parking benefit in 2025; 95% used it 4 times or less, and moving this to a choice allowed the program to retain it for members who value it and introduce other exciting new awards like the $200 Thompson Hotels Credit and the $500 Premium Suite Credit. If the benefit wasn’t being used, it actually wasn’t that expensive to offer! And not using it regularly doesn’t mean the option isn’t valued. It may not have been the most valuable benefit of Globalist for most people, but I wouldn’t personally make the tradeoff (in fairness, I’m someone that did use and get value from it). Of course, a parking award will be eligible for use a paid stay while it previously was only available on points. However, at 70, 80 or 90 nights where you can claim it you’re passing up 10,000 points or a suite upgrade to select it. A Year To Use Every Award Is Both An Improvement And A Cut Hyatt’s release presents the new expiration policy as giving members extra time. That’s true for some awards, but the effect runs in both directions. Hyatt tells me, For all awards issued on January 1, 2027 or later, expiration dates will be 365 days from the date of issuance. Milestone free night awards that presently expire after 180 days will get substantially more time. But suite upgrades, ordinary Milestone Guest of Honor awards and club access awards currently have much longer lives, generally through the end of the year earned plus another 14 months under Hyatt’s existing rules. A suite upgrade selected January 1, 2026 remained valid through February 2028. Under a 365 day rule, the same issuance date would produce a January 1, 2027 expiration. That’s more than a year of usefulness gone. Shortening the window makes it harder to hold upgrades for a major trip, to book far ahead, or to save awards from a heavy travel year for a quieter one. More Free Night Choices And Delta Status At Higher Milestones Here’s the rest of the 2027 chart: Qualifying nights   What you receive 70, 80 and 90, at each milestone   1 Guest of Honor Award, plus choose one: a Free Parking Award, 2 single visit Delta Sky Club passes, 10,000 points, or 1 Suite Upgrade Award. 100   Choose 1 Category 1–7 night, 2 Category 1–4 nights, or a $500 premium suite credit. Also choose one: Delta Gold Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. 110, 120, 130 and 140, at each milestone   1 Guest of Honor Award, plus choose one: Delta Gold Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. 150   Choose 2 Category 1–7 nights or an Ultimate Free Night Award. Also choose one: Delta Platinum Medallion, 10,000 points, 1 Suite Upgrade Award, or a Miraval Extra Night Award. The Ultimate Free Night at 150 nights isn’t going away. The two Category 1–7 nights are an alternative. Someone who wants two nights at less expensive hotels can choose those, while someone planning one especially expensive night can retain the Ultimate award, which covers participating Category 1–8 hotels, Category A–F all-inclusives and Miraval. The new hotel credits are more restrictive than points: $30 Inclusive Collection spa credit: for spa treatments at participating all-inclusive resorts. $200 Thompson Hotels credit: toward an eligible paid stay. $500 premium suite credit: toward an eligible paid premium suite stay of at least two nights. I’ve wanted a way to use two suite upgrades to confirm a premium suite. A discount on buying a premium suite isn’t as attractive to me. But there are times I might use it. Delta Gold starting at 100 nights and Platinum at 150 nights are interesting choices for someone who flies Delta without status. I still preferred the American partnership. The ability to redeem Hyatt points for American status for a trip was useful for people who didn’t have American status. And the earlier version earned American miles on Hyatt stays. I’d rather earn those than Delta miles. FIND credits are being pared back sharply. The $25 choices at 20 and 30 nights disappear, as do $150 choices at 40 and 50 nights and $300 choices at 70, 80 and 90. A $25 FIND choice appears at the new 10 night milestone. What Hyatt Gets From These Changes The strongest improvements are award stacking, more time to use free night certificates, an earlier first reward, and choices that let members avoid awards they won’t use. A member who doesn’t value concierge access can get something else, while someone who prefers two less expensive hotel nights can choose them. I expect members approaching Globalist will like the qualifying night choices. People who lose free night certificates to expiration should come out ahead, too. Existing Globalists who use all their suite upgrades, plan trips far ahead, or regularly choose FIND experiences have more to lose. Hyatt also gets more ways to influence where members spend. A Thompson credit encourages a paid Thompson stay. A spa credit encourages a treatment that may cost much more than the credit. The premium suite credit encourages someone to buy a room they might otherwise try to upgrade into. Shorter suite award validity should leave fewer outstanding upgrades available for future use. Making concierge elective lets members reveal whether they value the service more than points or another reward. And offering status credits makes the next milestone feel closer, encouraging someone with a modest number of Hyatt nights to keep going. For me, being able to confirm a suite on a free night certificate is the biggest improvement. I care much more about that than a spa coupon. There really is more choice and the ability to earn status faster with these changes. Stacking and combining rewards is great. So is longer expiration of free night awards, though sadly at the cost of shorter expiration for suite upgrade awards. The most consequential change for me might be something that isn’t really being announced. If changing My Hyatt Concierge to a choice benefit really does entail greater investment in the program, it would make the experience far more premium and secure even greater loyalty. I’d rather earn those than Delta miles. FIND credits are being pared back sharply. The $25 choices at 20 and 30 nights disappear, as do $150 choices at 40 and 50 nights and $300 choices at 70, 80 and 90. A $25 FIND choice appears at the new 10 night milestone. What Hyatt Gets From These Changes The strongest improvements are award stacking, more time to use free night certificates, an earlier first reward, and choices that let members avoid awards they won’t use. A member who doesn’t value concierge access can get something else, while someone who prefers two less expensive hotel nights can choose them. I expect members approaching Globalist will like the qualifying night choices. People who lose free night certificates to expiration should come out ahead, too. Existing Globalists who use all their suite upgrades, proposal trips far ahead, or regularly choose FIND experiences have more to lose. Hyatt also gets more ways to influence where members spend. A Thompson credit encourages a paid Thompson stay. A spa credit encourages a treatment that may cost much more than the credit. The premium suite credit encourages someone to buy a room they might otherwise try to upgrade into. Shorter suite award validity should leave fewer outstanding upgrades available for future use. Making concierge elective lets members reveal whether they value the service more than points or another reward. And offering status credits makes the next milestone feel closer, encouraging someone with a modest number of Hyatt nights to keep going. For me, being able to confirm a suite on a free night certificate is the biggest improvement. I care much more about that than a spa coupon. There really is more choice and the ability to earn status faster with these changes. Stacking and combining rewards is great. The most consequential change for me might be something that isn’t really being announced.     #30534. Latest Update: We Need a Better GOP

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (849 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: We Need a Better GOP

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (849 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The old Republican establishment could be out of touch, unimaginative, and too comfortable with revolving-door practices that enriched former officeholders and staffers, among other failings.
    • Beginning in 2016, Donald Trump burned this establishment to the ground and created a fresh one that has its own myriad deficiencies, some of which echo the failings of yore; the extremely online elements of today’s establishment, for instance, have found a whole new way to be out of touch.
    • We say this not to pine for yesterday’s establishment — parties never go back, only forward — but to make the point that every party elite reaches its point of exhaustion, and that’s where the Trump establishment is now.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The old Republican establishment could be out of touch, unimaginative, and too comfortable with revolving-door practices that enriched former officeholders and staffers, among other failings.

    Beginning in 2016, Donald Trump burned this establishment to the ground and created a fresh one that has its own myriad deficiencies, some of which echo the failings of yore; the extremely online elements of today’s establishment, for instance, have found a whole new way to be out of touch.

    We say this not to pine for yesterday’s establishment — parties never go back, only forward — but to make the point that every party elite reaches its point of exhaustion, and that’s where the Trump establishment is now.

    In a recent development, there is a robust intramural argument on the right over how to interpret the historic loss in the midterms. We have our own views, but the most elemental need is a better GOP — one that is not beholden to the will of one man, doesn’t tolerate corruption, insists on strict adherence to the rule of law, encourages Congress to take up its allotted role in our constitutional system, rewards policy entrepreneurship on the part of officeholders, and focuses on results rather than performative provocations.

    It’s possible to imagine any number of people leading such a national party, and it could have different ideological colorations depending on that leader and underlying circumstances. All that is TBD and should be a matter of fierce debate and competition. But unless the party moves beyond today’s establishment and renews itself, it risks subsequent devastating votes of no confidence from the American public.

    Industry observers note that consider the issue of corruption, which was one of the biggest concerns of voters in the midterms. It is one thing for a party to suffer politically in the course of making progress on an important priority — say, stepped-up immigration enforcement. It is another to suffer from the perception — and, sadly, the reality — that politically connected people are engaged in untoward schemes for their own enrichment. The former is an inevitable political trade-off; the latter is a party’s elite feasting on its power and connections with no heed to the consequences for the larger cause.

    President Trump, who has an overawing dominance over the party, is the source of many of the GOP’s current discontents. His influence is not going to drastically diminish anytime soon, and we know that many good Republicans have considered him better than the alternative, or have thrilled to his no-holds-barred assaults on the left. However one evaluates the Trump phenomenon, though, attempts to rely on the tropes that fueled his rise beginning in 2016, or ape his political style, will almost certainly fail — for the simple reasons that times change and Trump’s persona is not replicable.

    Industry observers note that the GOP could do much worse than look to the states, where Republican governors and legislators have cut taxes, restrained spending, pared back regulations, protected unborn children, and pursued reforms of schooling and housing. One reason that Florida constituted high ground beyond the reach of the blue wave is that it has been so well governed for so long, and it has had a series of reformist Republican governors focused on results.

    At the national level, the GOP obviously needs a cost-of-living agenda that addresses high costs in health care, medicine, and education, and there’s much work that’s been done on these complications at the state level and among conservative policy thinkers. But arriving at a coherent agenda will require a seriousness of purpose and substantive focus that have been lacking for years now. That doesn’t mean the party should be dull and conventional — much can be learned from Trump’s zest for combat and vivid political branding — but it needs to recover a sense of institutional self-respect.

    The new establishment, via President Trump, has worked its way back around to what were widely considered weaknesses of the old one. Republicans were once determined to make another push for amnesty after every election loss, and now, the president has floated that idea in response to the Democratic midterm victory; Republicans were once too soft on China, and Trump has been notably conciliatory in his second term; the GOP once talked a good game on deficit spending but didn’t do nearly enough to curtail it, while we are now adding to the debt hand over fist during a time of economic expansion and relative peace; the Tom DeLay–led Republican House was much too cozy with lobbyists, but prior GOP ethical lapses have been eclipsed over the past two years.

    The old establishment had reached its expiration date and, regardless, isn’t coming back, while the current establishment is harmful to the party’s image and interests and an obstacle to change.

    As Lincoln mentioned, it is a time to think anew and act anew. The GOP desperately needs something fresh and different, with ideas and policies designed to meet the challenges of the day.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that on the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”.

    “When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”.

    It has been revealed that “If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”.

    Industry observers note that the last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

    Industry observers note that meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

    #30529. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

    📅 16 Jul 2018 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1864 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

    📅 16 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses.
    • Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.
    • Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

    Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

    Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

    “Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

    All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

    But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s newly introduced endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

    Recent findings suggest that “Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at mentioned comedian’s dishonesty.

    Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

    This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney states in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

    Recent findings suggest that you can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

    Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

    According to recent reports, nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare blueprint. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

    READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show.

    One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

    Industry observers note that but this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

    (To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.).

    A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he states are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

    This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

    Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

    In a recent development, now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

    This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

    “Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

    Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

    But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

    Industry observers note that (Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.).

    A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

    According to recent reports, this has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

    Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”.

    The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

    And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

    Recent findings suggest that nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

    What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

    It has been revealed that yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

    Recent findings suggest that next week’s episode introduces one or two latest characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

    To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

    In a recent development, to other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.
    • In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.
    • As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

    In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

    As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

    Recent findings suggest that “Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

    When McDermott confirmed his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

    Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

    In a recent development, he attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

    Sources indicate that he continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

    Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a upcoming life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

    “I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

    As he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

    Sources indicate that then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

    “The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

    Sources indicate that mcDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

    Recent findings suggest that “Jim McDermott was as major as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

    #30525. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

    📅 23 Oct 2020 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1959 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

    📅 23 Oct 2020 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.
    • According to recent reports, compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one.
    • All it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

    According to recent reports, compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

    All it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

    Sources indicate that performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

    Industry observers note that and this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

    Recent findings suggest that tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

    Similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

    According to recent reports, america may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

    Recent findings suggest that when Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a upcoming mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”.

    This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one confirmed in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

    In the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

    In a recent development, now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

    The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”.

    Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half. Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

    Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

    In a recent development, there’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen revealed that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every newly introduced person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”.

    It has been revealed that what he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

    Nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for when he revealshis subjects’ prejudices.

    According to recent reports, but then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

    In a recent development, fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

    Recent findings suggest that then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”.

    Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?).

    But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

    In a recent development, there’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” says without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”.

    All of these are women, by the way.

    According to recent reports, this leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

    Evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

    In a recent development, the most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

    In a recent development, at the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

    Now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

    “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is at the moment streaming on Amazon.

    TPG's Nov. 2026 valuations peg Chase Ultimate Rewards points at 2.05 cents each, compared with 1.3 cents each for Asia Miles and Qantas Frequent Flyer points. However, that doesn't mean you can't get excellent value by transferring Chase points to either program for an award flight; transferable rewards are generally worth more because of their flexibility.

    Cathay Pacific and Qantas are part of the Oneworld alliance. This means that, in addition to Cathay Pacific and Qantas flights, you may also find award availability through these airlines on flights operated by other Oneworld alliance airlines, including American Airlines and Alaska Airlines.

    Recent findings suggest that chase already partners with several Avios programs, which provide access to many Oneworld award flights. However, the addition of Asia Miles and Qantas Frequent Flyer gives cardmembers more ways to compare award pricing and availability across the alliance. Of course, not all award flights are bookable through every partner program, so you'll want to check award pricing and availability with each program before transferring Chase Ultimate Rewards points.

    These two upcoming transfer partners also provide additional ways to book award flights across the Pacific. While Cathay Pacific premium-cabin award space can be extremely limited through other Oneworld programs, Asia Miles may offer access to additional award availability.

    Business and first availability between North America and Hong Kong is at the moment sparse even through Asia Miles, but you can fly in premium economy on some dates for as little as 52,000 Asia Miles one-way.

    Recent findings suggest that and if you have your eye on an around-the-world award, Qantas has a special Oneworld Classic Flight Reward that can cover up to 35,000 miles of travel on a single itinerary for 152,200 points in economy or 365,800 points in business. You'll need to fly at least two Oneworld airlines other than Qantas to qualify for this award.

    Recent findings suggest that you can also transfer points from several other transferable rewards programs to Qantas Frequent Flyer and Cathay Pacific Asia Miles. Now, Chase Ultimate Rewards points provide another way to top off your account when you're short of the miles needed for an award.
