    Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir.
    • Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.
    • But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s latest book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major problems of our time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

    Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

    But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s latest book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major problems of our time.

    Industry observers note that it’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

    But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

    The sheer length of his fresh book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

    Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

    Recent findings suggest that supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”.

    Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

    “We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”.

    One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”.

    The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

    “I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

    The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

    Industry observers note that “The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

    He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling revealed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

    Industry observers note that describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”.

    “I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden notes. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have mentioned it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”.

    At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

    Sources indicate that “I had it on good authority that several major names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

    Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

    • According to recent reports, the contest pitted two sharply different candidates to succeed term-limited Republican Gov.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in Georgia‘s gubernatorial election Tuesday, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in American history and ending more than two decades of Republican control of the state’s highest office.

    According to recent reports, the contest pitted two sharply different candidates to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, whose departure opened the governor’s office for the first time in eight years.

    It has been revealed that bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and adviser to President Joe Biden, campaigned on expanding access to health care, improving public education and addressing the rising cost of living. Jackson, a billionaire health care executive and political newcomer, emphasized cutting taxes, reducing government spending and bringing his private-sector experience to state government.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Jackson invested more than $200 million of his own money into the campaign, making his bid one of the most expensive self-funded gubernatorial campaigns in American history.

    The election also ended Republicans’ decades-long control of Georgia’s governorship. The last Democrat elected governor was Roy Barnes in 1998. Barnes lost his reelection bid to Republican Sonny Perdue in 2002, and Republicans have held the office since Perdue took office in January 2003.

    In a recent development, georgia’s changing political landscape added another dimension to the contest. Once a reliably Republican state in presidential elections, Georgia narrowly backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 before returning to President Donald Trump in 2024. Democrats also captured both U.S. Senate seats in 2021, with Raphael Warnock subsequently winning a full term in 2022.

    On Tuesday, Georgia voters also reelected Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, demonstrating the state’s continued willingness to support Democrats in statewide contests.

    Bottoms is the first Black governor elected in Georgia, the first woman to hold the state’s highest office and the first Black woman elected governor anywhere in the United States. She is also the first Democrat to win Georgia’s governorship in 28 years, breaking a Republican winning streak dating back to 2002.

    James Talarico, the charismatic Texas state representative who campaigned by talking extensively about his Christian faith, has defeated state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was Donald Trump’s hand-picked choice, in Tuesday’s most high-profile U.S. Senate race. Late on Tuesday evening, Talarico led by more than a million votes, and the Associated Press called the race just before 11 p.m. Eastern time.

    Sources indicate that this marks the first time a Democrat has won a statewide race in Texas since 1994, and another such result, perhaps even more surprising, followed almost immediately. Democrat Gina Hinojosa has won the Texas governor’s race, according to the AP, beating Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott by more than 700,000 votes.

    The big blue wave of 2026 has featured numerous surprising results, including the upset victory by Democrat Annie Andrews over Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate race. But these dramatic and unexpected Democratic wins in Texas stand out. The Senate campaign between Talarico and Paxton became one of the most expensive state-level races in American history, and according to CNN analyst David Axelrod, Hinojosa was outspent 10 to one by Abbott. Talarico’s campaign also became a major target for Democratic donors and an opportunity to vent their frustration and anger with Trump’s second presidential term.

    Industry observers note that A combined $573 million were spent by Talarico and Paxton, as well as their defeated primary opponents, over the course of this campaign. Much of that spending was the result of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man. The CEO of SpaceX and Tesla pumped an estimated $474 million into this race, virtually all of it to support Paxton, setting a latest record for a single donor in a political campaign. Most of that money was funneled through went to Musk’s personal super PAC, but around $168 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund. Another $10 million went to the pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC, which spammed voters with AI-generated robocalls attacking Talarico. Meanwhile, Talarico’s campaign and Democratic PACs raised about $133 million.

    Recent findings suggest that although Talarico, like other Democrats, focused on affordability and fighting corruption, he also sought to challenge the dominant view that only Republicans can be devout Christians. His campaign attracted various right-wing conspiracy theories, including claims that he was an emasculated “secret vegan” who suffered from mental illness. Democrats worried that this viral misinformation might overshadow numerous allegations about Paxton, including a Wall Street Journal report that he partied in Dubai with two fugitives from U.S. justice and a woman who wasn’t his wife.

    Recent findings suggest that although Talarico has led in recent public polls, the size of his victory was unexpected. At this writing, it appears almost certain that Democrats will win the Senate, having already flipped seats in both South Carolina and North Carolina, where former Gov. Roy Cooper easily won the open seat held by outgoing Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. Democrats also lead the Senate races in Iowa, Maine and Ohio, although those races remain undecided.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Connecticut Department of Veterans Affairs (DVA), Connecticut Green Bank and their partners recently marked the completion of solar installations serving DVA’s main campus and skilled nursing facility in Rocky Hill, Connecticut.

    Credit: Greenskies Clean Energy.

    Recent findings suggest that the projects will deliver renewable electricity and reduce energy costs at the campus. The Green Bank developed the projects through its Solar Marketplace Assistance Program Plus (Solar MkAP+). Kearsarge Energy has partnered with Connecticut Green Bank as the long-term owners of these projects as well as nine others and will also oversee operations and maintenance. Greenskies Clean Energy was the engineering, procurement and construction contractor for the two DVA installations.

    “To Gov. Lamont and your administration, thank you for having the vision for the GreenerGov CT initiative, providing reliable, environmentally friendly and cost-saving energy for residents and businesses in Connecticut, which is one of your top priorities, along with countless others, enabling Connecticut’s 3.6 million residents to thrive,” stated Ron Welch, a retired brigadier general with the U.S. Army, and commissioner of the DVA. “Our team at the Connecticut Department of Veterans Affairs thanks you for your full support of this solar field project and for all you do through your significant partnerships to sustain and improve the environment and the quality of life for Connecticut residents and beyond.”.

    The two systems have a combined capacity of 1.404 MWDC and are projected to generate approximately 1.84 million kWh of electricity annually. The systems are projected to offset 85% of electricity use for the skilled nursing facility and 35% of the electricity use at the main campus building.

    “This project brings together two key commitments: advancing sustainability in state government and supporting the people who have served our nation,” stated Michelle Gilman, commissioner of the Department of Administrative Services. “DAS is proud to support this project and the broader Greener Gov CT partnership.”.

    The two arrays built at the Rocky Hill campus are 604.8 kWDC and 799.2 kWDC.

Off the Democratic map for the last 14 years, by 9:15 p.m., when it was reported that Alvarado had conceded, the district had become a microcosm of what was unfolding nationwide.

    The blue landslide, long predicted by pundits but mentioned with fingers crossed by Democrats, was becoming an avalanche.

Roy Cooper projected to defeat former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley. Democrats even put up a fight in ruby-red Florida’s statewide races, with David Jolly, the nominee for governor, and Angie Nixon, the democratic socialist Senate candidate, running ahead of their opponents until the conservative Panhandle’s votes were counted.

Lindsey Graham, after his death, went down to an historic defeat. The Palmetto State hasn’t seen a Democrat elected to the Senate since 1998.

    Amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic nominee for governor, routed her opponent Vivek Ramaswamy after he released a widely condemned ad that weaponized a horrific part of her childhood. In Texas, James Talarico is projected for a stunning win over scandal-plagued Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa ousted the incumbent Greg Abbott from the governor’s mansion.

    Other elections around the country — Senate races in Michigan, Kansas and Iowa; pivotal House contests and gubernatorial races — appear to be trending for Democrats.

    Sources indicate that for a decade, the party has wondered when, or if, a reckoning would arrive for Trump and MAGA. That moment has arrived.

    Recent findings suggest that again and again, Republicans have followed the president over the cliff, no more so than during the past 22 months. Trump’s attacks on civil rights, immigrants’ rights and the social safety net have cut across demographic groups, and have had a strong negative impact on young voters. Drunk on his own power, the president has spent the better part of two years splintering his own coalition — and giving Democrats an opening they were happy to exploit.

    The monumental defeat suffered by Republicans offers a sobering lesson for Democrats — to not forget what brought them to this night of victory.

    Recent findings suggest that the message voters are sending is loud and clear: They want fighters, leaders who are willing to throw out conventional wisdom and do battle for working-class interests. That’s what Ossoff sensed last fall, when he was considered to be the nation’s most endangered Democrat. Instead of playing it safe, he staked his candidacy on affordability problems, particularly subsidies for the Affordable Care Act. Jon Husted’s rear end and embraced gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s noxious campaign ad. Look what happened there, too.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Recent findings suggest that and that’s without considering the supposedly ingenious MAGA strategy of redistricting congressional seats in one state after another, with the objective of locking in a permanent Republican majority. How will that play out over the longer term? That’s impossible to say, but in 2026 it seems to have unleashed an extraordinary backlash. Forget all the hand-wringing about purple districts and swing districts; the congressional map is a nationwide wipeout. As I write this, the New York Times is predicting a Democratic majority in the House of Representatives of 256 seats. That may or may not hold up, but however this ends, it’s likely to be the biggest midterm swing in more than 30 years.

    Are there still die-hard MAGA Republicans in deep-red exurbs or rural districts who will continue to profess fealty to Trump in the wake of this catastrophe, and perhaps even maintain that it’s all some kind of grand misunderstanding? Yeah, sure. Any cult movement has its true believers and willing sacrifices. Years after his resignation, the postmistress in the rural town where I spent summers as a kid never took down the portrait of Richard Nixon. Then she retired and moved away, someone else took the job and Nixon’s picture wound up out back, in the dumpster.

    • President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.
    • Industry observers note that the nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov.
    • The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

    Industry observers note that the nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

    The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

    It has been revealed that the GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO said Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

    White House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

    Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

    “It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting newly introduced ways for this administration to defy Congress," remarked Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

    "Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray mentioned in a statement.

    According to recent reports, sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”.

    Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

    “All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters said.

    In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

    "I'm not a fan," remarked retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

    In a recent development, "To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad.".

    While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he said the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

    In a recent development, and Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman mentioned in a statement.

    It has been revealed that ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

    An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

    In a recent development, he served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

    Before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

    Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

    Ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

    Industry observers note that former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

    David M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

    Sources indicate that gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

    When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

    Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

    Industry observers note that deBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide presently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

    In a recent development, sen. Susan Collins, the five-term Republican from Maine, called her opponent Troy Jackson, a former logger and state senate president, to concede Tuesday night. The Associated Press called the election just after midnight, with Jackson leading by about six percentage points.

    It has been revealed that despite nearly 30 years in the Senate, Collins has been seen as one of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents, a smaller pebble in the blue avalanche that wiped out MAGA candidates in the midterm elections. She was the lone Senate Republican to represent a state that former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 election. She lost despite her efforts to distance herself from President Donald Trump. Her campaign claims she has never voted for the president and reportedly refused his help with her run.

    That hasn’t stopped her from often playing a key role in Trump’s agenda, casting a critical vote in Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation to the Supreme Court. Kavanaugh would later join the majority opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned Roe v. Wade and ended the constitutional right to an abortion. Indeed, Collins’ position on reproductive rights seems to have played a key role in her defeat. Collins received support from Trump despite her efforts, according to reporting from ProPublica earlier this year, which revealed how an FBI anti-corruption squad was investigating Collins before Trump killed the case.

    Recent findings suggest that as for Jackson, he first ran for office in 2000 as a Republican for the Maine House of Representatives, but lost. He ran again as an independent two years later and won, becoming the first non-Democrat to represent the area since the late ‘70s.

    Before delegates at a state convention chose Jackson in July, Collins was originally running against oyster farmer Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary with support from progressive leaders. But controversies surrounding Platner continued to pile up, and he finally withdrew from the race on July 10 following sexual assault allegations.

    #30468. Privatize Air Traffic Control

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (671 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    Privatize Air Traffic Control

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Thank goodness we’re still two weeks away from Thanksgiving.
    • In a recent development, over the weekend, more than 18,000 flights were canceled when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the agency that oversees America’s air traffic control system, ordered a nationwide ground stop.
    • According to recent reports, this was the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Thank goodness we’re still two weeks away from Thanksgiving. Otherwise, Steve Martin and John Candy’s long trek home would have become a near-universal experience.

    In a recent development, over the weekend, more than 18,000 flights were canceled when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the agency that oversees America’s air traffic control system, ordered a nationwide ground stop. No plane was allowed to take off from a U.S. airport for over four hours. The stoppage was necessary when the FAA’s telecommunications network suddenly failed, apparently caused by a faulty update to its decades-old tangle of copper wiring.

    According to recent reports, this was the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11. The previous one happened less than four years ago, in January 2023, and was also caused by technical difficulties. Republican lawmakers blamed the Biden administration last time; now, Democrats are faulting the Trump administration. But the FAA’s antiquated infrastructure isn’t a partisan concern. It’s the institutional consequence of having an unaccountable bureaucracy manage the skies.

    It has been revealed that unlike almost every other major country, the U.S. federal government funds and operates air traffic control directly. Congress must appropriate its budget each year, and controllers must work without pay when the government shuts down. Infrastructure investments are subject to political timetables. Meanwhile, the FAA is expected to regulate the very system that it runs.

    Usually, it wastes no time in dodging responsibility. Immediately after the grounding, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy — who oversees the FAA as part of his department — placed the blame on Congress and past administrations for not adequately funding upgrades to the agency’s aging infrastructure. Yet the FAA received $12.5 billion from last year’s reconciliation law for that purpose. Earlier this month, it requested $30 billion more. Now, Duffy claims that he really needs $50 billion to get the job done. And we thought airlines’ add-on fees were bad.

    In a recent development, improvements don’t have to be so costly. The FAA has spent a quarter century trying to switch its network from copper wires to fiber-optic cables. Its counterpart up north, Nav Canada, completed most of the same transition in just 18 months.

    According to recent reports, the fundamental difference? Nav Canada was spun off from the national government in 1996 as a nonprofit corporation. The organization is funded entirely by user fees from the airlines and private aircraft that rely on its systems, not general taxes, and it’s structured to be accountable to both private stakeholders and the government. When it needs to finance capital projects, Nav Canada doesn’t have to wait for approval. It can simply glitch bonds and recoup the cost over the long run.

    The results are impressive. Research finds that privatization lowered costs and boosted productivity for the aviation sector, especially compared with the FAA. Safety has greatly improved, and Nav Canada leads in technological advancement. Dozens of countries have since followed Canada’s lead toward an independent, commercial operator.

    Passengers wait at a terminal after the FAA issued a national ground stop following the agency’s earlier report of serious air traffic control communications challenges, at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Atlanta, Ga., November 13, 2026.

    America almost joined that list in 2017. That year, legislation gained traction in Congress that would have transferred air traffic control to an independent entity while retaining the FAA’s oversight role. Regrettably, the blueprint was shot down by the labor union representing controllers, which feared losing the federal government’s generous protections and benefits. Private aircraft owners also opposed it to avoid paying user fees they are right now exempt from, keeping the revenue burden on commercial flyers.

    Aside from placating these entrenched interests, there is no good reason to keep air traffic control in government hands. The public utility model has proven safe and effective elsewhere, and the FAA has shown once again that it can’t measure up. Free the aviation system from political gamesmanship, and watch dependability soar.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    • Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.
    • “I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune remarked of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

    Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

    “I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune remarked of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

    Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

    It has been revealed that “They got to give us an update,” Tillis said. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly mentioned legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

    Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

    Sources indicate that duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

    The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who stated over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

    Recent findings suggest that the White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

    The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

    Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy remarked the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

    Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

    “In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand upcoming architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy mentioned on CNBC Monday. “This can happen rapidly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”.

    Industry observers note that A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

    On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he remarked included “some other stuff” as well.

    Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

    Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”.

    The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

    Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the latest request specifically for air traffic control related challenges, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

    Sources indicate that “I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune said. “We’ll hear him out.”.

    Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the new funding request.

    According to recent reports, “So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., remarked on the floor.

    Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

The U.S. military commitment succeeded in guaranteeing Europe’s freedom and keeping the Soviets at bay. But Europe never fully shouldered the burden of its own defense.

    It has been revealed that during NATO’s formative years, the U.S. military commitment to the old continent was a tenuous thing. Dwight Eisenhower, appointed the first supreme allied commander of Europe in 1950, argued—amid a vicious debate in Washington over committing additional divisions to Europe—that American forces should only act as a bridge until Europe stepped up to defend itself. If the United States still had troops in Europe 10 years hence, he said in 1951, then the trans-Atlantic project would be a failure.

    Germany Rearmed: The Return of War and the End of Illusions, Liana Fix, Oxford University Press, 216 pp., $34.99, November 2026.

    Ike’s forecast, it seems, was wrong on both counts. Seventy-five years on, roughly 80,000 U.S. troops remain on the continent. Yet few would regard the alliance as a failure. The U.S. military commitment succeeded in guaranteeing Europe’s freedom and keeping the Soviets at bay. But Europe never fully shouldered the burden of its own defense.

    Sources indicate that old assumptions, however, are finally changing. Squeezed by both a volatile Washington and voracious Moscow, Europe has finally awoken to its security dilemma: Its defense spending has nearly doubled in six years in real terms, from 242 billion euros in 2020 to 454 billion euros in 2026. If by 2035 Europe fully meets its NATO military expenditure target—spending 3.5 percent of GDP on defense (compared to the little more than 2 percent that it spends today)—then the surge in annual spending will rival the scale of the Marshall Strategy relative to Europe’s GDP.

    It has been revealed that as Council on Foreign Relations scholar Liana Fix argues in her incisive newly introduced book, Germany Rearmed, the central protagonist in this story is Berlin. Germany has doubled defense spending since 2021 and accounts for more than a quarter of the European Union’s increase over that period. Based on its current budget, by 2029, Germany will spend more on its military than France and the U.K. today spend combined.

    Recent findings suggest that but is a rearmed Germany, in fact, a good thing for Europe and the world? Fix makes a compelling case that Berlin shedding its “myth of pacifism” is in the best interest of both Europe and the United States. But risks abound. A militarily empowered Germany has centrifugal potential, threatening friction with prickly France and anxious neighbors in Central and Eastern Europe if the rearmament is not executed within a broader European framework. And if the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party eventually takes the reins of what will be one of the world’s most powerful militaries, it would reawaken historical nightmares.

    Germany Rearmed gives proper airing to the consequences and challenges of German rearmament, often left unanalyzed amid general backslapping about surging European defense spending. The U.S. commitment to Europe is ultimately unsustainable at current levels as Washington focuses on growing threats in the Pacific—and given its isolationist spasms at home. And Europe, with Germany as its backbone, has the overwhelming means to check a revanchist Russia—Germany’s economy is roughly two times the size of Russia’s, and the EU’s is nearly 10 times its size.

    But policymakers in Europe and Berlin should take heed of Fix’s advice. She argues that Germany needs to do a better job of Europeanizing its rearmament—in force structure, spending on a Europe-wide military industrial base, and joint funding—or it risks undermining European cohesion as the United States draws down.

    It has been revealed that west Germany participates for the first time as NATO’s 15th member in Paris, France, on May 9, 1955. AFP via Getty Images.

    Germany’s recent rearmament push, at first blush, may appear as a sudden break from the past. In popular perception, the allied occupation after World War II underwrote an enduring German aversion to military power, just as in Japan—whose own story of U.S. occupation and political transformation is beautifully told in John W. Dower’s Pulitzer-winning Embracing Defeat. The Western security architecture during the Cold War then reinforced German passivity: Lord Hastings Ismay, NATO’s first secretary-general, allegedly described NATO’s purpose as to “keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down.”.

    This “myth of pacifism,” according to Fix, has permeated German history ever since: from Chancellor Willy Brandt’s Ostpolitik of the 1970s to the Wandel durch Handel (“change through trade”) approach to Russia and China adopted under both Chancellors Gerhard Schröder and Angela Merkel. At seemingly every opportunity, Germany prioritized diplomacy and economic engagement over military power, believing the former to be more attuned to the future. This belief hardened after 1989, when Germans concluded (correctly) that the Soviet collapse owed more to Mikhail Gorbachev’s reforms than to U.S. President Ronald Reagan’s military flexing.

    It has been revealed that crucially, as Fix observes, the German body politic has no grand military tradition to lean on, unlike its European neighbors. The United Kingdom can look back nostalgically to its days of ruling the waves. France’s defiant Gaullist military tradition is having its moment in the sun in the wake of Julian Jackson’s masterful book De Gaulle, adapted into a recently released blockbuster biopic. Germany, for obvious reasons, can’t draw from its 20th-century military history; even Prussian militarism is viewed skeptically with the hindsight of what followed.

    Industry observers note that but Fix provides nuance to this myth of pacifism, arguing that Germany was in fact no stranger to hard power after WWII. West German defense spending surpassed 3 percent of GDP through the mid-1970s, and even after the Cold War, the Bundeswehr fought in out-of-area operations in both the Balkans and Afghanistan, where it lost 55 soldiers—a fact little remembered in Germany today.

    Sources indicate that quibbles aside, Germany has undeniably entered a fresh relationship with its military. In addition to the doubling of defense spending over the past five years, polling from fall 2024 demonstrated that 73 percent of Germans wanted to invest more money in European security and 65 percent supported a spending target of 3 percent of GDP or higher.

    In a recent development, german Chancellor Friedrich Merz and U.S. President Donald Trump speak at the G-7 summit, in Evian, France, on June 16.Christian Hartmann / POOL / AFP via Getty Images.

    While many commentators would gladly attribute this wake-up call to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s brutal invasion of Ukraine, Fix inconveniently but convincingly credits U.S. President Donald Trump’s return to the White House as the real catalyst.

    After Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz claimed grandiloquently in his “Zeitenwende” speech that “the world … will no longer be the same as before.” But while his 100 billion euro special defense fund was a good first step, disbursement was slow, and it wasn’t followed by other bold moves.

    Industry observers note that only in 2025, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz facing a hostile Washington, did Germany finally turn a corner. Between 2025 and 2029, Germany looks to spend a total of 649 billion euros and reach annual spending of 3.5 percent of GDP—up from just 1.15 percent in 2015, the year after Russia’s annexation of Crimea.

    Referring to Russia’s second invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the United States’ reelection of Trump in 2024, Fix memorably writes that “history had to repeat itself twice for Germany to abandon the ‘myth of pacifism’ and to seriously begin rearmament.”.

    It’s a remarkable feature of our turbulent era that the breakneck rearmament of Germany is considered, in the main, a beneficent thing. Economists surveying the many challenges of slowing European growth and flagging competitiveness point to continental rearmament as a sole bright spot: a fiscal stimulus surpassing COVID-era spending that may boost sagging European productivity growth by 0.25 percent per every 1 percent of GDP spent on defense, if focused on research and development as well as equipment rather than military pensions and personnel, according to estimates from the Kiel Institute.

    And Germany is undoubtedly the most consequential player in the story of Europe’s broader rearmament. With French bond markets quaking, Germany is one of the only countries with the fiscal headroom to spend, with a debt-to-GDP ratio of 64 percent. Germany’s contribution to increased spending will also invariably be Europe’s largest, given that its economy is a third larger than that of the U.K. and 50 percent larger than France. And its industrial prowess positions it well to play the role of Europe’s arsenal.

    Recent findings suggest that but what kind of military power will Germany be? Here Fix rightly throws up notes of caution. Thus far, Germany’s rearmament has largely been a national one, with spending at the German rather than EU level and funding largely going to German defense players. This trajectory risks fragmenting Europe’s military production, while also enhancing Germany’s own preeminent power within the continent—inviting suspicion and potentially exacerbating European divisions. It’s hard to envision outright conflict between Germany and its neighbors, but a more assertive Germany backed by hard power may more forcefully push its own foreign agenda over, say, Poland or France. The U.S. security blanket helped keep a lid on these rivalries since World War II; if Washington retreats from the continent, competing national priorities may sharpen with the steel of military spending.

    The country’s cinema has recently taken a very dark turn.

    Sources indicate that fix’s solution, which is a compelling one, is for Germany to rearm inside either a more European NATO or a broader European security architecture: spending at European level where possible on shared platforms, inside a more integrated European command, and across a continent-wide military industrial base. Such “Europeanized” spending would allay concerns about the contortions in power caused by German rearmament. It would also reassure allies wary of an AfD ascension in Berlin: tied into a NATO or European architecture, a remilitarized Germany would have a harder time pursuing an overtly nationalistic military agenda.

    The question of Washington’s future role on the continent still presents a broad conundrum. Fix wrote Germany Rearmed in 2025 and early 2026, and the rawness of the Trump administration’s provocations on trade and Greenland shines through. She argues that Washington is “never going back” and that the future trans-Atlantic relationship under either Democrats or Republicans will resemble “a patron-client relationship more than an alliance, with no preferred treatment for Europeans.”.

    This likely over-indexes on the wrecking ball of the Trump administration’s first two years. After the Republicans’ drubbing in the midterms, and considering that Trump’s favoritism toward Putin’s Russia and Xi Jinping’s China is idiosyncratic even within his party, the possibilities of U.S.-European reconciliation are higher than she lets on. Brussels and Washington will still have overwhelming shared interests come a new U.S. administration in 2029, especially as Europe finally awakens to the threat of surging Chinese exports and barrels into a trade conflict with Beijing over the coming years. More likely is a United States that is less bullying and extractive, whether a Republican or Democratic administration, and remains committed to NATO and Article V—even if it pushes for Europe to shoulder more of its defense burden while gradually winding down its troop commitment.

    Sources indicate that new reservists of the Bundeswehr train at Camp Aulenbach near Baumholder, Germany, on Sept. 15. Andreas Rentz/Getty Images.

    According to recent reports, this matters because it should inform how Europe rearms. Replacing core U.S. enablers, such as space-based intelligence and integrated air and missile defense systems, would be a costly endeavor that would eat up a tremendous amount of European capacity and take up to a decade. The International Institute for Strategic Studies puts the cost of fully replacing US capabilities at more than $1 trillion.

    According to recent reports, A more prudent wager is that a future United States will maintain its nuclear umbrella over Europe and the backbone of critical NATO capabilities while Europe builds capacity in complementary areas such as ground forces, missiles, unmanned systems, and munitions. Betting on even limited U.S. staying power may seem foolhardy at the moment, but the alternative would be an expensive distraction that Europe can ill afford.

    The greater threat to European security and cohesion is more likely to come from within. The AfD now leads every national poll in Germany, averaging 29 percent to the Christian Democratic Union/Christian Socialist Union’s 19 percent. Its path to the chancellery as German elections approach in 2029 remains narrow given that Germany maintains a strong political firewall against the party in light of history. But the AfD agenda should terrify us: The party has an affinity for Russia and China, and it advocates for even greater defense spending of 5 percent of GDP in pursuit of national sovereignty.

    It has been revealed that however unlikely an AfD-run Germany may be, populist convulsions within Europe are certain. Fix spends little time on the rise in France of the far-right National Rally, which appears poised to win the French presidency in the spring. How a right-wing France in the engine room of Europe would affect broader rearmament is a question that should be top of mind in Brussels today.

    The implications of German rearmament are vexing, and the recent surge in spending represents easy yards. But for a remilitarized Germany to truly enhance European security, it must surrender more of its own power, decision-making, and even defense-industrial spending to the rest of Europe. Otherwise, Europe will have answered Eisenhower’s challenge 75 years on only to produce a more fractured continent as the United States pulls back.

    #30463. Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This article was originally published on The Conversation.
    • Against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth declared on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone.
    • The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article was originally published on The Conversation.

    Against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth declared on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone. That, the department later stated, would include assessing symptoms of low testosterone such as “reduced libido, loss of spontaneous morning erections, erectile dysfunction, diminished energy and physical performance, impaired concentration, reduced muscle mass, and depressed mood.”.

    The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.

    For some time there’s been a contentious debate among writers, historians and public intellectuals over whether Donald Trump’s presidency could be considered “fascist.” Some have argued that such claims are hyperbolic or inaccurate, while others say it is a useful and accurate ideological label.

    Either way, it would be difficult to deny that the Trump administration frequently draws from the well of fascist imagery and symbolism in its official messaging.

    And that’s where the concept of cringe fascism fits in. In online parlance,“cringe” is a kind of embarrassment by proxy when someone posts something that should be embarrassing but which doesn’t seem to be to them.

    For their part, members of the Trump administration have relied on language and symbolism that borrows from the fascist or authoritarian playbook while doing so in a way that commenters often mock as patently ridiculous or embarrassing – or cringe.

    But the purported silliness of these ideas, as with Hegseth’s testosterone policy, hides a much more serious – and to some critics, fascist – reality. That, moreover, is why the deployment of cringe can be effective: It can generate enthusiasm among conservative voters by trolling the left while reducing deadly serious policy debates to the level of online memes.

    As Americans prepare for the midterms and a surely contentious presidential election in 2028, such considerations of Trump’s authoritarian tendencies are being put to the test. That’s especially true as he consistently threatens the integrity of elections, deploys immigration and other federal law enforcement officers on American streets in a highly contested manner, and attempts to target the press and restrict its access.

    As a scholar of conspiracy theories, I have been amazed at some of the more blatant efforts to repurpose fascist imagery by members of Trump’s inner circle.

    According to recent reports, consider, for example, the use of ethnonationalist and fascist imagery of “blood and soil” in sloganeering by the Department of Homeland Security, or encouraging U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits to “Defend the Homeland.”.

    In a recent development, and then there are the attacks on the press as the “enemy of the people,” echoing past totalitarian leaders, followed by Trump’s banning of mainstream media from the White House and the launch of Trump TV as the state channel. Critics view such moves to attack and restrict the press as hallmarks of fascist methods.

    Borrowing more obviously from fascist tropes was Trump posting on social media a mock-up of a potential fresh Space Force uniform. The post claimed to draw inspiration from Paul Verhoeven’s “Starship Troopers,” in which the soldiers are deliberately modeled on the fascist aesthetic and ideology of the Nazis.

    Alongside the authoritarian and fascist tropes, the Trump administration cannot seem to avoid “cringe.”.

    Recent examples include the White House tweeting images of Trump as a videogame character on a select screen with sleeveless blue suit and bulging muscles, or sharing an AI parody of the new Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time game with an awkward video of a pixelated Trump running around the White House lawn. Or consider the post depicting Trump as Green Lantern, using his magic ring to raise a spectral border wall, launch a military attack and fix American industry.

    On the one hand, the Trump administration seems determined to keep his party in power and enact a transformative MAGA policy agenda. On the other hand, Trump seems incapable of avoiding cringey riffs such as his digressions on men’s bodies in ways that seem strikingly at odds with his tough-guy persona. To see the commander in chief waxing poetic about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear feels deeply surreal.

    It has been revealed that trump’s seemingly incongruous comments occur at the same time that the secretary of defense is advocating hypermasculinity in the military through testosterone testing, reflecting a heady mix of masculinity and military supremacy that has long been a hallmark of fascism. Such a policy is also at odds with how the professional military has presented itself under previous administrations.

    The mixture of fascist aesthetics with cringe posting underscores the internal contradictions of the Trump administration.

    In a recent development, it is difficult to see critics’ view of Trump’s second term as “fascist” when observers get such awkward online displays of silliness. And when official communications from the White House and federal agencies are equal parts tough talk, trolling and cringe, the underlying policies can get lost in the shuffle.

    Sources indicate that is is hard to know whether this flood of cringe is always intentional, but it is certainly confusing and hilarious to both Trump’s supporters and his opponents. But that belies what many critics have decried as authoritarian actions by this administration, and these comparisons with fascism continue to animate public discourse.

    Masked ICE agents continue to operate with some legal protections from the White House in their sometimes-deadly efforts to pursue and round up people it broadly accuses of being in the country illegally.

    Likewise, the DHS announced that ICE agents could be deployed to polling locations, while the agency has reportedly attempted to get access to voter information to investigate alleged voter fraud through increased surveillance.

    The deployment of cringe might seems like a ridiculous, even unconscious, exercise by an administration that – as with the five-day tenure of former press secretary Katie Zacharia highlights – regularly exposes itself to derision and satire. Yet that’s why the use of such a concept can be so strategically effective: It turns potentially deadly serious policy consequences and ideological choices into a game of memes and online gamesmanship.

    Matthew N. Hannah, Associate Professor of Rhetoric, Politics and Culture, University of Wisconsin-Madison.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Roll-A-Rack, a developer of patented, on-site-manufactured solar racking systems, will introduce SunChord, its upcoming multi-purpose ground-mounted system, at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas.

    SunChord solar racking from Roll-A-Rack.

    It has been revealed that sunChord is a low-profile solar racking designed to use less land than conventional fixed-tilt racking or trackers. It is composed of two components: gutter channels and clamp brackets that attach to solar panels. SunChord assembles using what Roll-A-Rack has dubbed its “snap-slide-secure” system.

    In a recent development, “The next generation of solar technology needs to do more than produce clean electricity. It needs to make better use of land, minimize environmental impacts and create value beyond the energy generated,” stated Don Scipione, founder of Roll-A-Rack. “SunChord reflects our vision of harmonizing sun and earth, combining solar energy production with rainwater harvesting and soil conservation in a system that can unlock new opportunities for solar development on land where conventional approaches fall short.”.

    Industry observers note that roll-A-Rack claims an array using SunChord can capture 95% of rain that falls it using its racking channels to redirect the water. The tech giant sees potential for the racking in agrivoltaic applications, sites with land constraints, on brownfields and where ground disturbance should be limited.

    Sources indicate that sunChord is assembled on-site using a roll-forming device similar to producing roof-edge gutters. SunChord was developed with support from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Integrated Energy Systems Office and the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture. The company has two issued U.S. patents, a patent application pending, wind-tunnel ratings and UL 2703 certification.

    Roll-A-Rack is planning to supply SunChord for up to five pilot projects. Interested EPCs and developers can contact the manufacturer at [email protected].

    #30461. Latest Update: No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (824 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said.
    • Industry observers note that in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness.
    • Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”.

    Industry observers note that in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

    Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

    A major takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

    What may have looked like a upcoming GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

    With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

    Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

    Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

    Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ newly introduced populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

    Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

    White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

    Recent findings suggest that while there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

    If you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

    If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

    The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

    At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • The semiconductor manufacturer Nvidia, which had until recently been the most valuable tech giant in the world, was thrown into turmoil this past week.
