    #30441. The Journalists Who Left Russia—But Can’t Escape It

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2124 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignpolicy ↗ Open Full Page

    The Journalists Who Left Russia—But Can’t Escape It

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • What does a citizen owe to their country?
    • Such is the moral dilemma afflicting the characters of My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, Julia Loktev’s sequel to her acclaimed 2024 documentary about the unraveling of Russia’s last independent television channel, Dozhd (or TV Rain), in the wake of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
    • What does a citizen owe to their country?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Understanding the conflict four years in.

    What does a citizen owe to their country? And what if that country is Russia?

    Such is the moral dilemma afflicting the characters of My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, Julia Loktev’s sequel to her acclaimed 2024 documentary about the unraveling of Russia’s last independent television channel, Dozhd (or TV Rain), in the wake of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The first installment chronicles the channel’s final days in Moscow in March of 2022, and Part II follows its journalists into exile.

    What does a citizen owe to their country? And what if that country is Russia?

    Industry observers note that such is the moral dilemma afflicting the characters of My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, Julia Loktev’s sequel to her acclaimed 2024 documentary about the unraveling of Russia’s last independent television channel, Dozhd (or TV Rain), in the wake of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The first installment chronicles the channel’s final days in Moscow in March of 2022, and Part II follows its journalists into exile.

    Recent findings suggest that loktev’s protagonists, almost all women, fled as Russia imposed censorship laws that made their already dangerous jobs punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Within days of Dozhd’s disbandment, sometimes hours, they scooped up their laptops, pets, children, and underwear and flew wherever they could without a fresh visa—Istanbul, Tbilisi, Prague, Tel Aviv.

    They resisted Russian President Vladimir Putin and his government, yet wherever they go, they remain citizens of a country that is invading and killing its neighbors and are held responsible for the war it wages in their name.

    “You feel like it’s 1941 and you’re simultaneously the German and the Jew” says journalist Anna Nemzer, as she reloads her vape cartridge.

    Loktev’s subjects are buffeted by cognitive dissonance and must constantly explain themselves—to their Georgian and Latvian hosts, who urge them to “tell Putin to stop the war”; to their Ukrainian sources, who resent the very language that they speak; to their Russian parents who tell them to stop writing anti-government “bullshit” and come home; and even to themselves, wondering what they could have done differently to stop their country’s slide into fascism, and whether their work matters when Russian missiles continue to rain down on Ukraine.

    According to recent reports, loktev, who shot the film herself on an iPhone, gives these questions room. At six hours, this film is even longer than its predecessor—a bold choice—but the sheer accumulation of ordinary moments makes this exploration of exile intimate and compelling. For viewers willing to grapple with existential dilemmas and lucky enough to live near an art-house cinema, the movie’s length may be a boon. After all, its central questions are ones that take a lifetime to sort out.

    Perhaps no one takes up these questions more bluntly than Elena Kostyuchenko of the recently shuttered Novaya Gazeta, where, during her tenure, four of her colleagues were murdered. “All of us … spent many years, thoroughly, in great detail, in very good, well-written articles describing the coming of fascism in Russia,” she notes. “Well, there you fucking go. So we wrote all those articles.” Elsewhere, she is just as unsparing about the failure to stop Putin from turning Russia into what it is today: “We didn’t want to sacrifice our comfort.”.

    Alesya Marokhovskaya expresses similar unease as she recalls watching someone get beaten at a protest. “My job is to film,” she says. “You don’t rush in to defend the person. You film them, because, well, that’s your job.”.

    Recent findings suggest that despite those doubts, the journalists keep doing journalism. They provide truthful coverage of the war to Russian-speaking audiences through YouTube channels, podcasts, and eventually live broadcasts from Riga, Latvia, where Dozhd secured a broadcasting license. But they are walking on eggshells. A series of on-air missteps that led to questions about the station’s allegiances ultimately cost Dozhd its initial broadcasting license, forcing it to relocate to the Netherlands, where it operates today.

    Irina Dolinina continues to work in exile from Prague.Cinetic.

    Industry observers note that the hope of finding safety outside Russia does not last long. Alesya and her best friend Irina Dolinina, investigative journalists with IStories (or Crucial Stories), now based in Prague, receive oddly specific anonymous threats. The senders know their passport numbers, flight reservations, even about Alesya’s “snorting” bulldog. Latest friends are not always who they say they are: A supposed human rights lawyer Irina befriends previously worked for Moscow police. Alesya’s father, meanwhile, doesn’t understand why his daughter left. The war is in Ukraine, he notes, not Russia.

    Sources indicate that but for most of these women, war is everywhere. From a temporary shelter in a Swiss village, where cathedral bells mark the hours of another peaceful day, Kostyuchenko recounts the symptoms of what she believes was a deliberate poisoning in Munich in October 2022: foul sweat, disorientation, nausea, swollen extremities.

    In a recent development, months before, reporting from the Ukrainian city of Mykolaiv, Kostyuchenko had visited a morgue overflowing with victims of Russian shelling, which she wrote about with brutal clarity. “In the fridge, the bodies are stacked in layers. Two girls lie on top of each other. They’re sisters. The older one is 17—in the heap of bodies, all I can see is her hand, long thin fingers with a neat pink manicure. The younger is 3—she lies on top of her sister. … Her body is dotted with red shrapnel wounds. The girl looks alive.”.

    Recent findings suggest that despite atrocities that should have stopped the world in its tracks, life goes on, and Loktev’s film captures that well. Kostyuchenko loves, and loves deeply. Her partner is Yana Kuchina, a Moscow book editor turned disability-rights advocate who followed Kostyuchenko into exile. A newcomer to Loktev’s saga, Yana delivers some of the film’s most chilling insights into how Russia treats its own. Her cerebral palsy, she says, is considered an “intellectual inadequacy” in the eyes of the authorities, barring her from getting a driver’s license, becoming a doctor, or adopting a child.

    Sources indicate that you’d have to be fearless or a fanatic to persist in journalism in Russia. These women are both.

    So-called realists arguing for Ukraine’s surrender can’t let go of the past.

    How Moscow broke with the West—and unleashed a more chaotic world.

    Ksenia Mironova and co-director Julia Loktev speak after a screening of My Undesirable Friends: Part II: Exile at the Upcoming York Film Festival on Sept. 27.Michael Loccisano/Getty Images.

    Besides Yana, Kostyuchenko loves her mother—whose birthday she is missing for the first time—and her country. Her life there, she felt, was real. “I worked at the best newspaper on Earth. … All around me was my country, which I … value and love still.” Her love is definitely not blind, but for Ukrainians, whose country Russia is destroying, it may be difficult to comprehend, much less forgive.

    Unlike Elena and Yana, former Dozhd reporter Ksenia (Ksyusha) Mironova walks the road of exile alone, a melancholy kaleidoscope of taxi rides, dark staircases, and endless rented rooms; her fiancé, the journalist Ivan Safronov, is still being held in a Moscow prison on fabricated charges of high treason. Ksyusha returns to Russia for his sentencing, a trip Loktev also documents. Ivan gets 22 years.

    Sources indicate that in the midst of so much loss, there are brief moments of tenderness. In a rented apartment abroad, Ksyusha and her Dozhd friends sing along to a Russian song: “When you return … I hope we recognize each other … and I am not your wife and not even your girlfriend.” It is probably the most Russian scene in the entire movie—elegiac, haunting, yet oddly hopeful.

    After leaving Russia with her family, Anna Nemzer spent time in Tblisi, Georgia.Cinetic.

    According to recent reports, ksyusha is neither a victim nor a tragic heroine; behind her soft, girlish looks is a rod of steel. No longer with Dozhd, she moves from country to country, taking whatever freelance jobs she can find to keep herself afloat and working as an independent journalist covering political prisoners, their families, and the lives of Russians in exile. In 2025, we see her in the United States reporting on President Donald Trump’s second inauguration. “It’s really strange I’m now in America and the same things are happening here,” she says. She now works with Nemzer to archive independent journalism, including to preserve two decades of coverage in Russia against the Kremlin’s attempts to erase it.

    Sonya Groysman, another Dozhd journalist, finds ingenious ways to report on Russia from exile, directing anonymous camera operators, including wedding videographers. One of her reports features Sasha Skochilenko, an artist who was sentenced to seven years in prison for replacing price tags in a St. Petersburg supermarket with anti-war messages. The camera zooms in on a black-and-white tag above the coffee cans reading “Russia’s Army bombed Mariupol art school where 400 people hid from shelling.” It’s yet another reminder that in Russia, the price of truth is your freedom.

    Recent findings suggest that or your life. A sizable part of the documentary is devoted to the 2024 death of opposition leader Alexey Navalny. Dozhd, broadcasting from Amsterdam, ran videos of him from the day before his death, where he looks energetic and fairly healthy. In their coverage, the presenters called his death in prison what many in Russia knew but were afraid to say: a killing. Navalny went to prison to change people’s minds, indicates tearful Valeria Ratnikova, a Dozhd news anchor, between the airings of her show. He was a beacon for many. Now, all she sees is “total blackness ahead.”.

    Valeria Ratnikova stays in a hotel in Istanbul after fleeing Russia.Cinetic.

    Sources indicate that the only characters spared this Dostoyevskian moral anguish are, unsurprisingly, Ukrainian. “We don’t have the energy and time to worry and panic,” says Nataliya Gumenyuk, a prominent Ukrainian journalist and war correspondent who is married to a longtime former Dozhd journalist. “We live in our own country and continue to do our work.” Among the movie’s most striking images is that of Ukrainians dancing in a square in Kharkiv, where entire blocks are flattened by air strikes, the sound of Ukrainian folk songs mixing with the howling of the air raid sirens. Nataliya’s Russian husband, Peter, resolved his moral dilemma by joining the Ukrainian army and now records his Fuck the War! podcast between missions.

    Industry observers note that from its upcoming home in the Netherlands, the “optimistic channel,” as Dozhd was once known, still reaches 13 million as of 2023, according to Dozhd. Because coverage of the war not aligning with Kremlin narratives has been all but silenced, most watch through VPNs and proxies. For journalists, reporting on Russia’s war means living the Russian reality. This makes integration into their new countries nearly impossible; they are neither here nor there. But going home is not an option. Ratnikova, for one, was sentenced to seven-and-a-half years in prison in absentia by a Moscow court. Loktev records her hearing over a video call, where “witnesses” explain how the “false information” about the war “confused” them. This is how Russian justice works.

    In a recent development, for now, Ratnikova has a visa, a job, a place to stay. That could change overnight. Political exile is not war, but that’s a low bar for young men and women who could have lived a relatively normal life. By reporting independently, first in an increasingly authoritarian state, then from exile, often at considerable risk to themselves, they have given more to their country than its perpetually silent majority.

    It has been revealed that one of Ratnikova’s colleagues likens their mission to Sisyphus pushing his stone uphill: not as punishment, but by choice. They keep at it, hoping their work might still change minds in a country that seems irretrievably lost. Loktev’s immersion in their lives leaves us with hope for them, if not for Russia’s future.

    Anastasia Edel is a Russian-born American writer and social historian. She is the author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, a concise guide to Russian history, politics, and culture. Her writing has appeared in the Atlantic, the Fresh York Review of Books, the New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, Project Syndicate, and others. She teaches history at the Osher Lifelong Learning Institute at the University of California, Berkeley. X: @AEdelWriter.

    What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads.
    • However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S.
    • The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

    However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

    The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

    Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

    It has been revealed that “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom remarked. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”.

    In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

    Industry observers note that black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They revealed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

    When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

    Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

    Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

    In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

    Sources indicate that I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

    The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

    But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

    Recent findings suggest that "I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

    Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

    What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

    Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson initiative?

    Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials promptly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

    That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

    Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she noted.

    Recent findings suggest that colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”.

    Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

    I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

    • According to recent reports, “Management of PV wires and AC trunk cables is one of the most notable aspects of rooftop PV installation.
    • Sources indicate that DCSR is designed with a wire trough large enough to fit three-phase trunk cables, like those manufactured by Enphase, Hoymiles, and AP Systems.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Martin Solar‘s newly manufactured Dual-Channel Solar Rail (DCSR) was recently installed on a 70-kWDC solar project, marking its first real-world application.

    The Dual-Channel Solar Rail from Martin Solar.

    According to recent reports, “Management of PV wires and AC trunk cables is one of the most notable aspects of rooftop PV installation. Anyone who has ever experienced running hundreds, thousands of feet of conductors on a rooftop system knows what a hassle it is having to apply countless zip ties that are not really suitable for long-term wire management,” stated Preston Nelson, director of Martin Solar and co-inventor of DCSR. “What’s worse than the initial application of zip ties is having to pull up finished solar panels to apply even more zip ties after an inspector inevitably cites an installation for having wires that droop down to the roof surface.”.

    Sources indicate that DCSR is designed with a wire trough large enough to fit three-phase trunk cables, like those manufactured by Enphase, Hoymiles, and AP Systems. It can also fit up to twenty standard PV cables, without the use of zip ties. Instead of using specialized panel clamps, DCSR’s panel attachment channel is off to the side of the wire trough, where it separately accepts panel hardware.

    “The dual-channel design with separately dedicated features allowed us to increase the cross-sectional area of the wire trough to a size never seen before as a rail feature. In the past, we would install a separate wire tray to manage numerous long trunk cable runs, which was even more expensive and time-consuming. Now, this present project installation involves over 600 total feet of trunk, without a single cable tie. The separate wire trough can even allow access to wire runs without lifting panels, especially convenient when a worker simply needs to track a PV string,” Nelson noted.

    Recent findings suggest that DCSR is the first product accessory to Martin Solar’s Hidden-Fastener Solar Mount, which mounts to the roof surface without putting holes in shingles. While Martin’s proprietary solar rail and mount can be paired, both are compatible with other solar racking and mounts.

    Martin Solar will show DCSR and its solar mounting system at RE+ from November 17 to 19 at booth C5071.

    • This is a motif that features heavily in David M.
    • Industry observers note that some of the most enduring theories of power were born in its absence.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that some of the most enduring theories of power were born in its absence. Thucydides, exiled from Amphipolis for failing to ward off the Spartans, surmised that “the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.” Thomas Hobbes, forced to flee an England consumed by civil bloodshed amid an ailing monarchy, argued that only absolute authority can tame humanity’s primal “state of nature.” Machiavelli, tortured and driven from political life by the Medicis, opined that successful rulers must sometimes be ruthless. Circumstances vary, but when the right observer falls into the pits of powerlessness, they can see in human nature what others cannot.

    This is a motif that features heavily in David M. Sacks’ The Realist: Hans Morgenthau and the Purpose of American Power, a meticulously researched biography of the man who made international relations theory a field in its own right—by putting power at its theoretical core.

    Industry observers note that some of the most enduring theories of power were born in its absence. Thucydides, exiled from Amphipolis for failing to ward off the Spartans, surmised that “the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.” Thomas Hobbes, forced to flee an England consumed by civil bloodshed amid an ailing monarchy, argued that only absolute authority can tame humanity’s primal “state of nature.” Machiavelli, tortured and driven from political life by the Medicis, opined that successful rulers must sometimes be ruthless. Circumstances vary, but when the right observer falls into the pits of powerlessness, they can see in human nature what others cannot.

    According to recent reports, the Realist: Hans Morgenthau and the Purpose of American Power, David M. Sacks, Henry Holt & Co., 528 pp., $36.99, November 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that this is a motif that features heavily in David M. Sacks’ The Realist: Hans Morgenthau and the Purpose of American Power, a meticulously researched biography of the man who made international relations theory a field in its own right—by putting power at its theoretical core.

    Industry observers note that the Realist starts with a cold open: summer 1922 in Coburg, Germany, on a day Morgenthau would later describe as the worst of his life. A high school junior ranked second in his class, Morgenthau was slated to address his peers as part of a celebratory academic tradition. “But what should have been a triumph promptly turned to humiliation,” writes Sacks. The townspeople turned their backs, spat on Morgenthau, and barraged him with antisemitic vitriol for having the gall to participate in a “Christian Day” ceremony. All because, in their eyes, he was no more than a “stinking Jew.”.

    Recent findings suggest that while that day would leave an indelible scar on Morgenthau, it wasn’t his true awakening. Later that year, he would attend one of Hitler’s gatherings in Munich to witness with his own eyes the antisemitic tide said to be sweeping across all of Germany. It was “one of the most profound experiences of my life,” Morgenthau recalled. Soon after, the same scene played out in his own backyard: In defiance of local law, the führer sallied into Coburg with 800 stormtroopers and delivered two fiery philippics, whipping up a public paroxysm of threats, assaults, and mass street brawls, with tacit support from town police.

    According to recent reports, in just two days’ time, Morgenthau’s sleepy, parochial hometown became one of the Nazis’ earliest political proving grounds. From this, Morgenthau “drew a clear lesson,” writes Sacks. “He, and other powerless individuals, could not rely on the law or abstract ideals for protection.”.

    In a recent development, nazis in Coburg, Germany, in 1922. Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group via Getty Images.

    In a recent development, in one sense, The Realist is, as its title suggests, a study on an -ism—the school of thought that every international relations major must acquaint themselves with during their baptismal power-skim of Morgenthau’s 750-page syllabus staple, Politics Among Nations. The book sketches all the contours of political realism: Nations pursue power above all; peace depends on a healthy balance of it; and moral values must align with national interest and practical constraints.

    Industry observers note that but the basis of this framework, Sacks writes, was not incubated in an ivory tower; it was forged from a story of Sturm und Drang. Growing up Jewish during the rise of the Third Reich, Morgenthau endured a traumatic crescendo of antisemitism that “molded one’s whole life,” he wrote. He was the target of constant bullying and abuse, finding respite only in schoolwork, and sank into isolation and embitterment at a young age. Morgenthau’s father, too, was not spared: A doctor, he lost his medical license after the Nazis falsely accused him of professional misconduct, wiping away what little standing the family had left in Coburg.

    Industry observers note that after Morgenthau left for Frankfurt to pursue philosophy and law, he drew on the brutishness he’d seen among the common German volk—that “primitive” and “irrational” impulse—to elaborate his grand theory of power, one that was, in a sense, post-traumatic in character. It demanded constant hypervigilance and self-preservation. It doubted the durability of security commitments, and expressed a healthy skepticism toward rules, norms, and laws. And it saw the world’s default state as anarchy, ready to rear its ugly head yet again at any time. “The distribution of power,” as Morgenthau warned, “is always precarious.”.

    In the lead-up to World War II, this distribution of power wasn’t just skewing toward Germany; it was careening dangerously in Hitler’s favor. Few observers at the time saw this as lucidly—or as urgently—as Morgenthau, and Hitler’s expansionist designs were proof of concept.

    Industry observers note that but despite this prescience, it seems, Morgenthau mostly floundered as a young academic. He took whatever teaching jobs he could find in a Europe ravaged by the Great Depression with little appetite for his ideas, let alone his ethnic heritage. In Geneva, Sacks writes, colleagues found his Cassandra-like rhetoric a “disturbing influence.” At Brooklyn College, students felt his anticommunism was befitting of a hysterical “Hearst reporter.” In Kansas City, which Morgenthau called an “overgrown cow town,” his émigré ambition clashed with a culture in which academic standards were relatively modest—or, again in his words, “virtually non-existent.” Even when he first arrived at the tony University of Chicago, where he’d be a fixture for the next three decades, Morgenthau’s emphasis on theory over practice and empiricism put him at odds with his department.

    The school of thought doesn’t explain everything—but its proponents foresaw the potential for conflict over Ukraine long before it erupted.

    According to recent reports, what emerges from this account is a portrait of a man who was not just politically persecuted but constantly intellectually embattled. Yet he was never cowed by power. By Morgenthau’s own admission, he refused “to play the role of the suffering martyr,” and it’s hard not to agree. The book makes clear that Morgenthau met nearly every criticism he faced with an equal and opposite reaction. This is someone who took to prestige media to publicly pillory his detractors with a revolutionary’s zeal (“trash,” “hatchet man,” “fanatical wrongheadedness”), as if their objections were affronts to his own lived experience.

    Recent findings suggest that and perhaps they were. After all, Sacks spills relatively little ink on the thinker’s life outside of work. In this respect, the book seems to imply by omission that Morgenthau’s personal and intellectual identities were, by dint of his traumatic upbringing, fused. We are teased with tidbits about Morgenthau’s wife, who softened his hard edges among friends and whose family supported them financially; his mother, the “closest companion throughout his life”; his authoritarian father, who believed he would never amount to anything; his son, who appeared to suffer from various ailments; and his extramarital affairs, which were far from passionless.

    Recent findings suggest that but for the most part, these read like brief digressions with little bearing on the bigger story. This is a weak point for a first-ever biography of such a fascinating figure, let alone one whose intellectual mission clearly seemed to color his personal life in a number of ways, and vice versa. Consider, for example, Morgenthau’s sudden interest in the Jewish question: The theorist had never been observant, did not know his Hebrew name, and was largely agnostic on Israel and the plight of the Soviet Jewry until his early 60s, believing that the Jewish state fell outside his sphere of interest. But by the late 1960s, after his forced retirement from the University of Chicago, Sacks writes, something “elemental” had shifted in Morgenthau. Feeling “disillusioned and cast aside,” he suddenly found great meaning and purpose in the Jewish community. His personal involvement with Chabad in particular fueled a political zeal for aiding Soviet refuseniks as well as a fierce insistence on Israel’s right to self-defense following the Six-Day War. This is a highly intriguing turn in Morgenthau’s story, but it’s, again, one The Realist gives little airtime.

    It has been revealed that similarly, the book also could have lingered a bit more on Morgenthau’s bond with Hannah Arendt, another Jewish German émigré who fled the Nazis. The duo’s epistolary exchanges are rich with romantic intrigue—he may have proposed to her while still married—and intellectual compatibility. After all, they were both strangers in a strange land, hacking their way through the U.S. garden of liberal rationalism. When Arendt unveiled her infamous theory of the “banality of evil” while covering Adolf Eichmann’s trial in 1963, she provoked an intellectual maelstrom among colleagues at the University of Chicago, many of whom shunned her in response. Morgenthau, meanwhile, stood by Arendt and wrote to her gushingly, “Reality has protruded into the protective armor of illusion and the result is psychological havoc.” His use of the word “reality” was likely no coincidence.

    Morgenthau addresses an audience in Washington, D.C., on May 15, 1965, while taking part in a national, 15-hour teach-in on the Vietnam War.Associated Press.

    Recent findings suggest that over the past several years, conflicts from Gaza to Ukraine to Iran have prompted a great deal of debate among observers about whether the world is seeing the supposed return of realism. However, it’s worth remembering that aggression alone is not a good proxy for the presence of realism, which, as John Mearsheimer notes, is in large part predicated on restraint. Rather, the violence exposes a core realist truth: With no mechanism of holding great powers to account, the international rules-based order is still only as strong as those who abide by it.

    It has been revealed that the Realist, for its part, wisely avoids wading into contemporary politics, instead letting the resonance of realism’s history speak for itself. Nowhere is that more striking than in the book’s account of the Vietnam War.

    Sources indicate that one might assume that Morgenthau—who called for a very muscular posture toward the Soviet-backed Castro government during the Cuban missile crisis—was all for U.S. intervention in communist North Vietnam. However, Sacks goes to great lengths to show that he was an outspoken opponent from the jump: For two decades, Morgenthau waged a war of words with officials in the Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon administrations, including McGeorge Bundy, Robert McNamara, Walt Rostow, and Henry Kissinger (a frenemy of sorts). By the mid-1960s, as the conflict became clearly unwinnable, Morgenthau grew deeply distressed by the carnage on moral grounds. But his original argument had always been one of narrow political strategy: that the growth of communism in North Vietnam “simply was not a vital interest,” as Sacks writes. We must only intervene “where our national interest requires it and where our power gives us a chance to succeed,” Morgenthau wrote. “If the United States applies this standard, it will intervene less and succeed more.”.

    To say that the United States has done just the opposite would be a great understatement. In the aftermath of 9/11, President George W. Bush’s anti-terror war in Iraq created the conditions for the world’s deadliest terror organization to flourish, while the war in Afghanistan—which spanned four presidents—began and ended with Taliban rule. Though U.S. officials justified both interventions on the basis of national interest, prominent members of the neorealist school vehemently opposed them. Broadly speaking, this was because the conflicts were driven less by narrow strategy and more by either quixotic (nation-building) or chimeric (eliminating weapons of mass destruction) goals. When those goals could not be realized, the U.S. mission crept, and officials resorted to sunk-cost fallacies about credibility instead of retrenchment; the very same tack was taken by Kissinger, who attempted to argue on realist grounds that the United States would lose international “prestige” by pulling out of Vietnam. As for the current war in Iran, declared on the all-too-familiar pretext of imminent nuclear capability, the United States seems woefully bound to repeat the same cycle, and no amount of victory declarations from our commander-in-chief will change that.

    To be sure, these military misadventures do not suggest that realism reigns supreme in international relations. Instead, they point to one of its key weaknesses: the malleability of “national interest”—especially, and perhaps ironically, in the face of trauma.

    When Morgenthau published his first book, Scientific Man versus Power Politics, in 1946, Sacks notes that some critics found the term “national interest” too nebulous—a gripe that Morgenthau actually took in stride. U.S. military misadventures in the Middle East reveal that this problem remains in full effect. The country’s collective trauma after 9/11 gave the U.S. government a pretext to widen the aperture of “national interest” so much so that temporally or geographically distant threats—like simmering political instability in a region many Americans could not point to on a map—suddenly became existentially urgent. “As long as the Middle East remains a place where freedom does not flourish,” as Bush said in 2003, “it will remain a place of stagnation, resentment, and violence ready for export.” The United States met this specter of violence in much the same way it did Vietnam’s communism: with real violence. After two decades, our efforts to install a democratic regime resulted in nothing more than hundreds of thousands of civilian casualties. “The evil we wanted to prevent,” as Morgenthau wrote of Vietnam, was “nothing compared with the evil we left behind.”.

    Sources indicate that it may be tempting to see the “return” of realism in a world where the United States continues to pursue power brutally, by any means necessary. Yet if realist thought now predominates among U.S. foreign-policymakers, it is a far cry from the realism of Morgenthau’s making. Instead, it is a realism in which national trauma has turned national interest into an empty signifier, used for vengeful wish fulfillment at the expense of sober statecraft. If “great nations” like the United States are truly great because “they married … power to purpose,” as Morgenthau believed, then what has that purpose been over the last quarter-century of foreign policy? It’s hard to think of anything other than power itself.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, A judge mentioned he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

    Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

    “This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg stated.

    The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

    Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he noted next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

    Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”.

    The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

    “You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg remarked.

    Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump remarked last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

    Separately, Boasberg noted he may glitch rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

    The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

    For years Trump has stated he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that for all the horrible things Donald Trump has wrought upon the world — and there are so, so many — he’s also taught us some important lessons. Trump is proof of several truths: A red-meat-and-stress-addled heart can withstand otherwise unthinkable conditions with the federal government’s medical secrets; reality television ruined the world; and, if we’re not careful, we’re all liable to become parodies of ourselves one day, crying about it online.

    That latter bit is certainly true for filmmaker Taika Waititi, whose otherwise tacky-yet-progressive veneer cracked last weekend when he took to Instagram to condemn the poor reviews of his latest film, “Klara and the Sun.” After a torrent of bad press and worse box-office performance, the film’s distributor, Sony, opted to scale back the movie’s wide release, reducing the sci-fi dramedy’s reach from 2,000 theaters nationwide to 800, most of which returned a meager profit. Never one to take his mediocrity on the chin, Waititi deflected the negativity outward, which, as we know, always paints someone in a good light!

    Recent findings suggest that waititi’s childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Donald Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

    It has been revealed that waititi reposted a graphic claiming that “Klara and the Sun” was “rebounding” with a 78% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, a 53-point gap from the film’s 25% critics score. (For what it’s worth, neither number should ever be used to accurately measure a film’s quality.) “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in 15 years,” Waititi captioned the post. “But I do listen to the people . . . Let’s spare a thought for those sad, lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”.

    Reading Waititi’s emoji-peppered caption, I was surprised to find it so carelessly evoked the Trumpian crybaby approach to social media. Whether on X or his own Truth Social, Trump’s favorite way of addressing critics and opponents has long been to toss out adjectives at will. Tack a “SAD!” at the end of Waititi’s caption, and it could easily pass for one of Trump’s poetic musings. (If only Waititi had gone so far as to parrot my personal favorite Trump quip about Barney Frank by saying, “The critics looked disgusting, nipples protruding, in front of my movie. Very very disrespectful.”).

    Ironically, all those admonishments in Waititi’s caption are also fitting descriptors for the state of Donald Trump’s agenda, the one imitated by his legions of Republican cronies spread out across America, hoping to be elected in Tuesday’s midterms. But judging by the results, MAGA’s influence is waning fast. Seven Senate seats flipped, historically red states turned blue and a spate of monumental wins popped up nationwide. The MAGA bubble popped in real time. Americans have seen firsthand what little good fascist ideology does for the average, working-class person. And though the country may not become great again overnight, it appears the last 12 years of freefall have finally been suspended — at least for now.

    Not to be all, “Oh, won’t someone think of the celebrities?” about it, but such overwhelmingly positive election results left me wondering what happens to someone like Waititi, whose childish outburst is straight from the MAGA playbook. For over a decade, Trump has used social media to peddle broadly disparaging, dangerous rhetoric that has legitimate impact outside the phone screen. The reckless hatred comprising MAGA ideology is so potent that it’s bled into the ways even otherwise progressive people wield their power, like crude oil painting an ocean black. And while refuting film critics isn’t akin to Trump’s most damning sins, Waititi’s mockery is a symptom of a problem that won’t be washed away by one blue wave, no matter how sizable.

    It has been revealed that one would think that Waititi would know better. For one, the guy is 51 years old, certainly experienced and well-established enough to let a flop roll off his back. How fitting that his biggest success is the anti-fascist yet aesthetically tasteless political satire, “Jojo Rabbit,” which won the Oscar for best adapted screenplay in 2020, just as the Trump era was revving up for its second leg. That film, about a 10-year-old Hitler Youth who begins to grapple with the realities of life in 1940s Germany, examines propaganda’s influence and the power of hegemony, even if it often lacks the nuance and perspective such a satire warrants. For better, or more often, for worse, Waititi’s writing displays a self-possessed vulgarity that gets in the way of his more salient observations. Case in point: It’s downright ludicrous to stake your name on a film renouncing hate, then take aim at critics — people not exactly matched in influence to someone like Waititi — just six years later.

    But this is the rot that social media creates. Whether it’s Instagram, X, TikTok, or YouTube, these sites have incentivized and monetized incendiary opinions. Their algorithms push small people into major power. What was designed to ostensibly be a great equalizer has only divided the world more, making animosity easily accessible to anyone who gets their rocks off on sewing discourse through cruelty.

    Sources indicate that for some time now, arts critics have been easy targets on these platforms. Gone are the days of the critic playing dilettante, having intellectual conversations over martinis and cigarettes at the month’s salon for like-minded individuals. To be a critic today — to pursue one’s passion for art and writing and learning, all rolled into one — is to subject oneself to a pretty bleak existence. In most cases, the pay is meager. The hours are long. The job is demanding. And virtually no one has the patience or attention span to read an entire article anymore, let alone engage with its ideas. A legitimate critic doesn’t stumble into the job just to point and laugh; they write because they have real passion for what they cover. Surely someone like Waititi would say the same when he begins a latest project after a string of flops.

    If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person notes so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines.

    What Waititi fails to realize is that he’s not punching up or down, but laterally. This is artist versus artist. If the context is right, a good piece of criticism can be as life-altering as a good film. But that’s hard to see when the internet has built such a wide chasm between people, reducing the impact of writing in favor of scrolling. Along with social media’s effect on human behavior, it’s had a heavy hand in blunting the journalism industry. If everyone’s a critic, then no one is, and that’s precisely why monitoring Rotten Tomatoes scores like they’re poll numbers is futile and ridiculous.

    According to recent reports, but it’s not just Waititi who’s vulnerable to this unique form of MAGA-tinged, social media-brained psychosis; critics can fall prey to it, too. Whether it’s a filmmaker, a film critic, or just your average filmgoer, social media has confined us all to its machine. No one is exempt from consumer tech’s sway. And if a writer or filmmaker wants to make a splash, tossing out an inflammatory opinion aimed at a peer is a surefire shortcut. I’ve seen this affect critics’ prose over time, with certain writers (or their outlets) favoring button-pushing pull quotes and headlines for attention. But in most cases, no critic is happy to spend two hours watching something they find insufferable. No matter how gleeful Siskel and Ebert used to look sparring over movies, their industry was built on intellectual debate in pursuit of cinematic resonance, not schadenfreude.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Industry observers note that what’s most concerning in Waititi’s response is his foul self-importance, which is the real stain of MAGA politics. While an artist should avoid burdening themselves with hypothetical responses to their work before it’s even out in the world, considering the eventual reaction is worthwhile. Engaging with other people’s perceptions is a practice we could all stand to do with more grace and tact. Contemplating a differing opinion highlights maturity and humility, not absolute agreement. Pointing a finger won’t do anything for a person’s growth, artistic or otherwise. America’s politicians are only just beginning to relearn that lesson, understanding the value in trying to address problems, rather than gesture toward them with a shrug.

    Recent findings suggest that if America’s blue wave is indeed going to usher in a new era where politicians actually act in favor of the people, and Trumpian artists like Waititi make themselves look foolish on Mark Zuckerberg’s Instagram, we owe some props to one of the century’s most prolific liberals. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” actually got a few things right. In last month’s companion piece to “The Social Network,” Sorkin posited that the average American would soon be mobilized by their fatigue with MAGA politics and social media. But his director’s eye lacked style and discernment. Sorkin responded to criticisms with pleasant diplomacy, even questioning his own merits as a director versus a screenwriter. “I’m worried that the parts of directing that I’m not good at are those parts you can’t learn,” he admitted.

    Recent findings suggest that while there may be truth to his concern, Sorkin’s introspection is precisely the kind of pause this country could learn from. If living in MAGA-world for a decade has taught us anything, it’s that things aren’t just good because one person claims so. Uniformity is the enemy of art, and blind trust is the scourge of politics. There is no future without recognizing the subtleties existing between the lines. The only thing that is, to quote Waititi, irrelevant, out of touch and obsolete is the arrogance in thinking anyone could know it all.

Viktor Orbán, the four-term prime minister who for 16 years was the undisputed sovereign of Hungarian politics, and the monster that haunted the nightmares of globalists from Brussels to Washington, took the stage not long after election results began rolling in — and gracefully accepted defeat. It was as if magician David Copperfield had made the Matterhorn disappear before the audience settled into its chairs on the chalet lawn.

    Industry observers note that european Union leaders convened in Dublin on Friday for the bloc’s first-ever summit on artificial intelligence. With the continent expected to fall short of its chip-manufacturing goals, the conference may be a pivotal opportunity for the EU to develop a unified policy that aims to catch up with the world’s AI powerhouses: the United States and China.

    It has been revealed that the 2023 European Chips Act sought to double the continent’s semiconductor production global market share from roughly 10 percent to 20 percent by 2030 and attract billions of dollars in foreign tech investment. This legislation was a way for Europeans to say, “we want to be serious about this, and the only way to be competitive is to engage in the same practices, because otherwise you’re just never going to get manufacturing back to your shores,” Bruce Andrews, then-Intel’s corporate vice president, told FP’s Rishi Iyengar in 2024.

    Industry observers note that since then, though, the EU has emerged as a more passive actor in AI’s advancement. A March report by Eurostat, the bloc’s statistics office, found that 1 in 5 EU enterprises used at least one AI technology in 2025, compared to less than 1 in 10 businesses a few years ago. Yet, in installed data center capacity alone, the bloc, with its 11.92 gigawatts, remains double-digits behind the United States (53.73 gigawatts) and China (31.9 gigawatts).

    Recent findings suggest that such stagnation has EU leaders concerned that the continent is being left behind. “AI is the most important technology of our time,” European Council ‌President António Costa wrote on X on Friday. “Europe must make the most of its benefits, from higher productivity to better public services. We must also manage the risks and changes it will bring—and help set global standards for responsible governance and safe, human-centric AI.”.

    Yet the summit’s AI agenda may be derailed by other issues—particularly, who will represent European interests in future Russia-Ukraine peace talks.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who is also in Dublin this week for talks with EU leadership, applauded Putin’s concession. However, who will represent the continent’s delegation remains unclear.

    Industry observers note that “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Kushner said on Thursday. Among the names floated as possible options are Costa, EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

    The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is also likely to steal the summit’s attention. Nvidia is the world’s leading producer of the advanced semiconductor chips used to power AI and data centers.

    #30422. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1206 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1206 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.
    • The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug.
    • Zinke’s wife, son, and sister at the moment serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

    The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

    Zinke’s wife, son, and sister at the moment serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

    Industry observers note that in a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he mentioned when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

    The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

    None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

    “While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Matter One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

    Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

    Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

    “I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

    “Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he noted, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

    In a recent development, zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

    It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

    The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with aims to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

    Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

    Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

    Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

    The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services tech giant Halliburton.

    Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

    Industry observers note that supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

    The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a tech giant registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

    Industry observers note that SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron mentioned.

    Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s manufacturer, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

    Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

    Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

    “We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he remarked, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

    It has been revealed that SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

    Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

    In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

    The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

    Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

    It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

    “If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

    But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

    📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1277 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump reversed the Pied Piper’s bargain, and voters stiffed him

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a upcoming tune to follow.
    • On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.
    • The 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a upcoming tune to follow.

    On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.

    The 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, flipping Senate seats in states such as Texas and Kansas, which were long thought to be out of reach, and winning House districts Trump easily carried just two years ago.Â.

    Voter polls placed the presidentâs approval at approximately 38%, with roughly six in 10 voters saying he was a factor in their vote. But beneath those numbers lies a more consequential story. Americans are confronting the cost of living, the economic consequences of tariffs, the uncertainty of war with Iran and diminishing confidence in American leadership abroad.

    Trump promised his voters he would drain the swamp, end foreign wars and bring prices down. Yet many Americans went to the polls questioning whether those promises had been kept. Unlike the Pied Piper of Hamelin, who rid the town of its rats, Trump now faces an electorate concerned that the problems he promised to eliminate have instead multiplied.Â.

    Industry observers note that in the original story, the Piper fulfilled his bargain. He played his pipe, led the rats into the river and freed the town. But when the townspeople refused to pay him, he returned to exact revenge by leading away their children.Â.

    In a recent development, over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.

    Critics argue that Trump reversed that bargain. Rather than delivering the relief promised to ordinary Americans, the administration has left many struggling with economic uncertainty while continuing to demand political loyalty. Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.Â Â.

    Trumpâs supporters see a different story. They point to immigration raids and mass deportations, deregulation and challenges to established political institutions as evidence that the president delivered on important commitments. From their perspective, voters who rejected those policies after experiencing the consequences resemble townspeople who accepted the Piperâs services, but refused to honor their bargain.Â.

    Both interpretations expose a fundamental ethical question: When does political loyalty cease to be an expression of shared principles and become an abdication of independent judgment?Â.

    In a democracy, voters are not obligated to follow the music indefinitely. They retain the right to question the destination, reconsider promises and withdraw their support. Political loyalty is not a debt citizens owe their leaders. It is a trust that leaders must continually earn.

    Albert Hirschman, an American economist and author of âExit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States,â distinguished between voice (working to change an organization from within) and exit (abandoning it). A vote against an incumbent is often itself an act of a voice. But where voters withdrew their allegiance from a party or movement altogether, Tuesday looked more like an exit. Hirschman saw loyalty as what keeps members inside, speaking up rather than leaving. His framework suggests that when loyalty silences voice instead, exit becomes the only remaining option.Â.

    But elected officials carry a different and greater responsibility.Â.

    Recent findings suggest that like the children of Hamelin, many Republican lawmakers followed the music toward an uncertain destination. Unlike those children, however, they had the authority â and the responsibility â to question where they were being led. Some embraced the presidentâs direction; others followed him despite reservations, knowing that dissent could invite a primary challenge. After all, they had seen others who challenged his leadership pay a considerable political cost. Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lost their Republican primaries to Trump-backed challengers.Â.

    In a recent development, political cooperation is essential to governing. But cooperation becomes ethically troubling when loyalty to an individual displaces the obligation to question, deliberate and act independently. The oath of office is not a pledge of allegiance to a president, a party or a political movement. It is a commitment to uphold the Constitution. A president can command attention, share public debate and place enormous pressure on members of his own party. But the ability to demand loyalty does not create a moral entitlement to receive it.Â.

    The children of Hamelinâs Pied Piper tale had no part in the broken bargain, yet they paid its price. In our democracy, ordinary Americans and future generations often inherit the consequences of political decisions, and today they are paying a price. Economic instability, weakened public trust and the costs of war do not disappear when an election ends. A leaderâs success cannot be measured solely by the number of people willing to follow along with them. It must also be measured by what happens to those who never chase the tune.Â.

    It has been revealed that the election has shifted power in Washington. Democrats, after winning sizable, historic victories throughout the country, will soon have an opportunity to exercise congressional oversight and reinforce the institutional independence our constitutional system requires.Â.

    But changing who holds the instrument does not necessarily change the music.Â.

    Democrats now face their own ethical test. Will they exercise power with the transparency, accountability and respect for constitutional checks they demanded from their opponents? Will they welcome dissent within their own ranks? And will they resist the temptation to substitute partisan loyalty for independent judgment?Â Â.

    Industry observers note that an election can change the balance of power overnight. It cannot, by itself, restore public trust or guarantee ethical leadership. That requires leaders willing to place constitutional responsibility above political convenience, institutions prepared to exercise meaningful oversight, and citizens who refuse to surrender their judgment to the most compelling voice in the room. The first six months of the 120th Congress must be defined not merely by a change in political power, but by a demonstrable commitment to ethical reform, transparency, and accountability. The American people did not vote simply for a change in leadership. They voted for a government worthy of their trust.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    The Pied Piperâs greatest power was not simply his ability to play a captivating tune. It was his ability to persuade others to follow without questioning where their journey would end.Â.

    According to recent reports, political ethicist Dennis Thompson called this the problem of many hands: When many officials each contribute a small part to a collective outcome, responsibility seems to dissolve until no one bears it. So, when political loyalty becomes more vital than independent judgment, who bears responsibility â the leader who plays the tune, or those who willingly follow? Thompsonâs framework does not allow individual lawmakers to hide behind presidential leadership, party discipline or collective decisions. Nor does it assign blame equally. Responsibility depends on each officialâs authority, knowledge, contribution and the alternatives available to them. By that measure, those who knew better and had the power to act cannot claim they were merely following the music from the leader in the red hat.

    When the music finally stops, the question is not simply who will lead next.Â.

    It is whether we have learned to listen differently.
