    Lessons From the Watergate Babies for the ‘No Kings’ Congress

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Democrats scored a stunning victory in the 2026 midterms.
    • Now the question for Democrats is: What comes next?
    • Democrats scored a stunning victory in the 2026 midterms.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    Democrats scored a stunning victory in the 2026 midterms. Although many pollsters predicted a strong showing for the party out of power, few expected the map to look so blue by the end. In some ways, Texas looked as Democratic as Fresh York or California.

    Now the question for Democrats is: What comes next?

    Democrats scored a stunning victory in the 2026 midterms. Although many pollsters predicted a strong showing for the party out of power, few expected the map to look so blue by the end. In some ways, Texas looked as Democratic as Newly introduced York or California.

    Now the question for Democrats is: What comes next?

    Industry observers note that however large their majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate, they will face a Republican president who is extraordinarily aggressive in his use of executive power, as well as a Supreme Court that has been generally sympathetic to his vision of the presidency. If Democrats pass legislation, President Donald Trump will likely veto it. If Democrats investigate him, he will stonewall and wield his pardon power for allies who do the same. If they try to stop the war in Iran, he will draw on decades of accumulated presidential war powers to keep doing what he wants.

    Industry observers note that but the 120th Congress is not the first to face such a difficult situation. In 1975, the fresh class of House and Senate Democrats elected in the aftermath of President Richard Nixon’s resignation squared off against Republican President Gerald Ford. For all his talk of healing the nation and moving beyond the most contentious issues of the moment, Ford was also willing to use the veto to cut the Democratic Congress down to size. Though he understood that in Nixon’s shadow he had to scale back the presidency, he was not willing to give up the many tools at his disposal.

    Yet the 94th Congress—propelled by the Watergate Babies, as they were known—found ways to use its legislative power to pursue internal reform, advance a legislative agenda, and help create the conditions for Jimmy Carter’s election in 1976. Democratic members of the incoming “No Kings Congress,” as we might call it, should take notes.

    It has been revealed that in November 1974, the nation was reeling from division, scandal, and crisis. A decade of domestic conflict over race relations and the Vietnam War had opened deep rifts throughout U.S. society. Public trust in government had plummeted, largely as a result of the war. The economy was also in shambles in the early part of the decade, as the United States, which had enjoyed unprecedented economic growth after World War II, suffered from unemployment, inflation, and an oil embargo.

    Then came Watergate. Richard Nixon revealed what an imperial presidency looked like. Not only did he continue with secret military operations in Southeast Asia despite having promised to end the war in Vietnam, but he used the executive branch to intimidate, spy on, and threaten U.S. citizens; impounded money that Congress had appropriated; and engaged in dirty tricks against his opponents. As the scandal unfolded between 1972 and 1974, a story that began with a break-in at the Democratic National Committee Headquarters in the Watergate Complex grew into something much bigger: a revelation about the abuse of power that culminated in Nixon’s resignation, after being told that many Senate Republicans would vote to remove him from office if the House of Representatives passed articles of impeachment. After Nixon left office, Ford eroded the goodwill the public had for him by pardoning Nixon for any crimes that he might have committed. Ford’s approval ratings plummeted and many Americans came to see him as part of the problem.

    Recent findings suggest that the midterm campaigns had centered on the economy and on corruption in the political system. Democratic candidates promised a robust response to Americans’ pocketbook struggles and vowed to fix the problems the scandal had exposed in the political system. The midterms delivered a body blow to Republicans, even though they still controlled the White House. Democrats gained 49 seats in the House, bringing their total to 291, and a net of four seats in the Senate.

    In a recent development, A upcoming generation of House Democrats—such as Henry Waxman and George Miller (California), Tom Harkin (Iowa), Chris Dodd (Connecticut), Tim Wirth (Colorado), Thomas Downey (New York), and Paul Simon (Illinois)—came to Capitol Hill not wedded to older axioms and determined to bring about change. The day after voting, James Naughton of the New York Times wrote, “Democrats swept yesterday toward domination of the next Congress as voters across the nation apparently blamed Republicans for the Watergate scandal and for economic disruption.”.

    Industry observers note that looking back at the period, two of the Watergate Babies, Downey and Toby Moffett of Connecticut, recalled in a recent column in the Hartford Courant: “We were determined to challenge a sclerotic Congress where entrenched power sapped the idealism and creativity of newcomers. Led by the activism of newly introduced members — and supported by a key group of existing policymakers, dozens of newly empowered subcommittee chairs launched investigations on clean air violations, nuclear plant safety, pharmaceutical pricing and human rights abuses abroad — we had idealism, the staff, and the authority to change the way Congress functioned.”.

    But in November 1974, just as in November 2026, it was not clear what this fresh Congress would be able to accomplish. The government was divided, Democrats themselves were still split between a liberal northern and a conservative southern wing, and public distrust was so high that voters would be difficult to satisfy regardless of who was in power.

    Industry observers note that yet the Democrats found a way to keep moving forward. Their first step was to clean up their own institution before turning on to the presidency. In December 1974, Democrats pressured Arkansan Wilbur Mills, the powerful chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, to step aside as a result of a scandal that involved his relationship with a local stripper named Fanne Foxe and his addiction to pills and alcohol. In January 1975, the freshman class of Watergate Babies led the drive to depose three other House committee chairmen—F. Edward Hébert, W.R. Poage, and Wright Patman—after questioning every sitting chairman about how responsive he would be to the party caucus and finding them wanting. The spirit of reform also reached the Senate, where Democrats tweaked the committee system and also lowered the number of votes needed to end a filibuster from two-thirds of the senators present and voting to three-fifths of senators.

    It has been revealed that congress also investigated the Ford administration. In October 1974, Ford appeared before the House Judiciary Committee to answer tough questions about pardoning Nixon. Fresh York Rep. Otis Pike and Idaho Sen. Frank Church led high-level hearings investigating the Cold War national security state, producing bombshell revelations about how officials had abused their authority and lied to the public, building public support for reforms that ultimately passed in 1978.

    The 94th Congress also legislated. On some issues, it found points of agreement with Ford, who signed legislation providing tax rebates, creating the Earned Income Tax Credit, and establishing the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and CAFE fuel economy standards. In some cases, such as a bill funding public works jobs, Democrats overrode the president’s veto after scaling back the measure. In others, such as farm price supports, they passed bills that Ford successfully vetoed but that showed what the party might do in power. They had the effect of pushing voters to think about “what if?”—what if Democrats also had control of the White House? Some of the newly introduced Democrats, like Waxman, used their media platforms to promote issues, such as clean air legislation, that were only starting to gain attention.

    In 1976, former Georgia Gov. Jimmy Carter won the presidency with 297 electoral votes. Although Carter was not a Washington insider, his campaign built on many of the themes that the 94th Congress had advanced and kept the same agenda: government reform, transparency, help for working Americans, and restoring the balance of power in Washington. Democrats also maintained massive majorities, with 292 seats in the House and 61 in the Senate.

    The lesson from the Democrats of the 94th is that Congress can still accomplish a great deal in 2027, whether Trump chooses to govern in a transactional fashion with Democratic leadership or whether he decides to double down and fight.

    According to recent reports, given the election results, Democrats can investigate corruption, conflicts of interest, and decision-making on matters such as Iran. Congress can work on cleaning up its own house, including legislation to restrict stock trading by sitting members. As Moffett and Downey wrote in the Hartford Courant, congressional reform is even more essential than in 1975, due to the erosion of staffing, expertise, and institutional knowledge. They propose revitalizing subcommittees as a first major step toward the path of reconstruction.

    The No Kings Congress can look for legislation on pressing problems such as healthcare costs or Social Security that a lame duck president sees as being in his interest to reform, or that a shattered congressional Republican Party perceives as being in its own interest to join with the opposition on (thus making a bill veto proof). And Congress can keep pushing legislation on challenges such as affordability and immigration that lets voters see what unified Democratic control might accomplish in 2029.

    The one thing the 120th Congress can’t afford to do is nothing. A massive electorate and a diverse caucus, ranging from progressives in Michigan to preachers in Kansas, put Democrats into power. Voters have sent many signals that they want their leaders to do something about the crushing burden of affordability that weighs on U.S. families, the corruption that has afflicted Washington, and the sense of runaway presidential power. If Democrats live up to the moment, they could find themselves, two years from now, in an even stronger position to bring the era of MAGA to a decisive end.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.

    Recent findings suggest that the first made me go quiet at my kitchen table. Chris Pappas won election to the U.S. Senate in Newly introduced Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man ever sent to that chamber, and part of the margin that handed Democrats the Senate. In Indiana, J.D. Ford, the first openly gay person ever elected to that stateâs legislature, unseated a Republican incumbent and is headed to the House. In Texas, of all places, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than thirty years, after a campaign in which anti-LGBTQ+ messaging was reportedly Paxtonâs single largest category of advertising, and in which the vice president of the United States stood on a stage and used âgayâ as a punchline against him. Talarico is straight, and he won anyway.

    Industry observers note that and on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican. He conceded the election on Wednesday, down by roughly 6,700 votes in the closest race of the incumbent Republican Nick LaLotaâs career. In the same breath, Gallant called LaLota a brother in arms and told the district he was still their neighbor, which is to say he refused the shame he was supposed to feel from the photo leak to the very end. Whatever that is, it is not the story of a man sunk by leather. It is the story of a man who nearly won the unwinnable while carrying the exact weight that was supposed to be disqualifying.

    In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip.

    Recent findings suggest that put those results next to one another and a sentence forms that would have been unimaginable a decade ago: In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip. The oldest weapon in the drawer â the one that raised me, the one that could empty a lunch table in the 1990s â is losing its edge at the ballot box. Voters keep looking at the openly gay candidate and sending him to Washington.

    That is the headline, and it is real, and I am not going to let anyone talk me out of being moved by it.

    It has been revealed that but here is the second thing that happened Tuesday night. In the same hours, often on the same ballots, and it is the part the rainbow-wave coverage is already rushing past. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters approved measures to bar transgender girls from girlsâ sports. In Colorado, two measures aimed at transgender young people, one on sports and one restricting certain surgical care for minors, are narrowly passing. In Washington State, an initiative to keep transgender girls out of girlsâ sports passed comfortably. The same electorate that refused to punish a Senate candidate for being gay reached down the ballot and punished trans kids for existing.

    According to recent reports, this is the thing I need people to see before the celebration hardens into a story we tell ourselves. The contempt did not disappear on Tuesday. It relocated. A political movement that has learned it can no longer win by hating gay men has not given up the strategy. It has updated the target. The MAGA machine that aired the Paxton ads and laughed at Vanceâs joke is the same one now writing ballot measures about 11-year-olds, because cruelty still tests well when it is aimed at the group with the least power to answer back. Gays are simply the part of the community that got powerful enough to be left alone.

    I know this pattern in my body, because I have watched it my whole life. The fear moves. First it was the plague, then it was the gay man as predator, then it was marriage as the end of the world, and each time the broader culture eventually got bored or ashamed and the fear went looking for a new address. Right now the address is a trans child in a locker room. The people who found that child did not arrive by accident. They are the same people, running the same play, because it is the only play they have ever had.

    Sources indicate that so I want to be careful about the victory lap, even as I take one. It is a genuine and hard-won thing that Chris Pappas will be a senator and J.D. Ford will be a congressman, and that a straight man in Texas could not be destroyed by being called gay. Those wins are not small, and the people who did the work to make them real earned every bit of the joy.Â.

    But a movement does not get to accept its own seats at the table while the youngest and most defenseless members of its own community are voted off the field in four states on the same night. This is not a win we get to keep cleanly. It is a split screen, and if we only look at our half of it, we become exactly the kind of people who could be bought off with a little representation while someone else pays the bill.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    In a recent development, the refusal to be ashamed won some rooms on Tuesday. I felt it. The task now is to extend that refusal to the people the machine has decided to hunt next, to say as loudly for trans kids what the voters of New Hampshire and Indiana and Texas just mentioned for us: that you do not get to make a personâs existence a punchline, or a wedge, or a ballot measure. We learned that lesson about gay men the slow and brutal way. The whole point of learning it is to spare the next group from learning it alone.

    Recent findings suggest that chris Gallant did not quite win. But he came close enough to prove the old weapon is dulling. The question Tuesday really asked is whether we will hand the people wielding it a new one, or finally take the thing out of their hands.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the latest year, making the most of their coming majority.

    According to recent reports, that means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

    According to recent reports, arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

    “Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

    Recent findings suggest that still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

    The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

    According to recent reports, some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

    It has been revealed that there’s every indication that pressure will continue in the newly introduced Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, noted Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

    “Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres mentioned.

    Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the upcoming year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

    “There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

    According to recent reports, in addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the upcoming Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

    “For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a massive part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

    Industry observers note that lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

    For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

    Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

    Sources indicate that those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the fresh Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

    “But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin mentioned.

    The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

    Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

    Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

    In a recent development, U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

    “The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

    Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

    It has been revealed that “There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” mentioned Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

    As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”.

    “I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

    Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

    “We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

    Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

    Industry observers note that beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet confirmed — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

    In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

    “I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

    #30414. Can South Africa Tackle HIV Without the U.S.?

    Can South Africa Tackle HIV Without the U.S.?

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant.
    • Sources indicate that when Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, announced the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation.
    • It has been revealed that two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    It has been revealed that two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant. She had just led a major clinical trial in South Africa, the epicenter of the global HIV epidemic, testing a new form of prevention that was astonishingly effective. The drug, lenacapavir, is a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which blocks the virus from spreading in HIV-negative people. A twice-yearly injection could replace daily pills, offering longer-lasting protection and thus slowing the spread of the virus.

    Sources indicate that when Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, announced the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation. “There was huge anticipation and excitement. And then January came around, and suddenly that all disappeared,” she said, referring to the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

    It has been revealed that two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant. She had just led a major clinical trial in South Africa, the epicenter of the global HIV epidemic, testing a fresh form of prevention that was astonishingly effective. The drug, lenacapavir, is a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which blocks the virus from spreading in HIV-negative people. A twice-yearly injection could replace daily pills, offering longer-lasting protection and thus slowing the spread of the virus.

    When Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, declared the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation. “There was huge anticipation and excitement. And then January came around, and suddenly that all disappeared,” she remarked, referring to the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

    Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration took a chainsaw to global health programs, including the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which has provided around $8 billion to South Africa since 2003. South Africa pays for most of its own HIV programs, including 90 percent of its antiretroviral drugs. Still, the collapse of PEPFAR was devastating, shuttering clinics for high-risk groups and leaving thousands of health workers without jobs.

    According to recent reports, south Africa is home to around 8 million people living with HIV, or around 20 percent of the global HIV population. Approximately 6 million of them are on treatment, but the country still records around 170,000 new infections each year.

    Sources indicate that when South Africa began rolling out lenacapavir this summer, the landscape had changed dramatically. U.S.-South Africa relations have deteriorated, as Trump has objected to South Africa’s genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice and accused the country of committing genocide against white Afrikaners. Those tensions have compounded uncertainty for the HIV program.

    Last year, the United States provided South Africa with $115 million to keep core HIV services running, but in June, the Trump administration stated it would end all PEPFAR funding for the country in the coming months. Washington also excluded South Africa from global health financing deals struck this year with other African countries. Even as the United States supports the lenacapavir launch elsewhere, it isn’t doing so in South Africa.

    In an email, a U.S. State Department spokesperson confirmed that the political rift played a role in the decision to phase out PEPFAR funding. The spokesperson stated PEPFAR was never meant to be a permanent initiative and that South Africa is “more than capable of supporting its own health programs” as a middle-income country.

    It’s a departure from decades of U.S. foreign policy, said Jirair Ratevosian, a former senior PEPFAR official under President Joe Biden. “South Africa and the United States have never been perfectly aligned on foreign policy,” Ratevosian said. But the United States “was able to compartmentalize those disagreements and still cooperate on other major areas of interest that were aligned, and HIV was always one of those.”.

    According to recent reports, now, South Africa is left to manage its lenacapavir rollout without its historically biggest donor. It’s an early test of whether the country’s post-PEPFAR transition can become a blueprint for weathering the U.S. retreat from global health—or is a cautionary tale.

    Recent findings suggest that south African officials have downplayed the loss of U.S. support. In June, a health ministry spokesperson urged people not to panic, saying the government has “long been working on a self-reliance plan.” Officials have not released a formal plan, but they point to local drug manufacturing, stronger public health systems, and regional collaboration on HIV as vital steps.

    Sources indicate that south Africa had a head start in this effort, as PEPFAR already accounted for less than 25 percent of the country’s HIV prevention funding, compared with around 80 percent in neighboring Mozambique and Zimbabwe, according to the Joint U.N. Program on HIV/AIDS last year.

    At the launch of the lenacapavir rollout in June, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told a stadium crowd that the drug would mark a “turning point” for South Africa. Prevention remains a challenge in the country; until now PrEP has only been widely available as a daily pill, which can be difficult to access or stay on. South Africa planned to roll out a different shot that offers two months of protection last year, but high prices and PEPFAR disruptions stalled that effort.

    Experts think the twice-yearly lenacapavir shot could be a game-changer. Modeling suggests that if between 1.7 million and 2.9 million South Africans get on lenacapavir each year, upcoming infections could fall by as much as 31 percent, potentially allowing the country to eliminate HIV as a public health threat as soon as 2039. But first, South Africa must get the drug to people who need it.

    In June, Ramaphosa said 3 million people will be offered lenacapavir over the next three years. The government has already secured enough doses to cover 456,000 people, funded with $29.2 million from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria. The first tranche was allocated to 360 public health facilities in high-burden districts, but as of mid-October, just under 79,000 South Africans had started lenacapavir, according to health ministry data.

    Activists are frustrated by what they view as a sluggish rollout driven by funding gaps, insufficient planning, and regulatory bottlenecks. Some South African clinics have turned away patients seeking lenacapavir, some after running out of doses and others over logistical problems. Early in the rollout, facilities in the capital of Pretoria lacked HIV testing kits—a prerequisite to get the shot—or had not yet trained nurses to administer the drug.

    “It’s a drip feed of supplies,” said Fatima Hassan, a human rights lawyer and the founder of the Health Justice Initiative in Cape Town. The U.S. funding cuts and the pace of the rollout are “putting our entire health system in jeopardy and all the gains we’ve made in the last 20 years at risk.”.

    The government has tried to plug some of the funding gaps left by the United States. Last year, the South African Treasury allocated around $45 million in emergency funding to cover some HIV programs, roughly one-tenth of what PEPFAR contributed in 2024. But that money does not resolve the question of what will happen to these services in the long term.

    The State Department spokesperson remarked the United States would “reconsider future health assistance during the phase-out period”—but only if South Africa takes “concrete, demonstrable action” to remedy the Trump administration’s accusations that its government seizes land from white farmers, among other complaints.

    South African Health Minister Aaron Motsoaledi has said the country intends to eventually finance its lenacapavir program itself, with help from donors. “To establish a couple million doses-deep lenacapavir program in the next couple of years, we will need outside help,” said Gesine Meyer-Rath, a health economist at the University of the Witwatersrand and Boston University.

    Sources indicate that but it is not yet clear which donors will provide that help. The Global Fund, which supported the initial rollout, aims to cut South Africa’s HIV/AIDS funding by 26 percent in its next allocation cycle as it tightens its focus on the poorest countries hit hardest by HIV, TB, and malaria. A South African health ministry spokesperson did not respond to questions about the lenacapavir rollout or its “self-reliance proposal.”.

    South Africa is betting that a generic form of lenacapavir will hit the market just as the initial supply runs out, allowing the government to roll out the drug to hundreds more clinics. Gilead Sciences, the U.S. developer of lenacapavir, agreed to make a generic version available in 120 lower- and middle-income countries, including South Africa, for $40 per person per year; it is expected by the end of the year in Zambia and elsewhere in 2027. The Global Fund negotiated a confidential price with the drugmaker for the initial shots in South Africa and other recipient countries, but brand-name lenacapavir goes for roughly $28,000 per person per year in the United States. South African health officials say the generic price must be brought down to $25 to guarantee “universal access.”.

    In a recent development, eventually, South Africa wants to manufacture lenacapavir itself, but that effort has also encountered roadblocks. In 2024, three South African pharmaceutical companies asked Gilead for permission to make generic versions, but they were rejected because they could not handle the 28-step process of synthesizing the drug’s active ingredient. South Africa’s government is now working with Gilead and technical advisors to make local production possible.

    Clinicians and civil society groups warn that supply isn’t the only problem—it’s also about getting the lenacapavir shots to those who need it most, including sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender people, and injectable drug users. But the 12 PEPFAR-funded specialized clinics and community-based outreach for these key populations, which served more than 63,000 people, have not been replaced.

    In a recent development, “I do not think that the people who are suffering access problems because of the PEPFAR cuts are going to be the ones to get the drug,” noted Kate Rees, a public health specialist at the Anova Health Institute, which suspended its PEPFAR-funded programs. “We know how to reach key populations, and waiting for them in the clinic is not it.”.

    Meyer-Rath, the health economist, mentioned she has attended early planning meetings with government officials who want to reopen services for these populations and try to integrate patients into public health facilities—but that the budget available is “nonexistent or marginal.”.

    Another challenge: PEPFAR covered around 40 percent of South Africa’s HIV data workforce, which tracks infections and treatment uptake in HIV hot spots. With fewer of those workers, the patients who miss out on lenacapavir because they fall through the cracks of the traditional health system—as vulnerable groups tend to do—may go uncounted, making it harder to identify problems and surge support where it’s needed.

    The next phase of the lenacapavir rollout is fast approaching, and it will test the country’s infrastructure as well as its supply. The first South Africans to receive the drug are due for their second shot in December, and clinics must provide an HIV test and an injection for each of them every six months going forward.

    South Africa’s experience is likely to shape rollouts elsewhere, but other early adopters offer their own lessons. Kenya, which launched the drug in February, has used drop-in centers to reach key populations, though it has also struggled with shortages. Meanwhile, Zambia launched with just 500 doses in late 2025, and up to 85 percent of patients there and in Eswatini—which shares a border with South Africa—have returned on time for their second shot, according to Bhekisisa, a South African media outlet.

    It has been revealed that lenacapavir is now being scaled up in 12 low- and middle-income countries, with 17 more countries due to receive it by early 2027, according to AVAC, an HIV prevention advocacy group. The rollout of generic lenacapavir next year will be another turning point. It’s a reminder that even if South Africa sticks the landing, there’s still a long way to go to defeat HIV.

    In a recent development, “Right now, we are wobbling a bit, and the world is watching us wobble,” Meyer-Rath stated. “But basically, it’s either the [South African] government or it’s not. No one will fund the system. We have to.”.

    Gabriela Galvin is an award-winning freelance journalist in London. She covers health and social policy.
